item.title: Valie Export Was Ahead of Her Time and as Subtle as She Was Provocative - ARTnews.com
item.description:
One chilly but sparkling afternoon this past January, I made a pilgrimage. The destination was a somewhat unlikely site for work by one of the most iconoclastic (in every sense of that term) feminist artists of the last century: a Roman Catholic church. The Pöstlingberg basilica gleams atop the steep hill of the same name, looking out upon a wide vista of the Danube flowing through Linz—where VALIE EXPORT, born Waltraud Lehner in Nazi-era Austria, spent her formative years. 

I was led to the summit, admittedly not on foot, by Dagmar Schink, managing director of the VALIE EXPORT Center, established in the artist’s hometown in 2017, five decades after EXPORT changed her name in an acute rejection of patronymics and all they represented in her postwar milieu. After we reached the late-Baroque structure, brimming inside with billowing gilt ornament and trompe-l’oeil frescoes, my intrepid guide convinced a parish employee to lend us a key that unlocked a stairwell. We were greeted at the top by a shock of silver and the crisp, sweeping curves of a pipe organ designed by EXPORT and installed there in 2022. Across the instrument’s undulating facade, in cut-out letters backlit by colored lights, are words that began to appear in her work in the 1970s. Whoever understands has wings, the organ proclaims, projecting this sentence, like a piercing chord, toward the altar at the opposite end of the church.

A few months after this sojourn, the world lost EXPORT. Her death came during a time defined by compounding grief, especially for those invested in the feminist project out of which the artist’s work emerged. By comparison, the period of second-wave feminism can seem like—or, more accurately, can be idealized as—a moment of both endless possibility and political cohesion. 

In the wake of her passing, at least one prominent online obituary included a video of TAP and TOUCH CINEMA, first performed in 1968 and later becoming something of a synecdoche both for EXPORT’s work and feminist performance art writ large. The video shows passersby on the street reaching inside a box, figured as a miniature movie theater and worn around the artist’s torso, in order to feel her breasts. The surviving footage was originally aired by the ORF, Austria’s national public broadcaster. Just before a man reaches into the “theater” surrounding EXPORT’s upper body, there’s a quick cut to a shot from another part of the program (blink and you’ll miss it). In this other segment, EXPORT runs toward the camera while it tracks backward. Barreling forward, she chants a dizzying list: “…expanded movies… film objects… communication actions… multimedia programs…” 

Hiding in plain sight, in the midst of arguably her best-known work, EXPORT’s sprinting incantation speaks to the urgent yet playful experimentation that drove her practice, spanning performance, conceptual photography, televised video, publications, curatorial ventures, three feature films… you can lose your breath trying to keep up.

But what did participants (who were not only men, it should be noted) encounter in their confrontation with EXPORT’s body in this performance? The answers—a critique of male cinematic voyeurism, an assertion of female bodily autonomy—are important, but often come too quickly. Blunted certainty about the stakes of 1960s and ’70s feminism runs the risk of not only mummifying the period’s radically open-ended modes of questioning, but also fueling, in the process, our current fascist turn. For all its insistence on the gendered body, EXPORT’s work refuses too-easy answers to that insidiously transphobic question: “What is a woman?” 

In the prominent phrase on the organ she designed for Linz, the German verb for “understand,” begreifen, has the sense, resonating with English, of “grasping” something with the mind, acting like the hand. Understanding is here, if anything, a deeply physical, embodied act. But in EXPORT’s phrasing, primate fingers and opposable thumbs loosen, transforming into feathered wings. Her legacy, that most petrified of terms, resides precisely in the ways her art unsettles what we think we understand about the overlapping historical, political, and mediatic landscapes in which it intervened. Through some uncharted territory, I imagine her running breathlessly on, even to the point, eventually, of taking flight.

item.title: Christie’s to Auction Peter Simon’s $172 M. Art Collection, Led by Bacon, Mondrian, Warhol Works - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An art collection, estimated to be worth £87 million to £127 million ($118 million to $172 million), featuring works by Francis Bacon, Ben Nicholson, Barbara Hepworth, Piet Mondrian, Pablo Picasso, Jeff Koons, and more, is coming to Christie’s on October 14 and 15 during Frieze Week. The collection belongs to British businessman and art collector Peter Simon, who has appeared on each edition of ARTnews’ Top 200 Collectors list since 2005.

The sale of “Monsoon: The Peter Simon Collection” is the highest-value single-owner collection offered to date at Christie’s London. Comprising nearly 200 works, the sale will be spread across three auctions: an evening sale, a day sale, and an online auction.

Simon is the founder of fashion retailer Monsoon and Accessorize. In a statement, he explained that in the early days of Monsoon, he would sit with “fashion and textile designers sifting portfolio after portfolio” selecting work that could be converted onto fabric. Handpicking colors and prints, he added, informed his taste and ability to “zero in on the best combination of color and composition in a picture.”

When he was building his art collection, he first started with British artists, notably Bacon, Nicholson, and Hepworth. Simon’s aim was to always “build links and foster dialogue across different worlds” and now he wants to start collecting in “a new direction.”

The highlight lot includes two Bacon’s works: Figure in Movement (1978) estimated for £14 million to £18 million ($19 million to $24.4 million) and Study for a Figure (ca. 1945) estimated for £4 million to £6 million ($5.4 million to $8 million). The Mondrian Composition A, with Double Line and Yellow (1935) is estimated to go under the gavel for £8 million to £12 million ($11 million to $16 million), while Joan Miró’s Peinture (Les amants – Adam et Eve), 1925, is estimated for £7 million to £10 million ($9.5 million to $14 million).

The collection also includes works from Frank Auerbach, Leon Kossoff, Fernand Léger, Willem de Kooning, and Andy Warhol’s Diamond Dust Shoe (1980) estimated for £1.8 million to £2.5 million ($2.4 million to $3.4 million), which spans more than two meters in height and is a nod to the artist’s career as a commercial illustrator in the 1950s, where he had earned the moniker “Leonardo da Vinci of the shoe trade” by Women’s Wear Daily.

Katharine Arnold, Christie’s vice chairman of 20th and 21st century art in Europe, described Simon’s collection as “dynamic” and “unbridled by geography and time.”

item.title: Lonnie G. Bunch Has Had Enough - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Lonnie G. Bunch III has had it. After months of incessant harassment and political prodding from the Trump White House, the Smithsonian Secretary announced that he's quitting his job with “very mixed emotions." What a sad way to kick off the fall season. 

It's also sad to see New York artist Lucien Smith die at the very young age of 37. Once a market darling, he had abandoned the commercial art world for more community-focused work. Associate Editor Phillip Pyle looks back at his life and career.    

Also in the news: Another week, another museum heist in Europe. This time, two paintings disappear from the Renoir Museum in southern France. According to police, the thieves dropped two other paintings in the museum’s garden while officers chased them. 

Much more to read below, including John Yau on Law & Order writer and producer René Balcer, who also happens to be a photographer. Maybe Balcer can help Europe with its museum heist problem ... DUN DUN.  

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

The Law & Order Writer Who Moonlights as an Artist

Is René Balcer a street photographer, a documentary photographer, or a landscape photographer? All the above and more.

Despite his achievements as a producer and writer for Law & Order — including a Primetime Emmy Award and multiple Edgar Awards — the throughline of Balcer’s life was direct photography.

After studying poetry and photography at Concordia University in Montreal and taking a six-month seminar taught by the French New Wave filmmaker Jean-Luc Godard, Balcer worked as a cameraman, war reporter, editor, scriptwriter, documentary filmmaker, and film critic. Like Godard and other New Wave filmmakers, Balcer wrote reviews and made films, merging commentary and creativity. | John Yau

item.title: Irving Penn and the Afterlife of Fashion - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Fashion is more than clothes. It is a language of status, desire, identity and disappearance, a system in which bodies and objects are arranged to produce images that outlive their original moment. PENN & FASHION, opening the Maison Européenne de la Photographie’s 30th anniversary season, approaches this tension through Irving Penn’s six decades of work for Vogue, setting his photographs against a contemporary programme concerned with memory, intimacy and unstable forms of representation. Penn’s achievement lies partly in having made the commercial image feel strangely autonomous, stripping fashion of its narrative machinery until silhouette, gesture, surface and gaze become subjects in themselves. However, this apparent simplicity is not neutral: it raises questions about authorship, power and the complicated relationship between art and the industries that produce its images.

Penn’s photographs emerged from a particular modernist belief in economy. Trained in graphic design under Alexey Brodovitch, and later brought into Vogue by Alexander Liberman, he understood the page as a space of visual tension in which every element had to justify its presence. His response to fashion was consequently very different from the elaborate theatricality associated with earlier generations of image-makers, replacing fantasy settings with a concentrated encounter between garment, sitter and camera. Such restraint matters because it relocates fashion photography from spectacle towards attention, asking how little an image needs before it begins to acquire the authority of a portrait. Penn’s formal economy was not an absence of artifice, but a highly deliberate construction of it.

That question becomes especially vivid in the photographs made in Paris in 1950. Penn installed himself in a naturally lit studio on the Rue de Vaugirard and photographed designs by Balenciaga, Lafaurie and Rochas, frequently with Lisa Fonssagrives as his principal model. A dress such as Cocoa-Colored Balenciaga Dressdoes not depend upon elaborate storytelling; its power comes from the relation between Fonssagrives’s poised body, the architectural volume of the garment and the controlled space surrounding them. Balenciaga’s sculptural approach was particularly suited to Penn’s method, allowing fabric to become almost architectural rather than merely decorative. Here fashion approaches sculpture, while photography is an act of translation – converting movement, material and construction into a fixed image.

Fonssagrives also complicates the familiar hierarchy between photographer and model. She was not simply an anonymous body deployed to animate clothing, but a pioneering model, artist and collector whose relationship with Penn extended into marriage and whose photographs now form part of the exhibition’s wider archival story. Her presence is particularly striking beside Penn’s portraits of other figures from the fashion world, including Jean Patchett, Christian Dior, Elsa Schiaparelli and Charles James. Rather than separating fashion photography from portraiture, Penn repeatedly allowed the two genres to overlap, giving the sitter an intensity that could exceed the commercial purpose of the commission. His studio becomes, in this sense, less a backdrop than a psychological instrument – a controlled environment in which personality is made visible through posture, expression and restraint.

Such compression also explains why Penn’s work remains relevant to contemporary debates around the status of fashion photography. For decades, photography produced for magazines or advertising was treated as culturally secondary to supposedly autonomous art, even though editorial images often shaped public ideas about beauty, gender and modernity more powerfully than museum photography. Penn unsettles that distinction because his commissions retain their commercial origins while possessing the formal density of independent artworks. His later platinum-palladium printing practice intensified this contradiction, turning images first encountered through the disposable rhythm of the magazine into carefully considered photographic objects. What looks like an effortless image is therefore the result of sustained decisions about framing, printing, texture and scale.

The exhibition’s chronological structure makes this development legible without reducing Penn’s career to a sequence of stylistic periods. Curated by Pascal Hoël, in collaboration with Frédérique Dolivet, PENN & FASHION moves from 1947 to 2008, bringing together works from the MEP and Nicola Erni Collection alongside loans from the Irving Penn Foundation and the Miyake Issey Foundation. Facsimiles of Vogue place individual photographs back within their editorial conditions, an important curatorial decision because it resists the retrospective tendency to detach celebrated images from the systems in which they originally circulated. Penn is presented neither as a pure artist working incidentally for fashion nor simply as a master of commercial photography. Instead, the exhibition proposes a more complicated figure – one who transformed the constraints of editorial production into a distinctive visual language.

Penn’s travels deepen that complication. His 1948 journey to Peru began as a Vogue assignment, but his subsequent photographs in Cuzco shifted towards portraits of Quechua people whose clothing and presence became central to the series. The neutral backdrop, natural light and careful attention to posture establish an aesthetic continuity with his fashion work, suggesting that adornment itself can become a subject independent of Western couture. Yet this is where contemporary viewers may pause, because the language of beauty and the history of ethnographic photography are not innocent categories. Penn’s formal language may grant his sitters a powerful presence, but it subjects cultural difference to the same aesthetic system he applied to fashion – a tension that deserves to remain visible rather than resolved.

A similar tension runs through Small Trades, produced alongside Penn’s Paris fashion assignments. Street vendors, artisans and labourers entered the same studio space as celebrated models. Such equivalence can be read as democratic, since occupational clothing receives the same formal attention as haute couture, but it also reveals how easily different social identities can be transformed into aesthetic types. Penn’s gift was to see clothing as a carrier of character – yet his controlled compositions could also remove people from the environments that gave their clothing meaning. The result is both compelling and uneasy, a reminder that the studio’s apparent neutrality is always constructed.

That constructed quality becomes almost surreal in the 1974 project Inventive Paris Clothes. Fascinated by historical garments displayed in Diana Vreeland’s Costume Institute exhibition, Penn photographed designs by Poiret, Vionnet, Chanel, Schiaparelli and Madame Grès on resin mannequins inside a museum gallery transformed into a studio. Without living models, fashion becomes a study of absence, with fabric retaining its capacity to suggest a body even when the body itself has disappeared. Penn’s interest in clothing therefore exceeds its function as something worn: garments become vessels of memory, cultural history and imagined identity. His images anticipate a contemporary fascination with fashion archives, in which preservation can be as creative an act as design itself.

Issey Miyake offered another route into this relationship between garment and image. Their collaboration, extending from 1986 to 1999, was unusually intimate: Penn received Miyake’s clothes in New York without attending the designer’s shows, photographed them in his studio and returned the Ektachromes to Tokyo. Miyake’s sculptural forms seemed almost conceived for Penn’s reductionist eye, while the resulting photographs allowed the designer to perceive his own work through another medium. More than sixty posters created by Ikko Tanaka from Penn’s colour photographs further demonstrate how an image can become part of fashion’s design ecosystem rather than simply documenting it. Photography here is not an afterthought to fashion – it becomes one of the ways fashion acquires cultural memory.

Colour becomes increasingly important in Penn’s later work, particularly in photographs of John Galliano, Christian Lacroix and Karl Lagerfeld, where theatrical references and historical excess challenge his earlier austerity. His images for Vogue’s beauty pages push this further, using humour, Surrealism and visual disturbance to make familiar rituals appear strange. Beauty Treatment with Gauze Mask, for example, turns skincare into a kind of transformation, recalling Penn’s longstanding fascination with masks while questioning the conventions through which beauty is manufactured and consumed. These photographs demonstrate why the label of “fashion photographer” is ultimately too narrow: Penn repeatedly used fashion as a point of departure for investigations into performance, artifice and appearance.

The contemporary works at the MEP shift that instability from surface to memory. Curated by Victoria Aresheva, Nanténé Traoré’s pays des merveilles turns towards Brittany, where the artist’s return to a childhood landscape becomes entangled with recollection, attachment and disappearance. Expired film stock from the 1990s produces chemically altered colours, blurred contours and ghostly images, making photographic degradation part of the work’s emotional vocabulary. Bodies become landscapes and landscapes seem to dissolve into internal states, while a film made during a residency in Albania extends the project into moving image and voice. Placed alongside Penn, Traoré offers a different understanding of photographic control – one in which instability is allowed to shape what can be seen.

This dialogue matters because the MEP is not simply presenting a historical master followed by a younger artist. It is constructing a conversation between two approaches to photography’s relationship with time: Penn’s painstaking preservation of the image and Traoré’s embrace of its deterioration. David Gilbert’s practice, positioned between photography, installation and sculpture, extends that commitment to photography as something materially expansive, although the exhibition information gives less detail about his presentation than it does about Penn and Traoré. Together, the programme suggests that photography today is understood through printing, decay, installation, memory and circulation. Such an approach feels particularly apt for an institution marking three decades of collecting photography.

Penn’s enduring importance rests on a paradox. His images are amongst the most measured in 20th century photography, yet their subjects repeatedly point towards what cannot be controlled – ageing bodies, changing fashions, cultural disappearance, mortality and the unstable meanings attached to beauty. His celebrated cigarette photographs, made after he had become synonymous with couture, reveal how far his interest in surface could extend beyond glamour, transforming discarded objects into carefully printed meditations on waste and value. PENN & FASHION therefore becomes more than a celebration of an established photographic canon: it is an examination of how images move between magazine and museum, commerce and art, preservation and loss. At its strongest, this show asks us not only to admire Penn’s elegance, but to consider what it conceals, and what it permits us, with remarkable clarity, to see.

PENN & FASHION is at MEP, Paris from 30 September – 17 January: mep-fr.org

Words: Anna Müller

item.title: How Korean Paper Became War Collateral - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.

There are words that sit comfortably in the mouth.

Kozo is not one of them.

Every time I hear it used as the universal shorthand within East Asian papermaking, something in me tightens. Not because the word is incorrect. Not because Japanese papermaking is undeserving of admiration. I use the word myself. I teach it in workshops and have spent years working with the fibers, histories, and technologies associated with Japanese papermaking. My unease comes from somewhere more difficult to articulate. It comes from the growing realization that a field increasingly committed to the language of decolonization remains surprisingly comfortable with certain forms of historical amnesia.

I convinced myself this reaction was personal. Perhaps I was reading too much into a word. Perhaps this discomfort belonged solely to me, a Korean-American papermaker carrying family histories and cultural inheritances that others did not share. Then, I began paying attention.

I tuned in to workshop descriptions, artist statements, conference presentations, residency announcements, and educational materials. I could not stop seeing "kozo" appear not simply as a Japanese term or fiber source, but increasingly as a category through which East Asian papermaking itself became legible. I asked myself, “When did one tradition become responsible for speaking on behalf of all the others?”

The answer cannot be separated from history.

For many Americans, Japanese occupation remains a distant historical event. For many Koreans, it remains a living inheritance. Between 1910 and 1945, the Korean language was suppressed, Korean names were replaced, and Korean cultural traditions subordinated to imperial authority. This was not merely a political project; it was a cultural one. Language became one of the ways empire reorganized identity itself.

item.title: Well-Preserved Tomb of Ancient Egyptian Official Found Near Saqqara - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A joint Spanish-Egyptian archaeological mission has found a well-preserved tomb dating to the Fifth Dynasty of Egypt’s Old Kingdom (2494–2345 BCE), reports the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities. The find was made during the mission’s 2026 excavation season in the area known as the Mariette Necropolis, north of Egypt’s Saqqara archaeological site.

The tomb consists of a mastaba containing two funerary chapels. One chapel belongs to a man named Yunmen, a high-ranking official under the Pharaoh Djedkare Isesi (late 25th to mid-24th century BCE) whose positions included judge, court administrator, and chief scribe responsible for reviewing petitions and complaints. The second chapel is that of his father, Iti, who held clerical jobs related to the administration of agricultural lands and offerings.

Yunmen’s chapel is decorated with painted reliefs, some retaining their original colors, depicting various agricultural activities and processions of bearers bringing offerings to his tomb. Iti’s chapel features a traditional false door and offering scenes, though much of this decoration has been lost.  

The mission, a joint project of the Autonomous University of Barcelona (UAB) and Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities (SCA), is led by Josep Cervelló Autuori, a lecturer in the Department of Ancient and Medieval Sciences at UAB.

Hisham El-Leithy, secretary-general of the SCA, emphasized the importance of the tomb’s discovery, saying it offers new insights into the funerary traditions and administrative structures of the late Fifth Dynasty, a pivotal moment in Old Kingdom religion and politics.

He added that mastaba’s location been known since it was excavated by French archaeologist Auguste Mariette in the 19th century. However, the site had never been subjected to systematic scientific exploration and documentation, lending particular significance to the mission’s work.

item.title: Production Mold for Ancient Female Figurine Discovered in Jerusalem - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A mold used to create a clay figurine during the First Temple Period was discovered earlier this summer on the grounds of the Tower of David Jerusalem Museum. The excavation, at Kishle, a former prison and military base that is now part of the museum, was overseen by the Israel Antiquities Authority (IAA).

“Although many figurines from this period have been uncovered in Jerusalem, this is the first time that a mold used to manufacture them has ever been found in the city,” said IAA researchers in a statement. Archaeologists have long wondered if these ubiquitous figures, dating from the 8th to the 6th centuries BCE, were manufactured locally or imported; they now know that at least some were created within Jerusalem.

The mold in question depicts a woman’s face with defined features and an elaborate hairstyle. Sviatoslav Klindukhov, a conservation and restoration specialist working with the IAA, was able to cast a new figurine from the ancient mold.

Female figures are one of three main types found during this time periods; others depict horse-and-rider pairs or animals. Archaeologists believe that many were originally painted yellow, red, and black. Since these figures have been found in excavations of homes, streets, and tombs, it is believed they were used as everyday objects, perhaps to promote fertility or used as children’s toys or household amulets. Debbi Ben-Ami, a curator at the IAA, hopes that the newly discovered mold “will provide fresh insights and help answer some of the questions that continue to occupy researchers.”

This particular excavation site is one of the most significant in Jerusalem, according to Amit Re’em and Ayala Zilberstein, IAA excavation directors. “The Kishle excavation, which has been ongoing for several years, continues to surprise us time and again,” they said. It presents “the city’s history in a clear and continuous sequence—from the days of the Kings of Judah, through the many periods that shaped Jerusalem, and up to the British Mandate.”

item.title: Trump-Ousted Kennedy Center Chairman Buys Removed Shapiro Sculpture - Hyperallergic
item.description:
David Rubenstein, the former board chairman of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, has purchased Joel Shapiro’s "Blue" (2019) just days after the National Park Service deinstalled the iconic sculpture from center grounds.

The agency began removing late artist Joel Shapiro's 24-foot-tall sculpture from the Kennedy Center's REACH (Renew, Experience, Activate, Create, and Honor) campus on September 2, leaving its future to the Joel Shapiro and Ellen Phelan Foundation. Amid renewed attempts to stamp Trump's name on the Kennedy Center facade and grounds, the seemingly nonsensical removal of "Blue" prompted condemnation from artists, cultural workers, and organizations like Hands Off the Arts.

A billionaire philanthropist who has donated to organizations including the Smithsonian Institution and the National Park Service charity, Rubenstein reportedly purchased the work for a sum of $2 million and will ultimately move "Blue" to the sculpture garden at the National Gallery of Art, according to the New York Times.

Rubenstein was among several Biden appointees ousted from the bipartisan Kennedy Center board by President Donald Trump in February 2025. During his tenure, the philanthropist pledged $50 million to the center's REACH expansion project, which intends to honor President John F. Kennedy's vision of bridging divides between artists and audiences. When the REACH campus opened in 2019, Shapiro, who died in 2025, gifted "Blue" as an inaugural landmark that could be seen from Potomac Parkway and other major Washington, DC, thoroughfares.

Shortly after beginning his second presidential term, Trump replaced the former board with his own loyalist cohort and made himself chairman, the position formerly held by Rubenstein.

item.title: Artist Lucien Smith, Fixture of NYC’s Downtown Scene, Dies at 37 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Artist Lucien Smith, an abstract painter whose work as a nonprofit founder and restaurateur channeled the community ethos of 1970s New York, has died at the age of 37. The news of his passing was confirmed by Erin Goldberger, director of Half Gallery, which showed the artist's work early on. The cause of death has not been made public.

Smith was best known for his Rain Paintings series (2011–12), which he began making the year he graduated from Cooper Union by spraying canvases with acrylic paint loaded into fire extinguishers. Later subject to the rapid cycle of market growth and decline that defined the early-2010s movement reviving mid-20th-century abstraction and formalism, Smith quit commercial galleries in 2015 and began advocating for himself and others.

“I remember Lucien wanted to do a video of himself dressed as a ghoul in a tuxedo walking through Times Square as a joke about being the face of ‘Zombie Formalism,’” Bill Powers, art dealer and Half Gallery owner, told Hyperallergic. “He had a sense of humor about his place in the world. He will be missed terribly.”

Born in 1989 in Los Angeles, Smith was raised in the Lower East Side until his teenage years, when his mother, a fashion designer, and father, an artist and musician, moved him back to Los Angeles. Upon graduating high school, he returned to New York to study at Cooper Union, where he would develop the aesthetic language that would result in his two-person 2011 thesis show, Imagined Nostalgia, and his near-immediate market success upon graduation. “Hobbes, The Rain Man, and My Friend Barney / Under the Sycamore Tree,” a painting originally purchased for $10,000 from the thesis show, was sold at auction at Phillips for $389,000 in 2013.

Two years later, collector Alberto Mugrabi alleged that the work was practically unsellable, attesting to the market fluctuations that Smith openly acknowledged, stating on his website that he “battled with some of the pitfalls of gaining notoriety so early.”

item.title: Renoir Artworks Worth Millions Stolen in Five-Minute Heist in France - Hyperallergic
item.description:
A pair of thieves made off with two paintings from the Renoir Museum in southern France during a break-in early this morning, September 8. The duo initially stole four of Renoir's paintings from the galleries but dropped two in the museum's garden while being chased by police.

The operation lasted only five minutes, according to a statement from Mayor Bryan Masson of Cagnes-sur-Mer, who told French media that the burglars were “well equipped and well informed,” as the pair used an electric saw to cut through the museum's exterior fence and the clips securing the paintings' frames. The museum's alarm automatically notified the local police, who arrived on the scene and chased the burglars across the property on foot.

The pair made off with Pierre-Auguste Renoir's “Madame Colonna Romano” (c. 1910) and “Jeune femme au puits (Young Woman at the Well)” (c. 1886) — two lesser-known oil paintings by the Impressionist. They tried to take “Madame Stephen Pichon” (c. 1895) and “Coco Lisant” (c. 1905) as well, but ultimately left them behind. Per Masson's office, the value of the combined works, including the two that were not ultimately taken, starts at €9 million ($10.5 million).

Police are investigating the whereabouts of the thieves and the two paintings that remain at large. Still, the museum's proximity to the Mediterranean Sea poses an increased risk of a cold trail.

The Renoir raid is the latest in a spate of museum robberies sweeping across Europe. Just two weeks ago, two thieves smashed a display case and made off with a platinum and diamond necklace at the Museum of Applied Arts in Vienna.

A recent report from Europol warned that thieves are targeting museums and cultural heritage with “more direct and confrontational approaches,” especially highlighting the “growing use of violent force.”

Another one of Renoir's paintings, “Les poissons” (c. 1917), was stolen alongside works by Paul Cezánne and Henri Matisse during a raid at the Magnani Rocca Foundation in Parma, Italy, this March. Museum heists have garnered more media attention since last year's jewel heist at the Louvre.

item.title: Henry Wessel’s Candid California Photos Underscore the Art of Noticing - Colossal
item.description:
“There is the world, and there is the photograph. The photograph is not the world, it’s a completely different thing,” Henry Wessel (1942-2018) said in a “TateShots” short on the occasion of Tate Modern’s display of his Incidents series in 2014. Today, an exhibition of more than 65 prints titled Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books opens at The Grolier Club, a historic society celebrating the world of books and the graphic arts.

Wessel was a New Jersey native who, after borrowing a Leica camera during his studies at Pennsylvania State University, fell headlong into photography. He rose to prominence in the early 1970s for his black-and-white compositions that plumbed the possibilities of landscape and documentary imagery. Following the receipt of a Guggenheim grant, he moved to the Bay Area, where he taught at the now-defunct San Francisco Art Institute from 1973 to 2014 and captured the area’s characteristically glowing light, historic neighborhoods, and individualistic denizens.

Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes the artist’s Incidents and Traffic series in their totality, plus works from his Real Estate and Night Walks series. To make the latter, he would walk around neighborhoods with his tripod and take portraits of local homes after dinner or during the early morning hours.

In Traffic, Wessel snapped scenes and other drivers from his car, capturing candid moments as other vehicles passed or as he encountered roadside curiosities. But he quickly learned that there’s an inherent issue with having to stop the car, get out, and try to capture what you initially saw: it looks totally different.

Wessel began to capture what he saw directly from the driver’s seat, working quickly with the hope that the images would more closely translate his immediate experiences. In an SFMOMA interview he said, “You know, like they say, luck is impartial. You have just as much bad luck as you have good luck. But you can do things to prepare yourself to receive the good luck. And that’s part of the whole process of photographing.”

Henry Wessel — Photographs and Books includes some of Wessel’s earliest work, such as “Untitled” from 1968, plus the other series that were created throughout the 1980s and 1990s. The show opens today and continues through November 14 in New York, and a catalogue slated for release in October is available for pre-order from Chicago University Press.

item.title: Eiffel Tower Workers Strike in Outrage After Female Staffers Ordered to Leave Their Posts, Replaced by Men - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Eiffel Tower closed Monday due to strikes over outrage that female workers were allegedly ordered to leave and stay out of sight to comply with a special request from a traditional Hindu delegation that visited the monument over the weekend, reported Le Parisien. By Tuesday, the monument had reopened, and a representative of the Hindu religious organization BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha, which has close ties to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s nationalist party, issued an apology.

But it was too late to quell a viral storm over news that managers of France’s most iconic landmark appear to have agreed to effectively discriminate against its women workers. “Orders were given to sideline female staff at the Eiffel Tower, and female workers at contractor companies, [who were] replaced and made invisible because of their gender,” staffers who refused to work on Monday told Le Parisien. The situation “is serious and profoundly contrary to values of equality and non-discrimination,” they added. “The Eiffel Tower is the symbol of France, and we believe it must also be exemplary in the values it projects and the way it treats employees.”

Left-leaning Paris Mayor Emmanuel Gregoire said he agreed with protesting workers and announced the launch of an investigation into the incident. “Equality between women and men will never stop at the foot of our historical monuments, nor anywhere in this city,” he wrote on social media.

On Saturday morning, leading members of the BAPS Swaminarayan Sanstha were given a private visit to the Eiffel Tower’s second floor, to celebrate the inauguration of its first major temple in France, located east of Paris in Bussy-Saint-Georges. Prior to this, the delegation reportedly asked management at the monument to “limit” the group’s “interactions with women.” Another worker at the monument told Le Parisien that women were specifically asked to be “put aside,” to avoid “using the term ‘hidden.’”

Eiffel Tower management responded by asking female workers to leave their posts and to stay away from areas where the religious group was visiting. Men were then brought in to replace the women workers, and they escorted the BAPS delegates instead, according to staff.

Lawmakers across the political spectrum have taken to social media to express their shock. “In France, we’ll never accept that the presence of women be ‘limited,’” stated far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen.

Today, Ariel Weil, president of Société d’exploitation de la tour Eiffel, the city-owned organization that manages the Eiffel Tower, called the removal of female workers “totally unacceptable,” while speaking on BFMTV. He promised his own investigation into who was responsible for what he described as a likely “zealous” interpretation of the Hindu delegation’s requests. Meanwhile, in a statement on social media, the Hindu organization BAPS apologized for “anyone who may have been hurt or was inconvenienced.” The group also insisted that, “to the best of our knowledge, at no point was anyone prevented access to the Eiffel Tower.”

item.title: Rhiannon Adam on Space Exploration and Personal Identity - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In 1969, astronaut Neil Armstrong declared: “That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” This sentence became one of the most famous in history, marking the moment humanity first set foot on the moon. Since the Apollo 11 mission touched down on the lunar surface, 23 astronauts – all of them American – have been to the moon, and only 12 have walked on it. In 2018, almost fifty years after Armstrong uttered those immortal words, Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa announced a global search for eight artists to join him on a week-long lunar mission aboard SpaceX Starship: the first civilian mission to deep space. Irish photographer Rhiannon Adam answered the call and was selected as the only female crew member from millions of applicants, providing the chance to achieve the seemingly impossible: to become the first out queer woman to venture beyond the Karman line. 

The mission’s flight path was designed to echo Apollo 8’s 1968 journey, which led astronaut Bill Anders to suggest NASA “should have sent poets” to capture the sense of wonder he experienced. dearMoon, as Maezawa named the mission, sought to fulfil this vision by inviting creatives to reflect on humanity from space, aiming to inspire world peace. Adam immersed herself in the space industry for three years, preparing for the endeavour ahead and grappling with both her mortality and the responsibility of representing marginalised voices. It was an emotional and all-consuming process, defining both her personal life and her artistic output. However, in June 2024, Maezawa abruptly cancelled the mission, leaving the crew to try and pick up the pieces of their disrupted lives. 

The International Centre for the Image, Dublin, presents Rhi-Entry, an exhibition of works that Adam made to process the mission being scrapped. The series blurs fact and fiction through moving images, photographs and ephemera, reflecting on the artist’s “psychological recalibration” and her struggle to return to “normal” life. It is often cited that re-entry is the most dangerous part of spaceflight, and for Adam, this rings true, despite never having left our planet. Yet, this exhibition goes beyond just her individual experience, as the artist reckons with what it means to have been the first openly queer woman to be selected for a space mission, and how we better address representation in the field. As she describes: “this presentation stands as a shrine to lost dreams and an urgent call for alternative voices in the space industry.” Here, she joins other contemporary artists whose work highlights the lack of diversity within space programmes, including Mackenzie Calle’s photographic series The Gay Space Agency. 

Rhi-Entry also moves into a decidedly political direction, drawing connection between the end of the project and America’s shift towards more right-wing politics and figures like Elon Musk throwing their support behind Donald Trump. Adam is keen to bring attention to the wider ramifications of this. Her message is clear: space travel does not happen in a vacuum. In a recent interview with Dazed, she recounted how: “People don’t think space relates to them…but USAID is cut because Trump is in power, people are dying of HIV because Elon Musk helped win an election because he wants more rockets in space.” In one artwork, Adam reinterprets the 1950 book by Robert A. Heinlein, The Man Who Sold the Moon. The artist takes the original cover, which shows a close-up image of a man, looking back at a rocket that’s under construction, and replaced his face with that of Elon Musk.  

Adam’s series, and its currently display in Dublin, brings the often abstract and mysterious business of space travel and tells audiences why they should care. The artist’s deeply personal connection to the democratisation of space missions is a reminder of why representation matters, and how politics is inextricably tied up in exploration. Adam’s involvement and subsequent exclusion from a SpaceX mission acts as a warning to every person: space is the next frontier of exploration and expansion, and we must ensure that all voices are heard as we enter this next stage of scientific discovery. 

Rhi-Entry is at International Centre for the Image, Dublin from 11 September – 23 December: image.museum

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:
