item.title: Vietnam Veterans File Restraining Order to Block Progress on Trump’s 250-Foot Triumphal Arch - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A group of Vietnam veterans filed for a temporary restraining order on Friday to stop progress on one of Trump’s projects to alter the landscape of the nation’s capital, a 250-foot triumphal arch. 

The plaintiffs are veterans Michael Lemmon, Shaun Byrnes, and Jon Gundersen, along with architectural historian Calder Loth, who are represented by the Public Citizen Litigation Group, of Washington, D.C. They filed their motion for a 14-day restraining order on Friday, after Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X on Thursday that “excavation work” for the arch would come within two weeks, promising that the arch would be “one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World.”

The arch, however, has not received congressional approval. It is slated to go up at Memorial Circle, across the Potomac River, in Arlington, Virginia, from the Lincoln Memorial. The president debuted a model of the monument in October 2025, telling CBS News that the arch is dedicated to himself. Trump wants his arch, at 250 feet, to be taller than the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, which rises to 162.5 feet. The plaintiffs argue that the arch would disrupt sightlines between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The veterans first filed suit in February against Trump; Vince Haley, of the president’s office; and the National Park Service (NPS), aiming to stop progress on the project, absent authorization from Congress. In April, they agreed to dismiss their motion in exchange for assurances that NPS would not authorize construction without posting a notice of its authorization online and that NPS would provide at least 14 days’ notice prior to beginning construction or demolition ahead of construction. 

“The imminent course of action that Secretary Burgum has announced to the American people is unlawful many times over,” the Friday filing reads, further alleging that it violates the court’s April order. It adds that “once a building project has begun, a later order to reverse course raises ‘significant’ practical problems,” and that the defendants “have offered no evidence that beginning construction of a commemorative arch is a matter of such exigency that blocking construction until this Court has had the opportunity to rule on the project’s legality will irreparably harm Defendants or the public interest.”

“This court,” conclude the plaintiffs, “should enter a temporary restraining order blocking Defendants’ efforts to blaze ahead with an unlawful course of conduct in the hope that they can render the arch a fait accompli before this Court has had the chance to reach a final determination as to whether Defendants’ project is authorized by law.”

In a responding filing entered “to clarify Plaintiffs’ misunderstanding and avoid any potential for further confusion,” the Trump administration argues that the new activity will be “long-disclosed Phase 1B archaeological survey work,” conducted to ensure compliance with statutes such as the National Historic Preservation Act. “This activity is not construction, or demolition in preparation for construction, of an arch,” it says, noting that the work will consist of digging four test pits. 

The planning of the District of Columbia has been subject to great deliberation ever since it was founded in the late 18th century, notes the plaintiffs’ filing, with Congress responsible, since 1912, for authorizing any additional monuments and structures. 

The Trump administration has shown no regard for Congressional or any other authority in his campaign to remodel the White House and Washington overall to suit his taste. This has included gilding large monuments near the Lincoln Memorial, adding Trump’s name to the Kennedy Center in violation of its founding documents, and abruptly removing a major Joel Shapiro work from the center’s grounds.

Most dramatically, he razed the East Wing of the White House without warning last October to make way for one of his favored projects, a massive ballroom-cum-military bunker that preservationists say would be out of proportion with the rest of the White House. Nonetheless, the Supreme Court ruled this week, 5–4, that construction could go ahead absent approval from Congress, saying that the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a nonprofit chartered by Congress to guard public buildings, which brought suit against the administration, did not have standing.

item.title: Beyoncé Gives the Studio Museum in Harlem a $2 M. Gift on Her Birthday - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Beyoncé Knowles turned 45 on September 4, and to mark the occasion, the global superstar entertainer made an unusual birthday gift, of $2 million, not to herself but to the Studio Museum in Harlem. 

“Art tells all our stories; the past and the present, but is not always accessible to everyone,” said Beyoncé in a press release. “I have always been impressed with the Studio Museum in Harlem because of its intention to make the museum an integral part of the community. I have been introduced to several of my favorite young and upcoming Black artists through exhibits at the Museum. It is a place of inspiration where all audiences can discover new stories through the canvases of diverse storytellers that reflect our humanity.”

The museum did not immediately respond to an email asking how the funds will be used; this story will be updated with any new information from the institution.

Beyoncé is married to rapper, music mogul, and ARTnews Top 200 collector Jay-Z (born Shawn Carter). The couple famously shot large parts of the video for their 2018 single “Apeshit” at the Louvre Museum in Paris.

“Each time Beyoncé releases new music, it might as well be considered an art-world event too,” wrote Alex Greenberger for ARTnews in 2020. “She’s been known to include works by vaunted artists in her videos, and with her husband Jay-Z, she’s built up an important collection of Black art.” He was writing on the occasion of the release of an 85-minute visual album titled Black Is King, which is “filled with artworks of note, and includes contributions from art-world figures behind the scenes.”

One of the most-awarded performers of all time, Beyoncé has won 35 Grammy Awards, more than any other artist. As a solo musician, she has sold over 200 million records worldwide, and she is one of the highest-grossing live acts in history. Her net worth is estimated by Forbes to be $1 billion. 

Founded in 1968 in a temporary space on the second floor of a Fifth Avenue loft building, the Studio Museum opened its new $160 million David Adjaye–designed home on 125th Street in November after a seven-year closure. Writing for ARTnews, Maximilíano Durón called it “stunning.” In 2023, the financier Joseph Perella and his wife Amy gave the museum a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting, making it one of the few US museums to own one. Also among the masterpieces on view at the reopening were works by Barkley K. Hendricks, Kerry James Marshall, Howardena Pindell, Faith Ringgold, and Carrie Mae Weems.

“I am deeply grateful to Beyoncé, both for the generosity of this gift, especially on her birthday, and for recognizing the vital role that the Studio Museum plays in people’s lives,” said museum director and chief curator Thelma Golden. “Our institution was founded to shift the arts landscape and reimagine who that landscape serves. This gift will allow us to continue strengthening our work for Harlemites, New Yorkers, and audiences across the globe.”

item.title: Huiling Chen Documents Life in China’s Rural Communities - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In China’s Hengnan County, Hunan Province, long-term migration to cities is reshaping family structures and village life. As younger generations leave for education and employment, many older residents continue to care for homes, cultivate land and maintain everyday routines. Those Who Remain, a photo series by London-based Chinese visual artist Huiling Chen, focuses on older people living in agricultural communities like Hengnan. Through portraits taken in domestic spaces as well as scenes of daily labour, the body of work observes how rural existence is being reshaped by an ageing population.

“Rather than portraying these communities through nostalgia or decline, the project considers how everyday life continues and adapts amid social change,” the artist explains. “Those photographed are not simply presented as people “left behind,” but as active participants sustaining families, relationships and a continuing connection to place.” This is indicative of Chen’s wider fine art practice, which incorporates documentary observation of individuals to make broader cultural and socio-political shifts visible. Her previous projects include A House in Three Tenses, following three generations of women sharing one home, and The Lane Becomes a Table, in which a private birthday celebration expands into village streets. Chen’s subjects include rural societies and families in China, as well as migrants living and working in the UK.

The documentary genre brings with it a particular set of responsibilities: How do you tell someone else’s story? Who owns the photograph? How much are the pictures influenced by the person behind the camera? Chen explicitly aims to “avoid sentimental or victimising representations,” collaborating with participants to construct their own image – “rather than treating them as symbols of rural ageing.” The result is that the camaraderie between subject and photographer is often palpable. In one shot, a woman looks up from her phone, meeting Chen’s gaze with familiarity. Elsewhere, a man grins, walking by holding a bamboo cane. Other compositions take a wider view: depicting figures in the fields, a shock of yellow flowers behind them, or tilling the soil, deep in concentration. These are people with agency. Chen’s perspective moves between intimate portraits like these – taken in the home, or whilst individuals are at work – and empty interior spaces devoid of human presence. The latter shots are occupied solely by tools of their owner’s trade – buckets, stools and nets – and are reminiscent of still life paintings. Each featured object, perhaps passed down through generations, resonates with silent histories of family and labour.

In Those Who Remain, Chen places herself within a longer tradition of portrait photography concerned with ageing. Examples include Imogen Cunningham’s posthumous After Ninety (1977), Richard Avedon’s Portraits of Aging (1951–2004) and Martine Franck’s Le Temps de Vieillir (A Time to Grow Old) (1980). Today, a closer contemporary parallel can be found in the work of Joanne Coates (b. 1990). Whilst Coates does not explicitly focus on what it means to be “getting old”, her explorations of rural life and class in North East England – including The Lie of the Land and Daughters of the Soil – centre on portraying and telling the stories of farmworkers. Like Chen, she uses photography to give visibility to lives and experiences that are often overlooked, narrating “a story of gender and class that has long been forgotten, or never told.”

This collection of pictures is shaped by the absence of those who have left. Younger family members who have migrated are rarely physically present in the photographs, yet their distance influences the homes, relationships and routines Chen records. However, Those Who Remain makes it clear that these villages are not static, untouched remnants of the past. They are ever-changing environments in which older generations continue to adapt, work and sustain everyday life. That is where the series holds its power. And it has not gone unnoticed: Those Who Remain was recently named an Official Selection in the 2026 International Photography Awards (IPA), a major international competition which champions “the world’s finest photographers.” It’s a selection that establishes Chen as one to watch, positioning her alongside other acclaimed contemporary image-makers working in the space between fine art and documentary.

huilingchen.art

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

Image Credits:
All images courtesy of Huiling Chen, from the series Those Who Remain.

The post Huiling Chen Documents Life in China’s Rural Communities appeared first on Aesthetica Magazine.

item.title: Kehinde Wiley Responds to the Trump Administration’s Removal of His Painting With an ‘Aesthetically Terrifying’ T-shirt - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Kehinde Wiley’s artwork at the US Embassy in the Dominican Republic continues to cause a stir. Erin Scavino, director of Art in Embassies in a podcast interview with Sean Spicer, called the painting Young Artists After Siamesas 1960 (2013) “aesthetically terrifying” last week, but now in an unearthed radio interview from April, US ambassador Leah Campos described the painting as a lesbian picnic, according to the New York Times.

In the interview conducted in Spanish, Campos said that she saw a “huge painting of a picnic in a park with flowers and some lesbians.” She wrongfully contends in the interview that the Biden administration wanted being “that ideology here to the Dominican people.” The painting was commissioned during the Obama administration by the State Department in 2013.

Wiley hasn’t come out publicly to address the controversy around his painting, but on his official e-commerce Instagram, he posted a black T-shirt retailing for $120 with the words “aesthetically terrifying,” which he borrowed from Scavino, who describes his work as such. “A response. A reclamation. A reminder that art has never needed permission to be beautiful, provocative, or powerful,” Wiley’s post reads.

The Trump administration has been slowly changing artwork in its embassies to reflect “American patriotism and the beauty of our great country” as Campos put it in an Instagram post in August when describing the swap of Wiley’s painting for an image of the American flag accompanied by the Twisted Sister’s song We’re Not Gonna Take It.”

At the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., the same act is taking place as workers began to disassemble Joel Shapiro’s monumental 24-foot-tall sculpture Blue. The American sculptor gave the center the work as a gift in 2019. The New York Times reported that Shapiro’s work was “targeted for elimination after President Trump’s takeover of the center.”

In December, the center’s board, led by Trump and filled with his allies, voted to inscribe his name on the building’s facade, triggering an ongoing legal struggle with the federal court system.

item.title: Adam Lindemann Sued by Nature Conservancy for Allegedly Installing Julian Schnabel Sculpture Without Permission - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a lawsuit filed earlier this month, dealer Adam Lindemann is facing allegations that he installed a 25-foot-tall Julian Schnabel sculpture on a Long Island estate without permission.

Filed on August 20 in New York’s Eastern District, the lawsuit was brought by the Nature Conservancy, a preserve in Montauk. Lindemann, the founder of New York’s now-defunct Venus Over Manhattan gallery, has a property next to the vast preserve.

Newsday, a publication focused on Long Island’s Nassau and Suffolk Counties, first broke news of the lawsuit on Thursday.

Lindemann is accused of trespassing on the Andy Warhol Visual Arts Preserve, which the conservancy currently owns and which was once the property of Pop artist Andy Warhol. Lindemann is accused of installing Schnabel’s Ahab without the Nature Conservancy’s permission.

Known as Eothen (“from the East” in Greek), Lindemann’s adjacent estate is a six-acre property with a house and six cottages that Lindemann purchased from J.Crew CEO Millard Drexler for $50 million in 2015, according to the Real Deal. There was an additional 24-acre horse farm that Lindemann did not purchase.

The conservancy is an Arlington, Virginia–based nonprofit dedicated to environmental preservation. In 1992, the New York property was donated by the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts. As part of the donation at that time, the conservancy agreed to “preserve a section of the ecologically significant Montauk Moorlands and to promote the visual arts,” per the lawsuit.

After it discovered Lindemann had installed a sculpture on the preserve, the conservancy allegedly asked Lindemann to remove the sculpture in question within 90 days in an initial December 2024 letter, with additional correspondence about the sculpture’s removal. The nonprofit also found Lindemann parking personal vehicles in its lot, mowing its lawn, and planting shrubs, according to the suit.

“Despite TNC’s repeated demands and efforts towards amicable resolution, Defendant has refused to remove the Sculpture and continues to enter the property without permission,” William H. Taft V, the conservancy’s attorney, wrote in the suit.

According to the lawsuit, Lindemann agreed to remove the sculpture by August 31, 2025, after a meeting with conservancy officials in May.

On September 7, 2025, however, Lindemann sent the nonprofit an email, saying, “as promised I’m moving the sculpture!” He added, “Sure hope that makes you happy as it’s expensive and disruptive but it’s happening as you wished and I agreed. All the best to you and I’ll send pics as soon as the move is completed, we are currently organizing this with the local artist, the famous local artist Julian Schnabel’s team.”

Taft explained, “In a show of good faith — and with the intent to resolve these issues amicably — TNC noted that Defendant may not have been aware of the exact boundary lines between the Preserve and Defendant’s property and offered to meet with Defendant on site to walk their shared boundary.”

On February 6, 2026, conservancy officials allegedly sent Lindemann a cease-and-desist demanding he stop entering and parking on the property, as well as maintaining “any part of the preserve.” It also demanded the artwork’s removal within within 30 days.

The sculpture has allegedly still not been removed.

“To date, Defendant continues to park personal vehicles in the Preserve’s parking area, mow the Preserve adjacent to his property, and refuses to remove the Sculpture from the Preserve,” Taft said.

The conservancy has requested a jury trial and is seeking an injunction that would stop Lindemann from entering the property, a declaration that the conservancy has exclusive control of the preserve, a declaration that Lindemann does not own the sculpture, a declaration the conservancy can remove the sculpture, and attorneys’ fees.

The protection of the preserve is “important for migratory birds, rare species, and other wildlife,” the lawsuit claims. “The Preserve’s location along the Atlantic Flyway — a major north-south migration route used by birds in North America — makes it an important feeding ground and stop-over site for Neotropical migratory birds.”

Lindemann did not respond to ARTnews’s request for comment by the time of publication.

item.title: An Incisive Exhibition in Buffalo Defies Expectations of What Latinx Painting Should Look Like - ARTnews.com
item.description:
There is a painting at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum that I still can’t get out of my head, six months after I saw it. It only measures 40 by 30 inches, and I missed it on my first walk through the gallery. Made by Los Angeles–based artist Karla Diaz in thinned-out acrylic paint, it shows two Latino men, both with mustaches, one carrying the other on his shoulders. The painting’s joyful casualness belies its subject matter, clues to which can be found in the coyote on one of the men’s shirts and in the work’s title, Uncle’s Crossing (2022).

Diaz depicted her late uncle, who was a coyote, or someone who helps undocumented people cross into the United States. The role of the coyote is controversial in Latinx communities, often regarded as a necessary evil: someone who may help you get into the US but exploit you along the way. Growing up, Diaz recalled, talking about her uncle’s job was taboo at home. “He would whisper, ‘Okay, I’m leaving for work,’ and I was like, ‘Okay, why are you whispering? You’re just going to work.’” At the time, she didn’t know exactly what job her uncle was leaving for; it was only later that she learned the truth.

Four years ago, shortly after her uncle passed away, Diaz was recovering from a stroke and had to relearn how to talk, walk, and paint. Throughout this rehabilitation, memories of her uncle returned to her. “It was a vulnerable time,” she said. “I’m the type of person, when something is very vulnerable and scary, instead of running away from it, I confront it. Even if that means putting myself in a space that is scary emotionally, I feel I can grow and learn a lot from it.”

She felt compelled to make this tender work because it was an image she had never seen before in art history: a portrait of a coyote. “In a way, it’s something that has been erased. It’s a controversial story to tell. I hope that people come with questions more than anything. I know that my uncle, in the most humane way of being able to do that, was trying to help people.”

The work, she added, asks “What does it mean to make taboo stories visible and tell others about them?”

Uncle’s Crossing features in “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way,” which closes this weekend in Western New York. Painting surveys like “Let Us Gather,” which will soon depart on a national tour to Iowa, Phoenix, and Seattle, were once a standard feature of contemporary art museums, though they have recently fallen out of favor. The exhibition is an exciting intervention into the history of painting surveys, ambitious in scope yet thoughtfully executed in both its installation and its creation of new scholarship.

In focusing on one medium, Andrea Alvarez, the exhibition’s curator, wanted to explore “the breadth and the richness of that discipline—to reveal the richness of the Latinx population.”

Alvarez said she included works that most might not consider traditional paintings—oil or acrylic on canvas or linen—to “push the boundaries of what is painting and what that means today.” These range from Moises Salazar Tlatenchi’s Cruising Queens (2024), which imagines a queer version of Washington crossing the Delaware and features a crocheted frame; Manuela Gonzalez’s Inanna (2024), made of painted textiles sewn together into a diamond shape that reference the history of hard-edge abstraction and painters like Frank Stella and Mary Heilmann; and Nery Gabriel Lemus’s Querida Niña Migrante and This Is the Air We Breathe (both 2020), each consisting of 15 painted floor mats installed on the floor.

Works like these, Alvarez said, “resist the materiality of painting itself—what should and shouldn’t fine art be made out of. … Every single material choice is intentional and deliberate.” Speaking on an artist panel, Sarah Zapata, who contributed another textile-based work, said she welcomed her inclusion in the exhibition because “an important part of the lineage [of painting] is thinking about how textiles largely are the reason that painting exists.”

 “My hope is that what visitors take away is an experience of the richness, the diversity, and the complexity of what these artists are doing,” Alvarez said, and in doing so “they can also expand that in their mind to the population more broadly to understand that this population of the diaspora of Latinx people in the United States are similarly rich, culturally productive and diverse, and meritorious of all of this sort of celebration.”

Another legacy that Alvarez had to contend with is the perception of Latinx painting, more specifically the stereotypes that have historically been attached to it by outsiders: colorful, figurative, folkloric. “There are going to be people who walk through the exhibition with certain expectations that they will be surprised to see the breadth of work that they encounter,” she said. “But I didn’t see a lot of the artists still wrestling with that. It feels to me like a lot of the artists have liberated themselves from those historical obligations. The exhibition does do the work of undoing some of those stereotypes.”

Now curator at the Buffalo AKG, Alvarez joined the museum as a curatorial fellow in 2018 and shortly afterward began thinking about how she might introduce contemporary Latinx art to the people of Buffalo. After her promotion to assistant curator in 2021, she began planning the exhibition in earnest, conducting her initial studio visits across the country, from Los Angeles to Miami, Chicago to Phoenix, and Texas to Puerto Rico. “That’s when I started homing in on the discipline of painting,” she said. The museum’s deep holdings in 20th-century painting were also a plus, as frequent visitors might more easily begin to connect with the works on view.

“Let Us Gather” features 58 artists, though Alvarez could have included dozens more. “The question I asked myself over and over again is: Is this artist actively contributing to the discourse of what is contemporary Latinx painting?” As she continued her research, “I did start to observe shared concerns or interests among these different artists. In some cases, these artists weren’t in dialogue with one another—they might not even know each other’s work until this exhibition.”

These observations led Alvarez to organize the exhibition into seven themes, including “Identity/Place,” which looks at how the people who live in a place shape it and how, in turn, its topography shapes them, and “Pinturx,” a gender-neutral version of the Spanish word for “painter” that encompasses various genres of painting.

Each theme acts as its own microcosm of the overall exhibition’s approach, showcasing varied perspectives on a single topic. In the “Community” section, for example, artists including Aliza Nisenbaum, David Antonio Cruz, and Shizu Saldamando consider “community as a verb, community as a noun—different kinds of communities, whether those are blood relations or chosen family” and explore “the importance of community, in many cases, to marginalized groups for survival and thriving.”

Other artists subvert expectations of the themes, as illustrated by an abstraction by Eamon Ore-Giron featured in “(New) Histories,” which tackles the legacy of history painting; Kristopher Raos’s painted close-up of the Cheer laundry detergent logo in “Abstractions”; and still lifes by Salomón Huerta, featuring a gun paired with a glass of milk or a pink pan dulce, in “Bodies & Figures.” The latter works are actually portraits of the artist and his father, who each night would “take his revolver out of the holster, set it down on the table, and ask someone to bring him a snack,” according to Alvarez. “It’s a tender image actually that represents his father and the care that they had for one another.”

After settling on a final list in summer 2024, Alvarez felt it was important to involve the artists in selecting which of their works would be featured in the exhibition. Often, she explained, L.A.-based artists or artists from the Caribbean have shown together, but because artists from different places were going to be presented in the same galleries, “I wanted everyone to have a little bit more agency,” she said, noting that ultimately, as the curator, she did have the final say. “I wanted to hear what they had to say—I have my preferences; I have the works that have stuck out to me for whatever reason—but I wanted to know what’s more resonant for them.”

An example of this is also one of the largest works on view, Man on Trampoline (2023), by Larry Madrigal. Initially, artist and curator considered showing a selection of four or so smaller paintings before settling on this monumental canvas. Measuring 7.5 feet by 6.3 feet, it depicts a jumble of figures suspended in midair above the titular bouncing device, with the composition referencing El Greco’s The Resurrection (1597–1600) and the subject resembling something you’d see on America’s Funniest Home Videos. In blending these two sources, Madrigal said he aims to bring “humor, earnestness, and humanity—all in the painting.”

“His work is one that celebrates the improvised moments of family life—of a big family, a chaotic family—and what it feels like to be the father of a growing family,” Alvarez said. “It encapsulates all those elements [of community], while also still addressing the studied way the artist thinks about art history.”

Art history, meanwhile, factors broadly into the exhibition, too. “Painting has such a potent and undeniable history,” Alvarez said, connecting it not just to its primacy within the discipline but also how it was a tool of imperialist power in spreading aesthetic conventions to various colonies, like the Americas. “These artists are using painting, engaging with its traditions—and subverting its legacies—because of that history. Painting felt like a particularly loaded medium to unpack.”

Guadalupe Maravilla’s personal story of migration, from El Salvador to the U.S. during the 1980s, acts as a call to think about the ongoing mass deportations being conducted by ICE. In Pupusa Retablo (2023), the artist shows three women grilling masa for the titular dish and, in a painted caption, recalls how, while in Honduras on this sojourn, he ate pupusas: “A woman on the neighboring table told her friends that I was a Salvadoran refugee child because she noticed that I ate my pupusas with my hands. I remember feeling terrified of being sent back to El Salvador.” That experience, likely shared by countless others, was “an early lesson in assimilation,” Alvarez said.

While the works on view may all seem disparate, Alvarez said what connects the art and the artists together is “a deep sense of care for community, for heritage, for one another, lifting one another up.”

That sense of community informs the exhibition title, which borrows its name from Juan Felipe Herrera’s 2008 poem “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way.” Alvarez came across it early in her research for the show and felt a strong connection to it because of its fluid use of Spanglish. “I’ve always read poetry because I don’t understand it. I’m the kind of person who’s like, I’m going to bang my head against the wall because I want to understand why I don’t understand it. But for the first time, reading a poem in Spanglish, it felt like, oh, somehow, I understand this.”

In the poem, Herrera describes people coming together with “pearls / of corn flowing árboles de vida en las cuatro esquinas” where we are “contentos llenos de fuerza to vida / giving nacimientos to fragrant ríos / dulces frescos verdes turquoise…” Alvarez printed out his words and hung them up, contemplating them for months. “I started to understand the poem as a celebration of abundance, as this invitation to gather together,” she said. “As I was trying to figure out the title of the exhibition, I realized that was exactly what I was doing: inviting these artists to be present in their fullest expression in the galleries.”

To mark the exhibition’s realization, the Buffalo AKG commissioned Herrera to write a poem, “So Many Years We Dreamed the Colors / Tantos años soñamos los colores” (2024), that directly responded to the checklist. Printed on the walls of the exhibition and reproduced in the accompanying catalog, it reads, in part, “so many years we dreamt / the colors the shapes the gathering / … / so we stand on this wall you can see us / you can study our language & thought / never studied you can taste our colors / never loved…”

The exhibition also features three commissioned artworks by Zapata, rafa esparza, and Justin Favela. Zapata has made three textile-covered columns, two of which hang from the ceiling, while the third leans against a wall. esparza contributed Tratos: Después de Pedro Valtierra Entre Redadas (2025–26), an adobe painting inspired by Valtierra’s 1998 photograph taken after the Acteal Massacre of the Indigenous group “Las Abejas” (The Bees), in Chiapas, Mexico. Supported by a steel armature, the work encourages visitors to walk on the adobe path behind it, where a coiled US flag is embedded. Into the work, esparza’s has also added a scene from the Florentine Codex showing a Spaniard whipping an Indigenous person and images of ICE raids in LA and Chicago, connecting centuries of oppression together.

Favela’s contribution is St. Maarten (1972), After Marisol, installed on a large wall that faces a window overlooking the museum’s front lawn. The piece’s subject is difficult to see from the gallery, but when viewed from outside, its reference to a watercolor by Marisol in Buffalo AKG’s collection becomes clear.

St. Maarten is part of Favela’s “piñata murals” series, which he began in protest after being asked by an art school professor to “make something about being Mexican.” His fellow white classmates hadn’t been asked about that, but he took it as a challenge. He responded by making a piñata, “a symbol that represented Latinidad that I thought would be so corny, so cheesy, that they’d say, ‘Oh, he’s making fun of our request,’” as he recalled. His teachers loved it, though he suspects his critique went over their heads—and so did he, finding it a fertile artmaking mode for the past 20 years. When the exhibition travels to the Des Moines Art Center next month, Favela will make a new piñata mural based on a work in that institution’s collection.

I imagine “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way” will linger long after it comes down in Buffalo. Since 2022, the museum has been acquiring works for its permanent collection in anticipation of the show, beginning with Patrick Martinez’s Promised Land (2022), followed soon after by works by Guadalupe Maravilla, Ilana Savdie, and Eamon Ore-Giron. Since the exhibition opened in March, the museum has also added pieces by Felipe Baeza, Yvette Mayorga, and Salomón Huerta, as well as Alfonso Gonzalez Jr.’s towering Abogados Tierra Caliente (Billboard)—and it hopes to acquire even more in the coming months.

An exhibition like “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way,” with its layered and nuanced approach to discussing both painting and Latinx identity, was urgently needed even at the time of its conception five years ago. Given today’s political climate, one that’s only grows more fraught, its message will likely be just as necessary five years from now.

To that end, Alvarez hopes that “Let Us Gather in a Flourishing Way” is just the beginning for exhibitions of this kind. “This is just the tip of the iceberg,” she said. “By design, the project gives people a peek into the discipline, and it’s an invitation to want to learn more. This exhibition is not a comprehensive survey—I am resisting the word ‘survey’ because that comes with the connotation that it’s a complete story.”

item.title: Trump to Break Ground on “Triumphal Arch” Before Federal Approval - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Excavation efforts are set to begin within the next two weeks for President Donald Trump’s controversial “Great Triumphal Arch,” according to a statement Interior Secretary Doug Burgum posted on X on Thursday, September 3. The announcement was made before the project has even received the green light from a federal review panel.

The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), which evaluates design proposals throughout Washington, DC, preliminarily approved Trump's project on July 9, but issued several comments the president must address before earning the committee's final approval. The NCPC's primary concern is the height of the 250-foot-tall structure, which could violate the 130-foot cap imposed by the 1910 Height of Buildings Act and obstruct the sightlines of dozens of historical landmarks.

"This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World," Burgum added in his post on Thursday, a month before the NCPC's next scheduled review on October 1.

Sitting on the highly trafficked Memorial Circle near Arlington National Cemetery, the white granite-clad arch will include a “Military Observation Deck” and be topped by two statues of gold eagles and one of a golden winged figure. While the project has been presented as a celebratory marker of the country's 250th anniversary, Trump has also dedicated the monument, which many have deemed the “Arc de Trump,” to himself.

item.title: LA’s Lucas Museum Displays “Narrative Art” for the Few, Not the People - Hyperallergic
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — After nearly two decades of planning and construction, a spate of layoffs, and staffing controversies, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art will open its doors to the public later this month in South Los Angeles’s Exposition Park. This week, members of the press were invited to tour the new institution and get a taste of the random and facile smorgasbord of art that awaits visitors. 

Founded by filmmaker George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson, co-CEO of Ariel Investments, the reportedly $1 billion building designed by Ma Yansong/MAD Architects houses their collection of 40,000 works representing what they call “visual storytelling.” These include illustrations, history paintings, comic art, films, murals, and other genres that “have not always received the respect they deserve,” as press materials explain. The five-story, undulating, spaceship-like structure sits on an 11-acre campus of rolling green hills designed by Mia Lehrer of Los Angeles’s Studio-MLA, who also designed the building’s green roof.

“For thousands of years, that was the only way you could tell a story, with pictures,” Lucas said during a press preview on Wednesday, September 2 (seemingly disregarding traditions of oral histories or song). “Pictures and stories are very powerful. Put them together, and those two elements make a society.” 

“Narrative Art creates groups of people with common belief systems, which allows them to work together and not kill each other,” he continued, as if to finally resolve the question of what Narrative Art is, exactly, a query that has surrounded the museum for years.

Ironically, there is very little narrative at all in the Museum of Narrative Art, at least curatorially. The collection is spread throughout 100,000 square feet of gallery space, divided into 30 or so thematic galleries — Adventure, Romance, Motherhood, Civic Life, Science Fiction, Comics, Sports, and others — with a few dedicated to individuals such as famed fantasy artist Frank Frazetta, American regionalist Thomas Hart Benton, and Norman Rockwell, whose specific brand of folksy Americana can be felt throughout. Artworks are displayed free of context or even any wall text aside from shiny, metal letters announcing each section. The thematic arrangement mashes together artworks of different styles and eras, linked by the flimsiest of threads, as if to say “Look, we’re all the same: we play sports, we work, we raise children!”, with little interest in exploring the specific cultural or social conditions from which they emerged.

item.title: Ann Patchett and Crying at The Met - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Ever shed a tear in a museum? You’re not alone, my friend. There’s something cathartic about that rare moment, when you find yourself in front of a work of art that seems tailor-made for the very grief or joy or uncertainty you’re experiencing. Critic Lavinia Liang tries to locate this emotional connection with art — or a lack thereof — in Ann Patchett’s new novel, Whistler, which follows a single family’s unraveling and reunion bookended by the halls of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

Our reports on ICE’s seizure of 22,000 smuggled artifacts in Florida, coverage of the Chinese Pavilion’s withdrawal from the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea in protest of the Taiwan Pavilion, guide to Upstate New York art shows this month, and more in this edition.

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

item.title: Landskrona Foto FestivalForegrounds Powerful Imagery - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
“Displacement” has become a defining word of our times. According to the UN Refugee Agency, at the end of 2025, at least 117.8 million people were forced from their homes. That’s 1 in every 70 people on Earth. These figures are difficult to comprehend, but they represent individual experiences of conflict, human rights violations, persecution and violence. It is against this backdrop that the 10th edition of Landskrona Foto Festival emerges. Displacement is its overarching theme, bringing together artists from different parts of the world to approach these issues from multiple perspectives. This September, several exhibitions will unfold across the Swedish town, occupying public spaces, institutions and historically significant sites such as Landskrona Citadel, a former fortress marked by histories of refuge and confinement.

One of the most direct explorations of this theme comes from Dialect by Felipe Romero Beltrán (b. 1992). The Colombian artist, based in Paris, produces long-term projects rooted in social issues. This exhibition is no exception, documenting the daily lives of a group of young Moroccan men who have made a perilous journey across the Strait of Gibraltar into Spain. Romero Beltrán followed their experiences in Seville for three years, whilst their legal situation was reviewed. In these images, they find themselves in a state of limbo and uncertainty, waiting to obtain citizenship whilst estranged from their home country. Their real-life stories form a dialogue with Agnès Geoffray and Vanessa Desclaux’s They Stray, They Persist, They Thunder, in which fictional female figures confront or escape oppressive structures and institutions.

Conflict is one of the main reasons why people flee their homes. On February 24, 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. At the end of the year, Time named President Volodymyr Zelensky its “Person of the Year.” His portrait was taken by Alexander Chekmenev. Landskrona Foto Festival presents fourteen more images by Chekmenev, this time showing everyday people living and working in Ukraine: farmers, business owners, teachers, doctors. Each is accompanied by a comment: “We kept a diary. We wrote on the walls how many days we survived and how many people died.” Elsewhere, the video installation Repeat After Me (2022), by Yuriy Biley, Pavlo Kovach and Anton Varga, introduces refugees from the east of the country who, fleeing the threat of war, found shelter in a temporary camp in Lviv. They share their experience of the sounds of conflict, reproducing the noises made by various weapons. There is also a poignant contribution from Palestinian artist Taysir Batniji, who presents Just in Case #2 (2024): images of keys belonging to Gaza residents who have been displaced amid ongoing Israeli bombardments.

Ecological precarity is another primary driver of forced migration. The festival examines humanity’s fragile relationship with nature via several shows, including Zed Nelson’s celebrated The Anthropocene Illusion. This uncanny body of work examines how we immerse ourselves in increasingly choreographed and simulated environments – zoos, theme parks, safaris, alpine resorts and national parks – to mask our devastating impact on the land. Beauty and discomfort likewise collide in the work of Mandy Barker, an artist known for her mesmerisingly choreographed images of plastic waste. Still (FFS) takes that inquiry in a new, devastating direction. It transports viewers to Lord Howe Island, a remote location between Australia and New Zealand that is home to one of the largest colonies of Flesh-Footed Shearwater seabirds. They often mistake plastic for food and end up feeding waste to their fledgling chicks. Barker joined scientists on the Island in April 2019 to record the chicks’ migration to the Sea of Japan. Instead, the birds were found dying on the shoreline, unable to fly due to the weight of plastic in their stomachs. The photographs contrast the suffering birds with the stunning landscape, causing viewers to double take.

Crisis and instability are major throughlines of Landskrona Foto Festival, and this is communicated – with dark humour – in Alastair Philip Wiper’s (b. 1980) Cold Comfort. Here, the Hamburg-born photographer explores the “absurd theatre” of the atomic age: secret weapons labs, fallout shelters for politicians and comic books. One image reads: “it is 85 seconds to midnight”, in reference to The Doomsday Clock – which currently stands at the closest to global catastrophe it has ever been. “Set in 1947 by the Bulletin of Atomic Scientists, it has been updated every year since,” Wiper explains. “Back then it read seven minutes to midnight, when nuclear war was the main threat. In 1953, after the US and USSR tested hydrogen bombs, it moved to two minutes. In 1991, with the end of the Cold War, it stretched back to 17 minutes – the safest point ever. Since the 2000s, the clock has also counted climate change and, more recently, AI among the risks pushing the hands forward. Which brings us to now: closer to the end than at any time in history.”

Across these projects, and the many more that form the programme (there are further contributions from Alan Gignoux & Chloe Juno; Ana Núñez Rodríguez; Bharat Sikka; Debi Cornwall; Emil Heilborn; Fernando Montiel Klint; Gábor Arion Kudász; Inka & Niclas; and Lena Amuat & Zoë Meyer), displacement emerges as a condition shaped by conflict, political uncertainty and environmental destruction. From young men waiting for their futures to be determined, to communities living through war and ecosystems transformed by human intervention, the festival asks viewers to consider what it means to lose a sense of security, belonging or place. In doing so, Landskrona Foto Festival turns an overwhelming global statistic into something more intimate: a collection of individual stories that make the scale of the present visible.

Landskrona Foto Festival runs 4-20 September.

item.title: ICE Seizes 22,000 Antiquities in Florida - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) seized over 22,000 ancient artifacts in Florida last month, including Greco-Roman coins, terracotta and glass vessels, jewelry, and mosaic frames, yielding the largest object recovery in the department's ongoing probe into antiquities smuggling in the state.

Dated between 1,000 and 5,000 years old, the objects are said to have originated from sites across Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, Africa, and the Levant. The Tampa Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit partnered with archaeological specialists and researchers at the University of South Florida and the University of Pennsylvania to authenticate, contextualize, and conserve the objects yielded during the seizure.

ICE and its parent entity, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), continue to wage a campaign of brutality against immigrants in the United States that has also had consequences for the country's cultural heritage.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), under which ICE and HSI operate, came under fire this April after the Customs and Border Protection crew erecting Donald Trump's border wall “inadvertently disturbed” the millennium-old Las Playas Intaglio in Arizona, ultimately damaging a quarter of the Native American archaeological site with heavy machinery.

DHS followed up in July by waiving a majority of environmental, public health, and historical preservation barriers to expedite the construction of border barriers from the Big Bend region to Amistad Reservoir, Texas, threatening over 400 archaeological sites in the area.

item.title: China Withdraws from Gwangju Biennale in Protest of Taiwan’s Inclusion - Hyperallergic
item.description:
China withdrew from South Korea's Gwangju Biennale this morning, September 3, just nine days after event organizers restored the title of "Taiwan Pavilion" to a group show featuring Taiwanese artists. The announcement, which was first reported by the Korea Times, comes two days before the scheduled opening of the 16th edition of the biennale.

Rifts between Taiwan, China, and event organizers surged in mid-August after the biennale axed the name of “Taiwan Pavilion" in their promotional materials and replaced it with the English acronym for the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts, “NTMoFA.” Organizers initially refused the name reversal demanded by Taiwan's Ministry of Culture and participating artists, who condemned the change as political censorship, but later reversed their decision on August 25.

Responding to the name reinstatement, Chinese curator Ruan Yuelai announced the China Pavilion’s unanimous withdrawal during a Thursday morning press conference. 

“The Gwangju Biennale’s use of an incorrect name concerning the participation of the China and Taiwan regions has brought about a situation in which political factors intervene in the domain of art," Ruan said during the press conference.

item.title: 40 Filmmakers in 25 Countries Team Up for an Ode to Nature Shot Entirely on Super 8 Cameras - Colossal
item.description:
Before the iPhone essentially turned all of us into documentarians, the Super 8 camera offered a more democratic approach to filmmaking. Kodak introduced the analog format in 1965 with an eye toward amateurs and hobbyists interested in capturing the world around them, and today it remains a stalwart of the discipline, particularly for those drawn to the grainy, nostalgic qualities of shooting on film.

Ed Sayers, director and founder of the annual Super 8 competition and community called straight 8, tapped into the camera’s equalizing legacy for his latest project. Bringing together 40 collaborators in 25 countries across five continents, Super Nature is a collective ode to our planet. Rather than travel the world capturing the sights and sounds of far-flung locales, Sayers subverts the traditional documentarian approach by stitching together stories of people and creatures directly from their homes.

Participants include lauded photographers Gideon Mendel and Ami Vitale, who also founded Vital Impacts, alongside communities like the Enawene Nawe tribe in Brazil. Sayers invited several filmmakers from straight 8, and Greenpeace introduced his team to folks in the organization’s network, too. “I wanted them to feel very free. I made sure they were tuned into the spirit of what the film was trying to achieve, putting precious intimate moments and thoughts on a pedestal,” he tells Colossal. “Many had never used Super 8 before so we sent them cameras and taught them how to use them on video calls.”

Because the prompt had few guardrails, the difficulty came in making the final film appear cohesive and intentional. This meant finding where disparate segments fit together and which might offer an interesting and suitable segue to the next. “It was important that as an ensemble the stories came across as more than the sum of their parts,” Sayers says. “In the end, you’re watching one immersive story made and voiced by a chorus of people whom you meet and see in the film, captured on Super 8 just like all the animals and environments in the whole film.”

Alongside cinematic shots underwater, in air, and on land, Sayers also asked for glimpses of the filmmakers themselves, alongside narration that situates each frame into a larger portrait. He attributes the intimacy of Super Nature to this impulse as it showcases a sense of vulnerability and connection both in front of and behind the camera. Eleven languages and dozens of accents appear throughout, emphasizing the rootedness of each filmmaker.

In an age of AI and frictionless digital technologies, analog approaches to creation are ever more radical. Part of what continues to draw Sayers to film is that it requires more planning, intention, and an innate sense of when it’s time to act. “With Super 8 film, the roll only lasts a couple of minutes before it runs out, and there’s a cost to it. So suddenly you’re studying your subject and waiting for what you think it is a great moment, with the right light, before pulling the trigger,” he says. “Looking at your subject—be it a grasshopper or a glacier—with the eye or through an old camera with vintage glass is very different to whipping out your iPhone and taking 20 shots.”

This sentiment echoes the trailer’s opening line from one of the filmmakers, too: “It’s like it resets something in your brain. You feel part of things again.”

Released by BFI Distribution, Super Nature is screening in the U.K. and Ireland this month, with several London showtimes. Find one in your area on the film’s website.

item.title: 75,000 Patterned Paper Kites Cascade in Jacob Hashimoto’s Largest-Ever Installation - Colossal
item.description:
Created from bamboo and printed Japanese paper, Jacob Hashimoto’s elaborate installations cascade from the ceiling to create a vibrant “cloud canopy.” In his latest exhibition titled Giant Arc, ripples of color and pattern stretch from wall to wall as the nearly 75,000 kite-like elements cluster, repeat, and tease the floor. The monumental work, which just went on view at SFMOMA, marks the largest piece the artist has created to date.

As sun streams through the museum’s large windows and mixes with the light of the gallery, the feel of the installation changes throughout the day. Hashimoto conceives of the experience as a conduit to wonder for visitors of all ages, focusing on formal compositional elements like contrast, hue, and repetition to evoke the joy of the present.

“The gravity of Giant Arc is its universality,” Hashimoto says in a statement. “This essential nature allows people to find what they might need in the work—mysteries if people want them, stories if people desire them, narratives to spin and twist, experimental maps and aerial geographies to explore.”

Giant Arc will be on view through mid-2028 in the museum’s ground floor gallery. Find more on the Hashimoto’s Instagram, and revisit our interview with the artist from 2022.

item.title: Trump Somehow Mad at Stick Figure - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Trump’s National Park Service nonsensically removed a bright-blue Joel Shapiro sculpture from outside the Kennedy Center yesterday without stating a reason. The late artist is known for his quasi-abstract, dynamic stick-figure artworks that could not offend your most politically questionable uncle, but our president will find a way. Was it too happy? Too person-shaped? Or even better … “woke”?

Teju Adisa-Farrar’s must-read piece on Black American natural dyeing traditions is an antidote to cultural erasure. In the latest of our series on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows in collaboration with the Center for Craft, Adisa-Farrar traces the ways in which plants and organic fibers yielded a kaleidoscope of pigments whose histories are worthy of preservation and revival.

The Missing Colors of Black American Pigment-Making

As one of humanity’s oldest crafts, natural pigment-making occupies the intersection of science, agriculture, and art. It requires curiosity and ingenuity to see a marigold flower, for instance, and know that it can stain fabrics with beautiful shades of mustard yellow to gold; to know, as our ancestors did, that they also have anti-microbial and anti-inflammatory properties. The blue color of denim traces its roots to indigo, a dye crop cultivated and processed by West Africans and their descendants throughout the Atlantic world. The global indigo trade that made blue textiles possible was deeply intertwined with enslaved labor and African dyeing knowledge. | Teju Adisa-Farrar

item.title: Venice Biennale President Defends Russia Inclusion in New Interview - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In an exclusive interview with the Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera, Venice Biennale Foundation President Pietrangelo Buttafuoco stood by the decision to include Russia in the 61st Venice Biennale this year despite pushback from the Italian Culture Ministry and the European Commission.

The Venice Biennale Foundation faced immense criticism, calls for boycotts, and a widely circulated open letter demanding revision after it announced this March that Russia would return to its pavilion for the 61st edition amid the ongoing invasion of Ukraine, stating that the Biennale administration “rejects any form of exclusion or censorship of culture and art.”

Buttafuoco told Corriere della Sera that he would do “everything” again if he had to, adding that his handling of the pavilion was “more than fair and proper to the institution [he] preside[s] over” and that there was “not a single comma that violates laws and regulations.”

Italian Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli had asked the Venice Biennale Foundation to provide all correspondence with the Russian Federation to evaluate the pavilion installation's compatibility with the European Union's sanctions regime. The European Commission also condemned Russia's inclusion, threatening to freeze its €2 million (~$2.3 million) culture grant to the Foundation over the matter.

In April, the Biennale's award jury announced its intention to omit Russia and Israel from consideration for the Golden Lion awards, and Giuli publicized his intent to forgo the Biennale's preview dates over Russia's inclusion. Ahead of the Biennale's opening, it was revealed that Buttafuoco and the Foundation's administrators worked with the Russian pavilion curator as early as June 2025 to ensure that Russia's participation played by the rules. Ultimately, the pavilion would remain closed to the public for the Biennale's run after the vernissage dates.

item.title: Avian Beauties and Rarities Top the 2026 Audubon Photography Awards - Colossal
item.description:
Major expeditions, numerous attempts, and strokes of luck characterize how many of the top images in the 2026 Audubon Photography Awards came to be. Francisco Castro Escobar, for example, was surprised to see a rare lesser horned owl, sometimes referred to as “the ghost of the desert,” perched on a cactus in northern Chile during a dawn hike. “The largest owl in Chile gets this nickname because seeing one is so rare that it’s like an apparition,” Escobar says. The image also took the grand prize for the Chile/Colombia contest.

Audubon Photography Awards runs two parallel opportunities, one for photographers in the U.S. and Canada and the other for those based in Chile and Colombia. This year, the grand prize for North American entrants went to Jacqueline Burke for her bold capture of a bathing roseate spoonbill illuminated against the shadowed interior of a cove in Florida. Additional prize categories include Birds Without Borders, Plants for Birds, Youth, Conservation, and others.

The array of images capture the daily behaviors and habits of birds around the world, from hunting raptors to nectar-seeking woodpeckers. In addition to dramatic, sometimes humorous shots of avians in flight, eating, swimming, and more, we also discover some of the ways human activities put the animals at risk. Josh Galicki’s photo of nesting northern gannets in Shetland reveal how jettisoned old fishing nets have been scavenged for nests on a cliff face, but the same material poses a constant risk to the animals’ safety.

Across the board, the winning photographs illuminate the world’s immense avian diversity, from diminutive, jewel-like hummingbirds to seabirds that dive like torpedos to catch their prey. “Hours, days, or sometimes even years of patience and effort go into creating a scenario in which a photographer is in the right place, at the right time, to capture a fleeting moment,” Audubon says.

See all the winners and honorable mentions, including videos, on the contest’s website.

item.title: Serpentine’s Inaugural Fellowship Bridges the Gap Between Art and AI - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Serpentine’s artistic director Hans Ulrich Obrist called 2024 the “Year of AI” in an interview with ARTnews. Now, the gallery is diving further into technology by launching the Future Art Ecosystems R&D Fellowship.

The program picked four international applicants out of nearly 1,000 for a six-month fellowship commencing this month in London along with a cash prize of £10,000 ($13,480) each. The chosen applicants are artists Alice Bucknell from the United States, Alfredo Salazar-Caro from Mexico, and Auriea Harvey from Italy, as well as designer and researcher Reina Mun from the US. The four applicants will attend online sessions, tailored mentorship through specialist seminars and workshops, and in-person intensives in London. 

The program has been in the making since 2019 and operates on a three year partnership with the London arts charity Glass Castle Foundation. The deal with the Serpentine also includes a major commission each year.

Bettina Korek, CEO of the Serpentine, said in a statement that the fellowship will build “connective tissue between art and emerging technology, so they develop together rather than in sequence.”

Korek was part of the jury, alongside artists Refik Anadol, Cao Fei, and Holly Herndon; Google Deepmind chief AI readiness officer Lila Ibrahim; author and economist Mariana Mazzucato; writer and consultant Venkatesh Rao; chair of Glass Castle Foundation Suneil Setiya; and cofounder and CEO of Snap Inc Evan Spiegel.

Setiya, a UK billionaire that cofounded the hedge fund Quadrature Capital, described the fellowship cohort as a reminder that “artistic inquiry is not a purely speculative pursuit, but a vital tool for building public agency and keeping us anchored in our values.”

Ibrahim added, “By confronting the human dimensions of advanced systems, these artists are helping lay the bedrock for a technological future we can all be proud of.”

item.title: Two Artists' Odyssey Up the Erie Canal - Hyperallergic
item.description:
There’s wonder everywhere you look — especially the places you overlook. Maybe, in the apartment next door, there’s a library of 3,000 zines, as in Michelle Millette’s Sherwood Forest Zine Library in Austin, Texas. Perhaps, that canal that cuts through your town is the site of an upstream odyssey, as it is for Z Behl and Kim Moloney, who are spending six hours a day paddling up 350 miles of the Erie Canal. 

Speaking of overlooked wonder, let me introduce you to our Craft Archive Fellowship! In partnership with the Center for Craft, we offer $5,000 awards to support research on underrepresented craft histories around the United States, and publish fellows’ scholarship afterward.

Today, I’m proud to present the first piece in our series. Bilphena Decontee Yahwon’s passion, care, and personal stake in exploring the shared origins of Liberian basket weaving and Gullah sweetgrass basketry came through so clearly in our conversations. “I could hear Liberia in the way people spoke,” she writes of her first visit to St. Helena Island, off the South Carolina coast, five years ago. Here, she teases out how fannuh baskets serve as both cultural tool and cultural memory across continents.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

How Fannuh Baskets Connect Liberia to the US Lowcountry

I first visited St. Helena Island off the South Carolina coast in 2021. Like Louisiana, it was one of the few places I had traveled in the United States where I could hear Liberia in the way people spoke. I do not know how to fully explain it. It was in the rhythm of Gullah speech, what my mother would call “sing-songy.” It was in the syntax and cadence. As my mother would say, “my ears could hear it.”

It was also on St. Helena Island, at the historic Penn Center, where I first saw an image of two women fanning rice. I immediately thought of so many women I had seen in Liberia, standing over harvested grain with woven baskets in hand, separating rice from chaff through sweeping motions. Woven from local grasses, palmetto, and other plant materials found across the Sea Islands off the coast of the Southeastern US, these baskets have become one of the defining craft traditions of Gullah Geechee culture in the Lowcountry, a region along South Carolina’s coast. To me, they felt like something I already knew. | Bilphena Decontee Yahwon

item.title: Anthony McCall Pushes theBoundaries of Cinema and Sculpture - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
In 1973, Anthony McCall (b. 1946) broke new artistic ground with Line Describing a Cone, an installation in which a single projected line of light slowly traced the outline of a circle within a haze-filled room. Gradually, over the course of 30 minutes, it formed a luminous cone. The piece was revolutionary for several reasons, most of all because it transformed light into sculpture. It was a new blueprint for what a three-dimensional artwork could look like, and went on to inspire other landmark ideas, like Gordon Matta-Clark’s Conical Intersect (1975), which made circular “cuts” into two derelict Paris buildings.

McCall emerged from the avant-garde film communities of London and New York during the late 1960s and early 1970s. He rejected the conventions of narrative cinema in favour of an investigation into the essential properties of the moving-image: light and space. It was from this that his seminal “solid light” installations were born. He concluded: “If you want to make a film that’s really a film, and not anything else, you need to discard the image.” Line Describing a Cone was the first iteration of this idea. Rather than watching a projected scene on a screen, viewers entered the beam of light itself – walking through, around and inside something that appeared to simultaneously exist and not exist. The piece was initially shown in lofts across New York City, where it sliced through the dust and cigarette smoke circulating in the air.

Towards the end of the 1970s, McCall began a 20-year hiatus, stepping away from art-making to focus on graphic design. He returned at the turn of the millennium to a landscape transformed. Technological advancements since the 1990s – including the advent of digital projectors, the commercialisation of haze machines and the development of computer scripts and animation software – now offered different ways of manipulating light and space. These technologies have since enabled McCall to craft increasingly complex pieces, yet his practice remains rooted in the same fundamentals as always: perception, time and the relationship between the body and its surroundings. Today, McCall is widely regarded as one of the most influential names in his field. He has been the subject of major solo exhibitions at leading institutions worldwide, including recent retrospectives at Tate Modern, London, and Guggenheim Bilbao.

Line Describing a Cone is considered one of the defining examples of 20th century installation art. Now, it is at the heart of Sean Kelly Gallery’s latest exhibition, Solid Light, 1973, 2020, 2026, which brings together three key works spanning 50 years. Audiences will discover Skylight (2020), in which a signature illuminated cone materialises onto a plinth that can be experienced from every angle. It is accompanied by an original score by acclaimed composer David Grubbs, evoking a rumbling thunderstorm with flashes of lightning and steady falling rain. The third piece on view is Swarm (2026), McCall’s most recent offering. It responds to the increased presence of drones in daily life and is composed of two light volumes that rotate in opposite directions over fifteen minutes. Grubbs returns with a soundscape that intensifies over time.

In today’s increasingly digital landscape, where installations are shared online and go viral in an instant, Solid Light, 1973, 2020, 2026 does something special: it presents three works that can only be fully experienced in person. By combining visuals, audio and duration, McCall encourages audiences to participate fully, with all the senses. Moreover, the exhibition traces the artist’s journey from his breakthrough to the present day, highlighting how he has continually pushed the boundaries of his craft, embracing change whilst remaining true to a singular vision where cinema, sculpture and drawing overlap.

Anthony McCall: Solid Light, 1973, 2020, 2026

Sean Kelly, New York, from 11 September – 31 October.

skny.com

Words: Eleanor Sutherland
