item.title: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham Reverses Call for British Museum to Return Parthenon Marbles - ARTnews.com
item.description:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office in July, has reversed his previous calls for the British Museum in London to return the Parthenon marbles to Greece, the Financial Times reports.

Burnham had as early as 2002 said he supported the Parthenon marbles’ return to Greece, reupping that statement as recently as 2023. At the time, he added that their return should be “no strings attached.”

However, when asked by the FT in an interview last month about his current stance on the subject, Burnham told the paper, “Ultimately it’s an issue for the British Museum, isn’t it? Legally that’s where that issue rests, but I’m all in favour of using British cultural diplomacy. That’s something that I’m hugely in favour of.” 

The Parthenon marbles date to the 5th century BCE and were originally created for the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. During the first decade of the 19th century, Lord Elgin, who was then British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, received a permit from the empire, which had control over Athens for 350 years, to remove half of the remaining marbles from the Parthenon.

He then transported them to the UK, where they were subsequently acquired by the British Museum. Elgin’s “actions were thoroughly investigated by a Parliamentary Select Committee in 1816 and found to be entirely legal,” according to the British Museum. Because of his involvement, the collection, which includes 15 metopes, 17 pedimental figures, and 247 feet of the original frieze, has colloquially been called the Elgin Marbles.

The Greek government first made a formal request for the Parthenon marbles to be restituted in 1983. The Acropolis Museum, which houses the Parthenon marbles that remain in Greece, opened to the public in 2009. If the British Museum’s collection of the Parthenon marbles were to be returned, they would also go to the Acropolis Museum.

The British Museum has consistently denied Greece’s requests. In a previous statement, the museum has said, “The Trustees firmly believe that there’s a positive advantage and public benefit in having the sculptures divided between two great museums, each telling a complementary but different story.”

item.title: In the Face of European Colonization, Aboriginal Artists Created Images of Powerful Beings, Study Finds - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In the face of European colonization, Aboriginal artists created images of powerful ancestral beings, a new study has found. The results of the eight-year study, led by Paul Taçon, an archaeologist at Griffith University, were published online by the journal Australian Archaeology August 14.

Awunbarna is a landmark located in the northwestern region of Arnhem Land in Australia’s Northern Territory. The area, which is owned by the Aboriginal Amurdak people, is renowned for its Aboriginal rock paintings, some as many as 18,000 years old.

Also known as Mount Borradaile, Awunbarna is particularly known for its rock art produced in the 1800s and early 1900s, which is characterized not only by traditional images of local fauna, but by the introduction of new subject matter, including painted hands and depictions of European ships and firearms.

It is also notable for its numerous very large paintings of humans, animals, and ancestral entities, including Rainbow Serpents, likewise produced after the arrival of Europeans to the region. While extra-large paintings were made at various times in western Arnhem Land, the number of oversized figures increased during the contact period, both in Awunbarna and throughout the region.

To address the question of why huge paintings became common post-contact, Taçon and his colleagues worked with senior Amurdak traditional owner Charlie Mungulda to record rock art at 165 sites across the Awunbarna region. They concluded that the increased production of such paintings was a way of reasserting ownership of Aboriginal lands and culture, then under threat by colonization.

The team focused on images of Rainbow Serpents, including one 20 feet long with a fierce crocodile head, a long tongue, and razor-sharp teeth. They also reviewed a depiction of a giant man, and the only known rock art image in Australia of a whale. In addition to paintings of Rainbow Serpents, they additionally recorded a large, serpent-shaped stone arrangement measuring 125 feet in length.

While dating the large paintings is difficult, the researchers found that a number of images of Rainbow Serpents were rendered on top of older paintings in white pipe clay (kaolin). White clay paintings do not last long, usually eroding within a few hundred years and sometimes within a few decades, leading the team to conclude they were made post-contact.

Rainbow Serpents are ancestral beings believed to have the power to fold time and are associated with change. Learning to accept, cope with, and perhaps control change is one of the lessons taught by Aboriginal Rainbow Serpent stories.

Large paintings of these creatures and other entities, the authors of the study write, were a visually compelling way to make “authoritative declarations about the importance of maintaining Aboriginal tradition in the face of cultural change.”

item.title: An Unprecedented Look at Renowned Photographer Peter Hujar’s New York in “Hujar:Contact” - Hyperallergic
item.description:
“Hujar:Contact” offers a deep examination of the life, times, and creative evolution of  master photographer Peter Hujar. The exhibition features more than 110 contact sheets and 20 enlargements from the Morgan Library and Museum’s collection, which includes over 5,700 contact sheets from throughout the artist’s career.

Peter Hujar (1934–1987) began filing contact sheets and assigning them job numbers at age 21. His records make it possible to track his development — from two decades as a studio assistant (1955–67) when he pushed himself to try work of every kind, into the late 1960s and his work as a freelancer in fashion, music, and advertising, and finally through his mature period (1974–87) as a fiercely independent and influential artist in the East Village.

Many of the contact sheets bear editing marks that indicate ideas about cropping and printing and contextualize the exposures Hujar ultimately decided to enlarge. The intense, interactive quality of his portrait work comes to life in contact sheets that read as intimate pictorial narratives, revealing the nature of his attention and the unique personality of each of his subjects. As Hujar matures and struggles, and as the character of his social world changes from the 1950s through the 1960s, 1970s, and 1980s, his contact sheets tell the nuanced story of a lifetime, a community, and an era.

To learn more, visit themorgan.org.

item.title: The Artists Paddling 350 Miles Up the Erie Canal - Hyperallergic
item.description:
WATERFORD, NY — The scene in Waterford, Upstate New York, in early August: A group of kind elders sing with gusto under wilted American flags. Excited supporters hover over artist duo Z Behl and Kim Moloney — together, called “BALONEY STEEL” — as they prepare to embark on what they call the “Mule’s Passage,” and paddle 350 miles (~563 km) to Buffalo. 

After brief speeches and an emotional spoken-word piece by playwright Judy Tate, founder of the American Slavery Project, Behl and Maloney boarded their canoe at the end of the dock at the Eastern Gate corridor, the first in a series of locks that lift vessels from the Hudson and Mohawk Rivers into the canal system. The singers walked to the bridge above and were still belting their hearts out as the duo glided underneath — and thus began their journey against the current under a blazing summer sun. 

An artistic-cum-anthropological exploration of the Erie Canal, “Mule’s Passage” is a creative reimagining of the woman’s body as both an engine of industry and a narrator of history. With their canoe decorated like a mule, they honor the invisible labor that powered the early towpath canal that transformed the United States and the global economy as we know it. “Mule’s Passage” involves six hours of daily paddling and five weeks of camping for the duo, ending this Friday, September 5, when they are to land in Buffalo after traversing each of the counties along the waterway, also home to six territories of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

While retracing the old towpaths in a living study of work and folklore, “Mule’s Passage” also highlights the Erie Canal as a mechanism of Indigenous displacement: the development of the waterway carved through Native American lands, wrecking stewardship protocols and breaking contracts with Indigenous populations. The artists' expedition is punctuated by interviews with ecologists, historians, activists, and residents along the canal to foster conversations about the ecological impact of the manmade waterway. 

The project is supported by the Erie Canal Museum Artist-in-Residence (AIR) program and the New York State Canal Corporation, plus other sponsors including Bixpy (who supplied the electric outboard solar-charging motor for the canoe) and Camp Chow (who donated homemade dehydrated meals). The AIR program offers artists an opportunity to engage creatively with the iconic waterway “by blending art with storytelling to illuminate its cultural, environmental, and historical significance,” as its website puts it. Other project partners for the paddle include the Everson Museum of Art in Syracuse, which will host an exhibition of the “Mule’s Passage” documentation in spring 2027.

item.title: Art Gallery of Ontario Director Stephan Jost to Depart After a Decade - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Stephan Jost, the director and CEO of the Art Gallery of Ontario, will leave his posts at the end of the year, the Toronto museum announced on Tuesday.

Within the Canadian art scene, Jost’s leadership has been polarizing. He has drawn praise for making a significant investment in modern and contemporary art at the AGO, which acquired a range of important artworks in that area, including 450 works by Diane Arbus, 200 works by Peter Hujar, and 227 works by Hiroshi Sugimoto. In 2027, the museum will open a new gallery for modern and contemporary art that spans 40,000 square feet and five floors.

But Jost’s tenure was also marred by controversy over the past few years. In 2023, Wanda Nanibush, the museum’s first curator of Indigenous art, departed the museum amid scrutiny over her social media posts in support of Palestine; another curator exited the museum after she left. Earlier this year, a senior curator departed the AGO after reports that the museum had rejected a plan to acquire a work by Nan Goldin because the artist had described Israel’s war in Gaza as a genocide.

In 2024, meanwhile, more than 400 unionized workers at the museum led a strike over low wages that forced the AGO to close for a month.

In a statement, Jost framed his resignation as a response to the completion of a spread of long-term goals. “Over the summer, I reflected on arriving at the AGO 10 years ago and establishing the Strategic Plan we call AGO 2028,” he said in a statement. “I realized that we have met our goals ahead of schedule. Now is the time to set the AGO up for the future with new leadership.”

The museum’s release noted that Jost had expanded access to the AGO by altering its admission policy so that Ontario residents under the age of 25 get in for free. It also stated that Jost had played a role in gaining the museum $500 million in gifts.

“Stephan has transformed the AGO over the past decade,” Beth Horowitz, museum board co-president, said in a statement. “The collection is broader, deeper and more inclusive, the audience is younger and more diverse. His leadership of the Dani Reiss Modern and Contemporary Gallery project—fully funded and on track—is his legacy and will have a lasting impact.”

Prior to joining the AGO in 2016, Jost had been director of the Honolulu Museum of Art in Hawai’i. From 2024 to 2025, he also served as president of the Association of Art Museum Directors, an influential industry group that offers guidance to institutional leadership to museum directors in the US, Canada, and Mexico.

The AGO’s announcement did not detail Jost’s future plans. The museum said it would now begin a search for a new director and CEO.

item.title: ICE Unit Says It Seized 22,000 Ancient Artifacts in Florida - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Homeland Security Investigations unit of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE) said it seized more than 22,000 ancient artifacts in Florida as part of a smuggling inquest that counts “among the largest in the agency’s history,” according to a press release.

“The identification and authentication process for the large number of items will take time,” the release reads, “but preliminary evaluations indicate that some objects may have originated from ancient civilizations dating between 1,000 and 5,000 years ago, from sites across Europe, Africa and the Levant, and the Eastern Mediterranean.”

The seized treasures coming in for further study include coins, ceramic pots and vases, statues, weapons, jewelry, trinkets, and mosaic picture frames. As noted by the ICE unit: “Unlike narcotics, there is no field test for antiquities, so HSI partners with experts at local universities to identify and authenticate objects.”

In a statement, HSI Tampa acting Special Agent in Charge Micah McCombs said, “Preserving cultural heritage is not only a matter of law enforcement, but also a commitment to history and humanity. The trafficking of cultural property not only robs civilizations of their heritage, but also channels money into transnational criminal organizations, results in international financial crimes and, in some cases, even funds terrorist activities.”

HSI Tampa Special Agent Leanna Richardson said, “I never imagined I’d hold an object that may have been created more than 4,000 years ago. It’s like touring a museum with your own personal archaeologist as a tour guide and you get to touch all the pieces.”

The ICE announcement did not include any information as to the particulars of where, when, or how the ancient artifacts were seized.

item.title: Christie’s London Offers a Restituted Kandinsky, Long Displayed in a German Museum, for $30 M. - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A Wassily Kandinsky painting left behind by a Dutch family fleeing the Nazi occupation and later on view for decades in a German museum will come to the auction block at Christie’s London on October 14, during Frieze week. Estimated in excess of $30 million, Das bunte Leben (The Colorful Life, 1907) was restituted to the heirs of Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann in 2023 after a six-year legal battle. 

Measuring just over four feet high and five feet wide, it was Kandinsky’s largest canvas up until that point. In it, he aimed to sum up the richness of life, as other artists had done, for example Henri Matisse with his painting Bonheur de vivre (1905–06) or André Derain with La Danse (1906). Exhibited at the Salon d’Automne in Paris the year it was created, the painting shows a pastoral landscape densely populated by pilgrims, peasants, saints, nobles, and mothers and children, many inspired by Russian legend, folklore, and religious traditions. 

“Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben is much more than an early masterpiece: it captures a moment when different influences were coming together in the artist’s practice, and points towards the radical move into abstraction that would follow,” said Marc Porter, the auction house’s chairman for Americas, in press materials. 

The Russian artist’s auction record was established at Sotheby’s London in 2023, when his Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) fetched £37.2 million (then equivalent to $44.9 million). That painting, too, was stolen by the Nazis, was long on view in a museum, and had recently been restored to the rightful owners. 

Amsterdam sewing machine magnate Emanuel Albert Lewenstein and his wife Hedwig Lewenstein-Weyermann bought The Colorful Life in 1927. The collectors’ children lent it to the Stedelijk Museum for safekeeping before fleeing the Netherlands ahead of the Nazi occupation. The Nazis confiscated the family’s possessions and dispersed them in 1940, after which the work was sold at auction to collector Salomon B. Slijper. It was acquired by the Bavarian State Bank in 1972 and, the next year, placed on long-term loan to the Lenbachhaus in Munich, where it remained for more than five decades. 

Emanuel and Hedwig’s children, Robert and Wilhelmine Lewenstein, worked for decades to locate their parents’ collection. With the help of the Mondex Corporation, which specializes in the recovery of art and other assets looted during World War II, they sued for its return in a Manhattan court in 2017 (the company also does business in New York). When the Mondex Corporation approached the bank in 2016, founder James Palmer told Der Spiegel, “Essentially, they told us to ‘fuck off.’” But an independent German commission recommended in 2023 that the painting be restituted.

“Kandinsky is no longer simply depicting the world around him, but beginning to imagine how painting might communicate something beyond the visible,” said Keith Gill, vice chairman of the 20th- and 21st-century department, in a press release. “Colour assumes an unprecedented expressive intensity, while the figures and landscape become part of a larger vision of human experience.”

item.title: Minnesota State Fair Removes Anti-Trump Crop Art After Artist Was Harassed - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Minnesota State Fair took down a crop artwork containing an anti-Trump slogan at the artist's request this weekend, after she was doxxed, harassed, and threatened by right-wing agitators, as first reported by the Minnesota Star Tribune.

Against a backdrop of black and red beans, the artwork reads “8647” in yellow corn kernels, a sequence often used in protest of President Donald Trump. To "86" something, in the hospitality industry, means to get rid of it, and "47" has been interpreted as referring to Trump's status as the 47th United States President. After conservative news outlet Alpha News zeroed in on the artist's creation across social media, others allegedly targeted, threatened, and shared the private address and details of the artist, per the Tribune.

The artist has not yet replied to a request for comment. Hyperallergic is not reproducing the artwork image out of concern for their privacy.

Ike Whiting, another participating crop artist who is familiar with the incident, told Hyperallergic that the artist reached out to the fair “with regard to her own safety” after experiencing harassment.

"This particular situation goes way too far," Whiting said. "The need people feel to take matters into their own hands is shocking and unacceptable."

item.title: French Court Faults Deauville City for Removing AP Photograph of Gaza from Exhibition - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An administrative court in Caen, France, faulted the Deauville city hall on Monday for removing a photograph taken in Gaza from a local festival, reported AFP and Le Monde.

The image by Associated Press photographer Jehad Alshrafi features a soccer match being played by members of the Palestinian Ahli Gaza Club on a pristine, synthetic green field, surrounded by rubble from Israeli military attacks. But in mid-August, the image was quietly taken down from an outdoor exhibition that is part of this summer’s Deauville Sport Images Festival, which celebrates the “value of sports.”

The ruling effectively suspends the city hall’s prior decision to nix the photograph and follows an emergency motion filed by the Observatoire de la liberté de creation (Observatory for the freedom of creation, or OLC for short), which called for the protection of free speech and demanded the work be rehung. A lawyer representing the OLC told France 3 that the photograph, which first went on view June 6, was selected by a jury for the exhibition, as an artful example of the persistence of sports activity “including in the most terrible of situations.”

In the city’s defense, lawyer Marie-Thérèse Sur-Le Liboux claimed the photograph was taken down due to a perceived risk of public unrest and an alleged “wave of hatred” seen on social media against the images’ display. The latter, Sur-Le Liboux argued, could lead to “extremely violent” behavior. In a press release, the city also reportedly said that the photograph risked opening “new wounds,” while also adding that it was “in no way pro-Hamas,” as opponents of the photograph’s display apparently claimed online.

However, the court brushed aside the city’s arguments and ruled that removing Alshrafi’s photograph was “not a necessary, appropriate and proportionate measure, taken to preserve public order.” The image should be reinstalled before September 6, when the festival concludes, and the city must pay the OLC 1,000 euros ($1,160) in damages.

item.title: Inside the 3,000-Zine Library in a Texas Living Room - Hyperallergic
item.description:
AUSTIN — Last year, among a wave of protests against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violence, a gathering outside the Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas, took a turn when a demonstrator shot a police officer in the neck. Among the defendants handed lengthy prison sentences in connection with the incident is tattoo artist Daniel “Des” Sanchez Estrada. Estrada did not attend the protest, but he was sentenced to 30 years over a charge of concealing evidence. At the center of his case sits a box of zines.

Zines are self-published booklets. Often hand-bound and independently circulated, they are low-cost, easy to distribute, and can feature a range of art media. Zines surged in popularity with the 1980s punk scene, although informally disseminated pamphlets had been a significant tool in the liberation movements of prior decades.

“Zines, by nature, are supposed to be this open space to say whatever you want,” Michelle Millette, founder of Austin’s Sherwood Forest Zine Library, told Hyperallergic. “Zines have become one of the few spaces that allows someone to have their own opinion without having a comment section.”

The Sherwood Forest Zine Library is nestled in Millette’s living room, where a series of bookcases houses around 3,000 zines. She generally opens the library to the public over bimonthly, four-hour periods. Dozens of new and regular zinesters trickle in and out of her home during each open hour, some visiting for the novelty of the space, others taking a seat and catching up with familiar faces.

The culture and community surrounding zines have now been growing steadily across Texas for over 30 years. From picnic meetups in Houston in the 1990s to dedicated sections in public libraries, and through zine festivals, workshops and mixers, communities have sprouted everywhere from the border city of El Paso to the mid-sized, northern city of Denton.

item.title: Twelve Centuries of Documents Illuminate Humans’ Quest for Knowledge in ‘World Unfolding’ - Colossal
item.description:
When a portrait of aviation pioneer Ruth Rowland Nichols was taken while she stood beside her Lockheed Vega aircraft in 1931, she was already one of the most accomplished pilots in the world. That photo was captured the year she also became the first woman to hold simultaneous international records in altitude, speed, and long distance.

Nichols’ striking portrait is just one of hundreds of images and illustrations highlighting humans’ pursuit of knowledge in Worlds Unfolding: Science on the Page, published by Princeton University Press. The five-volume tome features more than 625 illustrations and an introduction by engineer and PBS personality Bill Nye. Moreover, it’s an exploration of global science, medicine, and technology through the remarkable archives of The Huntington in San Marino, California.

The Huntington Library contains a trove of research papers, natural history volumes, photographs, and ephemera that trace the human pursuit of knowledge over the course of centuries. From 18th-century human anatomy studies to aeronautic engineering, the book chronicles our understanding of natural history, electricity, space, geology, flight, and much more.

Compiled by Jennifer A. Watts, Daniel Lewis, Joel A. Klein, and Natalie Lawler, Worlds Unfolding spans the 10th century to today. Readers will discover incredible photos like an uncanny double-exposure portrait of Nikola Tesla sitting calmly in a lab while an enormous electrical current moves through his namesake coil. And Eadweard Muybridge’s iconic early photographs capture animals and figures in motion, marking the first time photographic methods were used to essentially record the passage of time.

The set comprises individual volumes titled Above, Below, Within, Beyond, and Alive, all of which are presented in a slipcase. “Across centuries of trial and error, illusion and triumph, the history of science is a continuously unfolding quest,” says a statement.

Worlds Unfolding will be released on October 10. Pre-order your copy from Bookshop.

item.title: How Fannuh Baskets Connect Liberia to the US Lowcountry - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This article is part of a series focusing on underrepresented craft histories, researched and written by the 2025 Craft Archive Fellows, and organized in collaboration with the Center for Craft.

I first visited St. Helena Island off the South Carolina coast in 2021. Like Louisiana, it was one of the few places I had traveled in the United States where I could hear Liberia in the way people spoke. I do not know how to fully explain it. It was in the rhythm of Gullah speech, what my mother would call “sing-songy.” It was in the syntax and cadence. As my mother would say, “my ears could hear it.”

It was also on St. Helena Island, at the historic Penn Center, where I first saw an image of two women fanning rice. I immediately thought of so many women I had seen in Liberia, standing over harvested grain with woven baskets in hand, separating rice from chaff through sweeping motions. Woven from local grasses, palmetto, and other plant materials found across the Sea Islands off the coast of the Southeastern US, these baskets have become one of the defining craft traditions of Gullah Geechee culture in the Lowcountry, a region along South Carolina's coast. To me, they felt like something I already knew.

Much of the conversation around lineage has centered on African Americans tracing their ancestry back to the African continent. As someone born in Liberia, with ancestry that includes Bassa people from the Grand Bassa, Montserrado and River Cess regions and those who emigrated from the Caribbean, I have long been interested in tracing those lineages in the other direction as well. I have been searching for the strangers and kin created through the ruptures of slavery — the “commoners, the unwilling and coerced migrants who created a new culture in the hostile world of the Americas and fashioned themselves again, making possibility out of dispossession,” as Saidiya Hartman writes in Lose Your Mother: A Journey Along the Atlantic Slave Route (2008).

I am drawn to the ways language, dance, food, and material traditions become reflections of cultural survival and continual refashioning.

“In Liberia,” dancer and anthropologist Pearl Primus reflected after spending two years in Monrovia as director of the Konoma Kende Performing Arts Center in the late 1950s to early '60s, “I found the very root of … dances like the Charleston, Lindy Hop and the old plantation dances … the same used during religious services in some churches in the South.” On St. Helena Island, and throughout my travels across the US South, I have found myself looking for those same connections that Primus traced back to Liberia.

item.title: John Galliano Withdraws From Met Show - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Staging a retrospective at the Met Museum for a fashion designer convicted of antisemitic and anti-Asian hate speech was not the Costume Institute's best idea. After serious backlash, British designer John Galliano finally withdrew, and the show was officially canceled. Staff Writer Anna Lee has more about this debacle. 

Speaking of unsavory characters, billionaire Peter Thiel, who makes Lucifer blush, received red-carpet treatment at a VIP preview of the 11th-century Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum in London. We're still trying to figure out why.  

Also today: Jennifer Higgie imagines a year in the life of painter Richard Dadd — who was famously institutionalized after killing his father — in a new novel; John Yau visits Catherine Murphy in her studio; and Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia reviews a performance by Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez at Manhattan’s Little Island.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

John Galliano Withdraws From Met Exhibition After Backlash Over Racist Comments

The British fashion designer John Galliano has withdrawn his upcoming exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute, set to run concurrently with the 2027 Met Gala, after intense criticism of his past racist behavior.

A French court convicted Galliano of antisemitic and anti-Asian hate speech directed at a French couple in February 2011, and a barrage of antisemitic slurs against a woman in October of the same year. He was fined a total of €6,000 ($6,962). A video of Galliano declaring “I love Hitler” was also circulated by the British tabloid, The Sun, leading to Dior firing the designer from his post as creative director in March 2011. | Anna Lee

item.title: Chris Killip’s Enduring Snapshots of Northeast England - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
“I wanted to remember people’s lives because I valued them. I wanted them to be remembered.” Chris Killip (1946-2020)’s work throughout the 1970s and 1980s made him one of the most influential figures in British photography. His stark documentary approach and sympathetic eye produced enduring and impactful images of those living in the North of England. It was a period of huge political turmoil, with deindustrialisation and the closure of mines destroying many traditional livelihoods in the area, resulting in economic hardship and mass unemployment. Yet, Killip’s philosophy was not the capture the urgency of the moment, but to authentically record the lives of those he saw has having “history done to them.” 

A new publication from Thames & Hudson looks back at his monumental career. Author Mark Holborn, an internationally recognised editor and writer, knew Killip personally, and produced this book with exclusive access to the photographer’s archive. The result is a defining presentation of Killip’s work in the northeast of England between 1975 and 1986, with over half its images published for the very first time. It’s essential reading for those interested in the social power of photography. But what makes is particularly unique is its ability to reconcile the world as Killip documented it with the one we live in today. Holborn draws parallels between the two, offering nuanced explorations of why he continues to cut through today and speak to those living through contemporary hardships. As he notes: “we live in a world as fractured as that Killip witnessed forty or fifty years ago … Stare at the pictures and you might recognise a place that touches you with the most intimate memory of an earlier era, or else, gather yourself because you are, indeed, looking beyond the invisible borderline to what Killip himself once suggested was another country.”  

Chris Killip: North centres on a time when shipbuilding was still a point of pride on Tyneside; bitter miners’ strikes protested the closure of the region’s pits, although by the end of the 1980s, only six collieries were left; and unemployment neared 20%. The artist was unflinching of his portrayals of this lived reality, confronting it in a way few of his contemporaries managed, and this is evident throughout the book. In Wallsend, Tyneside old home are shown in the midst of demolition, whilst in the West End of Newcastle, blocks of flats stand burnt out and inhospitable. Often in these images, huge industrial infrastructure and factory towers belch out smoke loom over terraced houses and high streets. Everyday life was carried out in the shadows of these sites, with one shot showing a woman pushing a pram alongside huge concrete buildings, whilst children play right beside ships in the docks. Readers are reminded on every single page that in the 1970s and 1980s, heavy industry was the lifeblood of the region. 

Killip’s images of the miner’s strikes are particularly arresting. The mass dispute began in 1984 as a response to the planned closure of 20 coal mines, although it was later found that authorities planned to close 75 over a three-year period. The yearlong protests profoundly shaped modern British history, politics and society, with around 187,000 miners walking out of their jobs across the country. One of the suggested sites of closure was Herrington Colliery in County Durham. In Chris Killip: North, images show rows and rows of riot police lined up beside a row of terraced houses, as family looks on from the doorstep. Elsewhere, men gather in a local club to show solidarity for the strikes. Killip really succeeds in demonstrating how the industrial dispute permeated all parts of northeastern life, simultaneously uniting a community in their backing of the striking miners, and tearing away its foundations as an industrial heartland. His work earned him a commemorative lamp from the Monkwearmouth Miners Lodge.  

In the early 1980s, Killip lived for months in a caravan on a Northumberland beach to photograph Seacoal, which according to Holborn is “perhaps his most memorable and graceful work, where the harshness of gathering from industrial detritus for survival was tempered by his observations of tenderness.” Here, dogs, horses and children – often the focus for the photographer – come to the fore. Life is inextricably tied to the sea, as Killip captures families searching for and collecting coal, directing their horse and carts across the beach, or spending time with their animals in caravans. These are images with personality, where young boys carried huge corrugated steel on their backs like a shield or pick through pebbles “in the very good fur coat.” Killip succeeds in painting a complex portrait of a community whose existence is centred around the ocean, with conditions that are often harsh and unforgiving. Yet, whether it’s a puppy nestled on a man’s chest, or schoolkids running home in the snow, he also spotlights the small, soft moments of humanity that shine through in even the severest environments.  

 Mark Holborn does a remarkable job of bringing fresh perspective to Killips era-defining career. Chris Killip: North presents a portrait of a region and an artist’s intense ties to it. The photographer dedicated his lens to a community facing economic and social hardship, refusing to do so with anything other than the utmost dignity and nuance. His oeuvre is unquestionably a masterclass in documentary photograph, but this book reveals it to go one step further, offering us all a blueprint for empathy and compassion. 

Chris Killip: North is published by Thames & Hudson on 3 September: thamesandhudson.com

Words: Emma Jacob

item.title: "Marina" Dares You to Laugh at Technology - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Artistic attempts to contend with technology’s ever-tightening grip on our attention, institutions, and social abilities too often take the form of post-human fever dreams of the Black Mirror school — works that, while intended to be critical, easily devolve into discursive, cyborg-filled feedback loops. Julio Torres and Martine Gutierrez’s Marina, which premiered at Manhattan’s Little Island last week as part of the 2026 Whitney Biennial program, opts for a radically different tack: laughing at technology instead of fearing it, and winning our hearts rather than rotting our brains. 

The air is humid with a storm that never materialized as audience members stream into The Amph, Little Island’s open-air amphitheater, on Thursday, August 26. Onstage, a figure in a burgundy pinstripe suit mouths wordlessly into a payphone set on a wooden dock suspended above a vaguely apocalyptic underwater mise-en-scène. Framed video screens playing water-wave patterns rise from coral outcroppings encrusted with rubber-tire bits, junk, and debris. 

Down in the murky waters of the Gowanus Canal, we learn, reside a sea wench named Marina (played by Gutierrez), her overprotective older sister, and an anglerfish named Nano. They lead a parasitic existence, accruing the trash that sinks to the floor to reinforce their shells. No one seems to question their lifestyle until a distracted construction worker, barking his insecurities to his AI girlfriend while pacing the dock above them, drops his smartphone into the water. (“Is this a rectangle?” Nano asks, unironically.) Entranced by the device, Marina is drawn into a world of endless scrolls and highlight reels, where influencers peddle the familiar doctrine that a woman can find self-worth only through a man's validation. If this is all sounding very truth-universally-acknowledged so far, that’s because the plot of Marina is Frankensteined from paradigmatic tales of women scorned, from Homer’s Odyssey to Euripides’s Medea to Jennifer’s Body (2009).  

Our protagonist sets out with good intentions at first, snapping a candid selfie atop her garbage pile and uploading it to OkCupid, a platform that feels as dated a reference as the payphone. But no one swipes right, so she does what we all do online, to some degree or another: She pretends to be someone else. Marina finds her perfect alter-ego in a more conventionally attractive sea dweller, Ariel of Disney’s The Little Mermaid (1989), whose wide eyes and frizz-free red mane lure thirsty suitors like Jared, a “man of faith” who swears he’s 6’5 and a CEO but “will not be tasked with the emotional labor of dealing with your trauma.” In other words, they are not exactly a catch. When they realize they’ve quite literally been catfished and grow aggressive, they face the homicidal ire of Marina, their Apple Watches and motorcycle jackets becoming absorbed into her ever-growing junkyard ecology. 

Back on terra firma, our pinstriped narrator, a detective, is determined to crack the case of the fuckboys going missing down below. She recruits a randy garbageman named Dino to go undercover (“I’ll make it worth your while, but not by a lot — I’m solving this case on spec,” she tells him.) But as the saying goes, there’s a lid for every pot, and in a twist of fate, Marina turns out to be exactly Dino’s type: large claws, “kinky,” no interest in deodorant.

Throughout this journey, Marina is faced with one of the greatest challenges of becoming oneself. She must learn to locate a sense of identity in her own existence, not in the men she kills or in the man she falls in love with, and certainly not in the carefully constructed chaos of the screen.

item.title: Jennifer Higgie’s Empathetic Elegy for Richard Dadd - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In English painter Richard Dadd’s “The Fairy Feller’s Master-Stroke” (1855–64), the ghostly, gray faces of well-dressed Victorians nestle among human-size dandelions and shrubs, partially obscuring a shrouded figure raising an axe overhead. The eerie work was painted at Broadmoor Hospital, a high-security psychiatric institution where Dadd was confined after his tenure at the famed Bethlem Royal Hospital, also known as “Bedlam.” Writer and art critic Jennifer Higgie captures a similarly uncanny world in her novel of the same name. Originally published by Sternberg Press in 2006 and re-released by Verso in July, Bedlam reimagines the painter’s infamous 1842 expedition through Europe, Southwest Asia, and North Africa as a draughtsman for a British nobleman, a journey that spurred a period of psychosis and resulted in Dadd committing patricide at age 26. 

It’s this dark odyssey that propels Higgie’s fragmented, first-person account. Through diaristic, idiosyncratic snapshots, she translates Dadd’s uncanny, often Orientalist paintings and drawings into “his” own writing. Higgie’s bold approach illuminates the fragile boundaries between historically marginalized minds like Dadd’s and those of people who may never see the inside of a psychiatrist’s office. Truth and fiction merge and disjoint as Dadd moves toward crisis, a visceral and strange descent emphasized by Higgie’s choice to embody — not mediate or describe — his perspective. As Dadd says in Bedlam’s opening salvo from Broadmoor Hospital, “Perhaps it is the story that chooses the man … I did not write my life.” 

But Higgie did. In her telling, Dadd’s psychosis emerges from the artist’s increasingly off-kilter understanding of the relationship between reality and its representations. Tasked with capturing his international trip in sketches for Sir Thomas Phillips, Dadd wonders why he should “bother” to recreate the Alps in front of him if his drawings “can’t help but be inferior to the original,” ultimately soothing himself with the idea that “a drawing is simply another mountain.” He agonizes over the differences between what he draws and what he sees: “In every wave a picture hides from me, but none I can mention or describe to my companion,” he says, traveling across the Gulf of Corinth. Later, near En Gedi, a desert near the Dead Sea and present-day Occupied West Bank, metaphors collapse into hallucination. “I see scorpions the size of men haunting ruins,” he says. “I crash into walls I do not see.”

item.title: New Discoveries at Egypt’s Saqqara Necropolis Show Its Use Over Time - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An Egyptian archaeological mission working at Saqqara has uncovered the tomb of Sekhentiu-Ptah, a high-ranking official of Egypt’s Old Kingdom (ca. 2700–ca. 2200 BCE). In a separate discovery, the archaeologists also found a network of burial shafts containing human remains and funerary objects from later periods.

Heritage Daily reported the news following an announcement by Egypt’s Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

The finds were made during the mission’s first excavation season in an area west of the Bubasteion necropolis in Saqqara. Taken together, they point to the ancient cemetery’s use over centuries.

According to the mission, Sekhentiu-Ptah’s tomb contained the remains of a funerary chapel with its false door still in its original position. Alabaster objects arranged in front of it included an offering table, an offering implement, a purification basin, a vessel, and a mat.

Mohamed Abdel Badi, head of the Egyptian Antiquities Sector, described the discovery of these objects as particularly important. Because they were still in their original positions, they provide researchers with a clearer understanding of Old Kingdom burial practices.  

In addition to Sekhentiu-Ptah’s name, hieroglyphic inscriptions on the false door and funerary objects also recorded several of his titles. They included royal chamberlain, supervisor of the king’s works, supervisor of royal documents, keeper of royal secrets, priest of the goddess Maat, and supervisor of the library.

The tomb stands alongside a group of later burials containing human remains, painted funerary cartonnage, three sealed sarcophagi, and over 100 faience ushabti figurines. Preliminary explorations indicate these burials were looted in antiquity; passages linking them are thought to have been made by ancient robbers moving between the tombs.

Amr El-Tayeb, Director-General of the Saqqara Archaeological Area and head of the archaeological mission, said the surviving material will offer researchers insight into funerary practices, particularly those of Egypt’s Late Period (664–332 BCE).

Located 20 miles south of Cairo, the Saqqara archaeological site was the main necropolis for the ancient Egyptian city of Memphis, which was founded around 3100 BCE and abandoned in the 7th century CE. The latest discoveries add to growing evidence of its extraordinary longevity as a burial ground.

item.title: Otto Muehl Retrospective at Vienna Actionism Museum Courts Controversy in Advance of September Opening - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Vienna Actionism Museum (WAM) has been controversial since it opened in March 2024, which is perhaps not an entirely surprising outcome given the postwar movement’s penchant for violent, graphic performance art.  

A new scandal is brewing as the museum prepares for its fall exhibition, dedicated to the work of Otto Muehl, one of the co-founders of Viennese Actionism. The show “Otto Muehl: Art on the Precipice” will feature 150 paintings, objects, film, and prints, some from the museum’s own extensive collection, others loaned by private collectors. It’s set to open on September 10 and will be on view through January 10, 2027.

The controversy goes beyond the fact that many may find Muehl’s artwork involving graphic nudity, violence, and the use of blood and excrement as materials distasteful. He also founded a notorious commune in Friedrichshof, outside of Vienna, that was active in the 1970s and ‘80s. In 1991, Muehl was convicted of sexual offenses against minors, rape, and illegal drug use; he ultimately served seven years in prison, and then moved to Portugal, where he died in 2013.

As documented in a pair of articles published earlier this month in the daily newspaper Der Standard, the controversy is wrapped up in the insensitive way in which the show is being marketed. Former victims of the Friedrichshof commune, many of whom are alive, have spoken out against the museum for glossing over Muehl’s crimes in favor of the art historical significance of his “perpetrator art.” The Der Standard articles poke holes in the idea that one could reasonably separate “the life of the cult leader and his art,” and question the ethics of organizing an exhibition that stands to grow the market for Muehl’s work.

The Vienna Actionism Museum, for its part, acknowledges that an Otto Muehl retrospective is a “challenging project,” to say the least. The press release emphasizes that the show does not include images that depict abuse, and that no works from the painting series “Accidents in the Home” (1986), in which teenage victims posed as models in scenes of domestic violence, are in the show. The museum also claims that any recognizable subject has given permission to be in the show, though Der Standard questions if and how heirs of certain identifiable figures gave consent.

Klaus Albrecht Schröder, the former director of the Albertina and current director of the WAM, hopes that visitors will feel empowered “to form their own judgments regarding Otto Muehl’s art.”

item.title: Auction Houses Won’t Sell a Keith Haring Drawing That Faced a Lawsuit - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A Keith Haring drawing deemed authentic by a Superior Court judge but lacking sufficient provenance records to sell at Christie’s and Sotheby’s was the subject of a trial in Connecticut. The gallery that sold it ended up proving victorious.

As reported by Greenwich Time, Nevada businessman Vernon Hartung bought the drawing of flying saucers from Martin Lawrence Galleries for $165,000 in 2018. But when he inquired about selling it at Christie’s and Sotheby’s, the two auction houses said the artwork’s documented history “did not meet their requirements for selling a Haring drawing as an authentic work,” according to trial records.

Martin Lawrence Galleries then attempted to sell the work for Hartung, but he deemed potential prices ranging from $20,000 to $30,000 too low and sued the gallery for breach of contract and other claims related to the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act.

In a written decision in May, Judge Robert L. Genuario described the drawing “by a preponderance of the evidence, to be authentic,” citing a 2002 letter from Richard Hambleton, a friend of Haring’s known for collecting the artist’s fleeting subway works. But when its credentials did not pass similar muster on the market, Hartung “argued the gallery effectively sold him something that could not be authenticated to standards required by top auction houses.”

After he could not prove that the drawing was inauthentic and the gallery had violated its warranty, however, Hartung lost his case and was found responsible for the defendant’s attorney’s fees related to the suit.

item.title: Catherine Murphy Has Her Cake and Eats It Too - Hyperallergic
item.description:
POUGHKEEPSIE, N.Y. — I first saw Catherine Murphy’s work at the now-defunct Xavier Fourcade gallery on Manhattan’s Upper East Side in 1980, and I have admired it ever since. Her career began when her paintings were included in the 1972 Annual Exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art (a precursor to the Biennial). Since then, Murphy has characterized herself as an “observational painter” who bases her work on what she sees. Throughout her career, however, she would move from what she saw to setting up situations based on dreams and memory, broadening the definition of realism as well as breaking with the realist painting convention of working on a one-to-one scale. With these two innovations, Murphy single-handedly pushed observational painting into a fertile territory that is all her own. Like Alex Katz, whose paintings she saw as a student, Murphy wanted to make large paintings that could hold their own next to the Abstract Expressionists and, in opposition to them, reject style and working in series.

While I have written about Murphy many times, including in the only monograph on her paintings and drawings, I continue to find the richness and perceptual complexity of her works wonderfully daunting. Whether I am looking at two clear plastic bags filled with used clothes, stacked on a broken office chair; stacks of books with yellowed pages, seen from the side; or a wallpapered corner of a room with baseboard and red wall-to-wall carpet, I always feel like I am just scratching the surface. While I have long focused on her attention to detail within the overall view, it recently struck me that I had not paid enough attention to the structure of the paintings, and that the friction between the entire picture and its parts was another of the innovations for which Murphy deserves recognition.

What I am proposing is that after breaking with the conventions governing realism, Murphy recognized that her ambition was even larger than her accomplishments. To keep moving, she had to take on the modernist conventions controlling abstraction, including the grid and the two-dimensional picture plane. Could they be reconciled with one-point perspective while being transformed into something fresh? Simply put: Murphy wanted to have her cake and eat it too. This meant she had to further articulate a trajectory that was hers alone, even as it brought pictorial challenges none of her contemporaries were addressing. To attain a rapprochement between realism and abstraction that had not been thought possible, she had to forgo the certainties she earned in her singular paintings and break new ground.

Murphy is a subversive painter who has made work in dialogue with Renaissance painters and classical subjects, such as the nude, as well as work by her peers and generations before, including Lois Dodd and Robert Mangold. Refusing to embrace the postmodern ideology that all is rubble, or that the utopian ideal of progress is dead, Murphy rejected the by-now-familiar strategies of parody, citation, and irony. She was not interested in mocking high modernist motifs, but rather in utilizing modernist compositional devices, such as the grid, to revamp the mundane into the unexpected. In making realism (the three-dimensional) and modernism (the two-dimensional plane) inseparable, she could shape and honor time passing without seeking sanctuary from inevitable destruction; this became a lifelong preoccupation. It is what makes her paintings so engaging. Confronted by her scrupulously formal arrangement of telling particulars, at once isolated and connected, we see something of ourselves in her work — the inevitability of mortality and solitude.

item.title: What in the Devil Was Peter Thiel Doing at the British Museum? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The British Museum hosted Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel for a VIP viewing of the Bayeux tapestry on August 18, drawing concerns among staff, per a report from the Guardian.

The museum declined to comment on the matter in an email to Hyperallergic, and it remains unclear if Thiel was part of a larger group privileged with viewing the 11th-century tapestry before its coveted public exhibition starting September 10.

Thiel's VIP visit puzzled some, as the billionaire has never donated to the British Museum individually or through any of his businesses. Certain staff were concerned that Thiel's private viewing potentially limited public access to the historic weaving, as the museum must limit both the amount and intensity of light exposure on the tapestry to prevent damage.

Thiel's visit to the museum is said to have been facilitated by its director of development. Board chair George Osbourne neither met with nor attended the VIP viewing with Thiel. A limited number of private viewings have been made available to various museum stakeholders while the exhibition gallery is still undergoing construction.

item.title: Marka27 Superimposes Pop Culture, Graffiti, and Political Critique in Urgent Portraits - Colossal
item.description:
Animated characters, patterned textiles, logos from iconic fashion labels, graffiti, and more coalesce in the vibrant portraits of Victor Quiñonez. Born in Mexico, raised in East Dallas, and now based in Brooklyn, the artist, who works as Marka27, is interested in the ways activism and pop culture converge, and he infuses the visual language of contemporary street art with Indigenous imagery and Mexican mural traditions. Whether working on large-scale walls or more intimate canvases, Quiñonez taps into his own experiences of living between cultures and the arbitrary nature of national borders.

Portraits like “Luchando Por Mi Alma” superimpose the signature Louis Vuitton pattern, desert flora, a striped weaving, a masked Lucha Libre figure, and a stereotypical, low-wage character from the television show Family Guy atop a portrait of a man in a wide-brimmed hat. This pastiche is emblematic of what Quiñonez dubs his “neo Indigenous” style in which potent cultural symbols and a critical consideration of the social and political landscape converge.

In his solo exhibition Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá, which translates to “not from here, not from there,” the artist presents several portraits alongside a collection of sculptures and immersive installations. Following its debut at Boston University in 2025, the exhibition traveled to the University of North Texas in Denton, where it was on view briefly before being shut down by the administration. Now at its third venue, Ni de Aquí, Ni de Allá will open at Institute of the Arts and Sciences in Santa Cruz this October.

The censored show is explicitly critical of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, with the artist’s I.C.E. Scream series confronting the mandate. This particular body of work includes a street vendor’s pushcart and sculptural paletas, one of which encases handcuffs in its translucent resin body with a faint image of a person in a cage imprinted on the oversized stick. Smaller acrylic iterations contain photographic portraits of street vendors embedded within. Etched onto the wooden sticks are a government logo paired with a mock agency called “U.S. Inhumane and Cruelty Enforcement.” By placing portraiture at the center of every work large and small, the artist directs our attentions to the very people most impacted by these actions, while emphasizing our shared humanity.

“At first glance, you’re like, ‘Oh, wow, that’s a popsicle.’ You want to approach it. It brings back nostalgia for everyone. It symbolizes something fun, innocent and childlike,” Quiñonez told The Los Angeles Times. “But then when you get closer, you see the writing on the popsicle sticks. … I wanted to show the two different sides of the world that we’re living in.”

In addition to his studio works, the artist has painted murals in cities across the U.S., which you can explore more of on his website and Instagram.

item.title: Contradiction and the Unknown Permeate Isaiah Lee’s Imaginative Dollhouse Paintings - Colossal
item.description:
With a teal roof and gabled windows, a colonial-style dollhouse is at the center of Isaiah Lee’s practice. In his current body of work, the Chicago artist renders childhood toys that transition from objects of play and nostalgia into uncanny, animate entities. Set in the scaled-down rooms and landscape around the miniature home, Lee’s scenes channel the wonder and theatrics of the adolescent imagination, while confronting the ways these early experiences permeate one’s life.

Born into a fundamentalist Christian family in Missouri, the artist grapples with the contradictions within the teachings of his upbringing, alongside the lived reality of being a Black man in the U.S. In “Shepherd I,” a tiny green astronaut evokes Moses as he leads livestock through the house, while an enormous skull and concealed man loom in the shadows. The vast differences in scale within a single scene gesture toward the outsized impact of some encounters and how our memories have the capability of exaggerating the scope.

Narrative ripples throughout Lee’s paintings, with “Romeo and Juliet” and “Juliet” capturing two different points of view of the same scene. The artist’s ability to shift perspectives is a compelling world-building technique and, like his heavy use of shadow, positions each composition as an illuminated nook amid a vast network of the unknown. “They arrive at a moment when it feels necessary to return to childhood as a way of uncovering who we are and what good we are still capable of bringing forth,” he adds.

Darkness pervades many of the pieces, not necessarily in a sinister way but instead to suggest the omnipresence of the unknown and a sense of underlying fear. He writes that “faith cannot simply be abandoned but must be understood as an inheritance wrought into the body and the imagination.”

Lee is preparing for a solo exhibition this fall at crosswalk in Chicago. Titled A Thief in the Night, the show nods to the Biblical notion that people need to repent in order to be “right with the Lord.” “For many, this warning creates a persistent sense of unease, fostering the belief that no amount of faithfulness is truly enough,” the artist says. “Life becomes a race against time, a race that cannot be won.”

If you’re in Chicago, you can see some of Lee’s works through November 1 in an exhibition celebrating the city’s emerging artists at Hyde Park Art Center, and A Thief in the Night opens on October 16. Find more on Instagram.

item.title: Met Museum Cancels John Galliano Exhibition Amid Controversy over Designer’s Antisemitic Comments - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In a surprising turnabout, New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art canceled a John Galliano exhibition that was due to open next spring, in what would have been the Costume Institute’s big May 2027 show, held in tandem with the notorious Met Gala.

The show had faced controversy from the start, as many fixed on antisemitic and anti-Asian comments made by Galliano more than a decade ago. He was convicted of a hate crime in France in 2011.

The designer previously apologized for those comments and sought mental health counseling, and the Met said it had conferred with Jewish groups in the making of its Galliano exhibition. But neither was enough to assuage the concerns of politicians and public figures who had pushed the museum to cancel the show since its announcement at the end of July.

The cancelation came just a few days after the New York Times published a report detailing those criticisms, which had been largely waged in emails to curators and leadership at the Met. One of those critics was Pace Gallery founder Arne Glimcher, who reportedly threatened to withhold artworks that he was planning to donate to the Met following his passing. According to the Times, board members were going to meet to discuss the shape of the exhibition going forward.

As the Times report noted, the Met Gala, an extravagant event held in tandem with the Costume Institute’s spring show, is typically held on the first Monday in May. In 2027, that Monday is Yom HaShoah, the day of international Holocaust remembrance.

In a statement, Met director Max Hollein said the museum had called off the show amid “thoughtful discussions with John Galliano.”

The release about the cancelation also featured a three-paragraph comment from Galliano, who reiterated his apology for his prior comments.

“After much reflection and discussion with The Met and all those involved, I have decided, with great sadness, that it is best for the exhibition not to take place at this time,” Galliano said in a statement. “I remain fully accountable for the pain caused by my words in the past, particularly the hurt I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I remain deeply sorry for it. I understand that meaningful atonement is not achieved through an exhibition, institutional recognition or a single public gesture. It is a continuing responsibility, demonstrated through listening, learning and one’s conduct over time.”

The British designer continued, “I do not want the debate surrounding me to place The Met in a difficult position or to distract from the remarkable work of the Costume Institute. I also recognise and respect that an exhibition honouring my work would be painful for some. I would also like to express my deepest gratitude to all those who have guided, supported and accompanied me throughout these fifteen years of sobriety and recovery from alcoholism and addiction. Your wisdom, patience and humanity have helped me more than I can ever adequately express.”

Andrew Bolton, the curator in charge of the Costume Institute, said that he recognized “the pain and concern this exhibition has caused. After extensive discussion, I support the decision not to proceed.”

Former Vogue editor-in-chief Anna Wintour, a Met trustee who chairs the Met Gala and has helped shape the Costume Institute, called the move “the right decision” in a sparse, two-sentence statement. She also described Galliano as “courageous.”

It was not clear what would replace the Galliano show, but it appeared that the Met would still stage its Met Gala next year. The museum promised further details on that gala and the Costume Institute show staged alongside it at a later date.

item.title: Seeing Krasner and Pollock Together - Hyperallergic
item.description:
As an editor, occasionally a pitch lands in your inbox that makes your heart rate quicken. That’s what I felt when artist and writer Lia Strasser emailed me a few weeks ago, attaching a very personal and moving essay about her relationship to the story of Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock. You may be familiar with the critique that Krasner’s oeuvre has been overshadowed by that of her husband — the alpha male, the household name, the frankly abusive spouse. When Strasser first saw a post announcing The Met’s upcoming exhibition dedicated to both artists, she winced. “Give her a solo show!” 

Then, Strasser retraced her steps — from the Abstract Expressionist couple’s home in East Hampton to the formative moments that shaped her own artistic identity — and discovered a different reading, one that centers rather than diminishes Krasner’s agency.

Also today, the art world pays homage to Yayoi Kusama, who died last week at the age of 97; a Bruges exhibition that claims to de-center Europe fails to live up to its premise; and thieves make off with a diamond necklace from a museum in Vienna.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

What I Got Wrong About Krasner and Pollock

Earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming exhibition Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous on Instagram, alongside a photograph of the artists by Hans Namuth. Seething, I looked to the comments for affirmation. I didn’t have to scroll for long.

Months earlier, I had visited the Pollock-Krasner House in Springs, East Hampton, knowing far more about Jackson Pollock than I did Lee Krasner. I am a painter myself, and I had come to Springs in the wreck of yet another failed relationship … with a painter. I thought I already knew Krasner’s story. I thought her story was partly my own. | Lia Strasser

item.title: The Edge of Certaintyat Foam Amsterdam - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Photography is often treated as a form of visual evidence, its authority resting on the belief that what the camera records can be understood as fact. However, every photograph is shaped by selection, perspective and interpretation, complicating the certainty it appears to offer. Nadav Kander works within this tension, creating images of striking precision that resist definitive interpretation. Across more than four decades, his practice has moved between portraiture, landscape, still life and the human figure, using each form to examine the distance between what can be seen and what can be known. The Edge of Things, at Amsterdam’s Foam, brings these strands together, but Kander’s significance extends beyond any single exhibition; his work offers a sustained examination of what photographic authority can achieve.

That question is particularly pressing in a culture where images are consumed at extraordinary speed. A photograph can identify a person, establish a location or appear to document an event, yet none of these functions guarantees understanding. Kander’s images frequently exploit the gap between recognition and comprehension, allowing information to remain present without becoming the whole meaning of the picture. His landscapes may be geographically specific while seeming psychologically displaced; his portraits may identify their sitters whilst leaving their inner lives inaccessible. The effect is not obscurity for its own sake, but an insistence that looking is an active process rather than the passive receipt of facts.

Kander’s career makes this position especially interesting because he has worked so successfully within both art and editorial photography. London-based, he began taking photographs at 13 and has developed an international practice encompassing fine-art photography, portraiture and moving image. His honours include the Prix Pictet for his Yangtze River photographs, an Honorary Fellowship of the Royal Photographic Society, the Sony World Photography Organisation’s Outstanding Contribution to Photography award and a 2025 Pollock-Krasner Foundation Grant. In 2009, The New York Times Magazine commissioned him to make 52 portraits of members of Barack Obama’s administration – the largest number of portraits by a single photographer published in one issue – whist his sitters have also included Rosamund Pike and David Lynch. His work is held in collections including London’s National Portrait Gallery and the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago and has been shown at institutions including the Barbican Centre, Somerset House and Palais de Tokyo.

Editorial photography usually depends upon immediate recognition: the image must establish its subject quickly, whether that subject is a politician, actor or cultural figure. Kander’s portraits satisfy that requirement while simultaneously undermining it, turning the familiar face into something less secure. In a 2019 exchange with Kander, curator David Campany described a portrait as “a fragment from an ongoing life”, pointing to the impossibility of fully knowing the person represented. That distinction matters because a portrait activates the viewer’s assumptions about who that person might be. Kander’s photographs become compelling precisely where identification gives way to projection.

Kander himself offers a useful counterpoint to the conventional idea of the photographic storyteller. “I don’t photograph to tell stories,” he tells Campany, “I photograph to make stories possible.” The distinction shifts responsibility from photographer to viewer, suggesting that meaning is completed through looking rather than delivered by the image. It also explains why his portraits can feel intimate without becoming confessional: the photograph does not claim privileged access to another person’s interior life. Instead, expression, posture and lighting create conditions in which the viewer imagine what cannot be seen.

This becomes particularly evident in Kander’s portraits of public figures. Barack Obama arrives already burdened with an enormous accumulation of photographs, speeches and representations, meaning that the sitter is never encountered without the weight of an existing public image. Kander’s 2009 portraits therefore operate within a space between historical document and individual encounter. David Lynch presents a different but related problem: the cultural associations surrounding his name are so strong that the photograph must negotiate an image of the artist that already exists in the imagination. Kander introduces stillness and distance, allowing the recognised figure to become momentarily unfamiliar.

Landscape removes the pressure of celebrity but not the problem of interpretation. Kander’s photographs of the Yangtze River were made during a period of rapid industrial and social transformation, bringing together human activity, altered environments and the immense scale of the river itself. Yibin I (Bathers) places small human figures against water, rock, industrial structures and atmospheric haze, producing a scene that is neither straightforward document nor pure abstraction. The factory and smokestack provide evidence of transformation, but composition and light prevent the photograph from becoming a simple statement about industrialisation. What matters is the instability between these readings.

Environmental photography has increasingly questioned the assumption that showing damage is sufficient to communicate ecological crisis. Images of polluted rivers, collapsing habitats and industrial landscapes can provide powerful evidence, but they can also reduce complex histories to familiar visual symbols. Kander’s approach is less declarative, allowing the altered landscape to remain visually seductive while retaining its political implications. The Yangtze pictures are therefore not simply about environmental degradation; they ask how a viewer reads a landscape in which natural and human histories have become inseparable. This ambiguity makes the work relevant to a broader shift from documentary photography towards practices that acknowledge the camera’s role in constructing the world it depicts.

The same tension runs through Kander’s photographs of the Thames and Chernobyl. These are locations already saturated with history, but photography does not automatically make that history visible. A place may carry political, industrial or personal significance without offering an obvious visual language. Kander responds by attending to atmosphere and physical detail. The resulting images leave room for history to operate as a pressure within the frame rather than a caption imposed upon it.

Such an approach places Kander within a wider post-documentary conversation without requiring him to abandon the documentary function of photography. His pictures remain grounded in actual people and places. Light, scale, colour, framing and sequencing determine what becomes visible and what recedes. The photograph consequently records reality while acknowledging that recording is already an act of interpretation. This is where Kander’s editorial experience becomes significant: his practice demonstrates that an image can communicate clearly without pretending that clarity is equivalent to truth.

Curator David Campany’s role at Foam provides a useful structure for seeing these connections across Kander’s career. The exhibition brings together landscape, portraiture, still life, studies of the human body and moving image, with Campany serving as guest curator in collaboration with the Foundation for the Exhibition of Photography and Foam. Rather than treating these forms as separate specialisms, the selection makes it possible to consider the relationship between surface and depth. A face, a stretch of water and an industrial site can all become subjects through which Kander tests the limits of photographic description. Curation therefore matters as a means of placing visual questions beside one another.

The inclusion of moving image extends that investigation into duration. Alongside photographs, The Edge of Things includes video accompanied by music composed by Max Richter and a projection incorporating Kander’s own voiceover. These works introduce sound and movement into a practice often associated with highly controlled still images, making time itself part of the encounter. Yet the shift is not as radical as it first appears: Kander’s photographs have always depended upon the viewer. A still image may stop the clock mechanically, but interpretation continues to unfold long after the shutter has closed.

That demand for attention has force within contemporary image culture. Digital photography has made visual production almost continuous, while platforms reward speed, familiarity and immediate response. Kander’s work operates according to a different rhythm, one in which the first impression is deliberately insufficient. His photographs can initially attract interest through their formal control – the precision of light, the measured compositions – but visual pleasure becomes an entry point rather than a conclusion. The longer the encounter lasts, the more the photograph reveals its refusal to settle into a single meaning.

Kander’s achievement lies in making that uncertainty productive. His photographs do not abandon evidence, but neither do they allow it to become the final word; instead, they move between the recorded world and the meanings viewers construct. Campany’s extensive scholarship on photography provides a valuable critical context for Kander’s approach to portraiture, particularly its tension between observation and interpretation. Kander’s own assertion that photographs “make stories possible” extends this principle across the wider practice. At a moment when the medium is increasingly asked to deliver certainty at speed, Kander’s work offers a more demanding possibility – images can remain open, allowing viewers not simply to receive meaning but to participate in its construction.

Nadav Kander: The Edge of Uncertainty opens at Foam, Amsterdam on 18 September: foam.org

Words: Shirley Stevenson
