item.title: Colourful Portraiture from the Aesthetica Archives - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
From the early use of charcoal and soil 40,000 years ago to the vivid digital compositions of contemporary photographers, humanity has always used colour to express emotional and cultural depth. Colour is far more than a decorative element; it is a primary language of storytelling. This selection explores the work of contemporary photographers previously featured in print editions of Aesthetica Magazine who place bold palettes at the heart of their work. From the energetic “Hueism” of Derrick Ofosu Boateng to the surreal landscapes of Sanja Marušic, these artists harness light and contrast to reshape our visual world. The work featured here is inspired by cultural and physical spaces by photographers that are redefining portraiture.

Sarfo Emmanuel Annor 

Sarfo Emmanuel Annor (b. 2002) is fascinated by colour. Based in Koforidua, Ghana, the photographer launched his career on iPhone by making portraits of family and friends. At the time, the goal was to express the dreams and stories of other young people living in his home city. Now, Annor shoots editorial for UNIF and is listed amongst i-D magazine’s “hottest creatives.” He remains drawn to the subject of African youth and its “power to shape the continent’s future,” crafting images bursting with potential. Everyday moments are heightened by glowing backgrounds, rendered in magenta, majorelle blue, orange and scarlet. Objects are brought into focus, with vases balancing on heads and leaves obscuring faces.

@sarfogh_

Sanja Marušić

Sanja Marušić (b.1991) is a Dutch-Croatian artist, based in Amsterdam, who builds otherworldly images in which collage, painting and photography collide. The artist travels extensively, capturing performances where figures – often Marušić alone in costume, sometimes accompanied by others – move through surreal landscapes. Mirrored cubes, triangle headdresses and glittery bodysuits create a space-age look and feel. Subjects navigate pink and turquoise flower fields, as if traversing the surface of a new planet, or leap through giant yellow squares, revelling in freedom and play – like completing a video game level. Some of Marušić’s stories are autobiographical, whilst others evade explanation. Folk and naïve art are wellsprings of inspiration here, influencing composition and palette.

sanjamarusic.com | @sanjamarusic

Derrick Ofosu Boateng

“Without effort no harvest will be abundant.” It’s a fundamental message, and one of many African proverbs at the heart of Derrick Ofosu Boateng’s (b. 1998) practice. Traditionally, these sayings were shared orally and seldom written down; this led to a lack of wider documentation. The Ghanaian photographer’s energetic pictures close the gap. Shot on iPhone, they interpret each maxim by bursting with colour and joy. Boateng calls this approach Hueism: “self-expression through colour therapy and visual poetry.” Figures hold balloons or flowers, making shapes in tandem against blue, red and yellow blocks. Each teaches a lesson, from humility and modesty to patience. “Launching an art movement is a powerful way to share your message, and, in my case, to address the misinterpretation of Africa.”

@derrick_o_boateng

Yannis Davy Guibinga 

Yannis Davy Guibinga (b. 1995) is passionate about storytelling. The photographer, originally from Libreville, Gabon, now based in Montréal, Canada, creates visual histories centred around Africa and its diaspora. Whispers in the Twilight (2024), takes cues from classical painting to tell the tale of a developing relationship – adversaries to friends – set against a backdrop of deep blue and vivid orange skies. In Moonsilver (2024), Guibinga follows two mermaids who emerge on the shores of a secluded village in west Africa, whilst other portraits depict figures who reach for the moon or stand hand-in-hand against the setting sun. Most recently, the artist has been experimenting with surreal collage techniques in images that resemble heat maps. In these, feathers and butterfly wings merge with the human body. 

yannisdavy.com | @yannisdavy

Sarah Doyle

In 1923, Wassily Kandinsky handed out a questionnaire to his Bauhaus students. Their task: match the three primary colours with basic shapes. The responses fed into the art- ist’s wider investigations into colour-form theory, which linked yellow to triangles, red to squares and blue to circles. Today, contemporary photographers, including Dublin-based Sarah Doyle, are continuing to play with the relationships between geometry and palettes. Multi-toned spheres are suspended against stark black backdrops, models hold scarlet rings aloft, whilst various shades of thick paint spill out across portraits. Doyle’s work, which is defined by its bright aesthetic, has been featured by Hunger, The Observer, Tatler, Time, Vogue and others. Her clients include Max Factor, Sony, Universal & Urban Outfitters. 

sarahdoylephotography.com | @sarahdoylephotographer

Words: Sophie Bullivant

item.title: Dawoud Bey Bringsthe Past into the Present - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
“How can one reimagine and visualise African American history and make that history resonate in the contemporary moment?” This question, posed by American artist and educator Dawoud Bey (b. 1953), underpins Material Histories, Living Landscapes, his latest exhibition of photography and film at the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO). Bey began his career as an image-maker in 1975 with the series Harlem, U.S.A, which took viewers on a journey through the historic New York neighbourhood. It was exhibited to critical acclaim, and Bey’s work has since been the subject of numerous major museum and gallery presentations throughout the US and Europe. The artist, who is a MacArthur Fellow, grew up in Queens during the Civil Rights Era. Today, he is focused on bringing the past into the present, and that is the crux of AGO’s show.

Material Histories, Living Landscapes is presented in partnership with the 2026 Toronto Biennial of Art (26 September – 20 December), and its focus is on “the tenuous relationships between North American landscapes and Black diasporic experiences.” The first artwork encountered in the gallery is Untitled #25 (Lake Erie and the Sky) (2017), a large-scale shot from the Night Coming Tenderly, Black (2016-2017) series. In this body of work, Bey reimagines rural Ohio landscapes as they would have appeared to enslaved people moving along the Underground Railroad – a network of people, routes and safe houses, which helped enslaved people escape to the North – in the dark. The image is all water and sky, absent of figures. Audiences are encouraged to pause and consider the unspoken narratives that still live in these locations.

The exhibition features further photographs from Bey’s equally powerful series In This Here Place (2019) and Stony the Road (2023). Both are set within historical sites and landscapes through which enslaved Black people were forcibly moved during the transatlantic slave trade. The former comprises images made in Louisiana, along the west banks of the Mississippi River and at the Evergreen, Destrehan, Laura, Oak Alley and Whitney Plantations. The latter follows the Richmond Slave Trail, which begins at Manchester Docks, a major port that made the city the largest hub for the trafficking of enslaved Africans on the east coast of America between 1830 and 1860. Today, it is a pedestrian route that traces the harrowing journey thousands were made to march to auction houses. On view are the haunting gelatin silver prints Branches in the Bayou (2020) and Untitled (Tangles Branches) (2020), which immerse observers in lush vegetation and a sense of unease. It’s an unshakable feeling as you move through the space, where images are hung tightly to “magnify constraint.” Bey says: “I hope that viewers will come to a deeper consideration of history and realise that it does not stay in the past, it very much informs and shapes the present as well.”

At the centre of this installation is the black-and-white two-channel video 350,000 (2023). It also takes the Richmond Slave Trail as its starting point, reimagining the journey made by 350,000 enslaved Africans during the 19th century. Cinematographer Bron Moyi immerses viewers in dense foliage, creating further tension which is only amplified by a soundtrack of staccato breaths and body percussion, made in collaboration with choreographer and Virginia Commonwealth University Professor E. Gaynell Sherrod. By combining lens-based art with sound, as well as African sculptures from the wider AGO collection, Material Histories, Living Landscapes becomes a truly multidisciplinary exhibition that engages the senses.

The show is curated by Allison Glenn, who is also Curator of the 2026 Toronto Biennial of Art. “What Bey’s monumental photographs, presented in situ at the AGO, enable us to do, is to visually represent the enduring dialogues between North America and Africa, and to consider the importance of global waterways to those dialogues,” she says. “A call and response between West African histories in the United States and Canada, seen from the shores of the Great Lakes, this exhibition highlights the historical rupture made manifest by the Middle Passage.” Material Histories, Living Landscapes feels like required viewing. Its power lies in what it doesn’t say. Instead, it encourages us to sit with these landscapes, demonstrating how they can hold, evoke and transmit uncomfortable histories. Here, Bey does not simply look back at the past; he asks audiences to consider how its traces remain embedded in place.

Dawoud Bey: Material Histories, Living Landscapes is at Art Gallery of Ontario until 4 July.

ago.ca

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

Image Credits:

item.title: Pace Gallery Founder Arne Glimcher Criticizes Met Museum Over Planned Galliano Show: Report - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A range of politicians and public figures have criticized the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York for its forthcoming controversial John Galliano show, including dealer Arne Glimcher, the founder of Pace Gallery, one of the biggest such entreprises in the world.

A New York Times report published on Friday revealed that the Met has privately faced criticism over the exhibition for Galliano, a fashion designer who was convicted of a hate crime in France in 2011 for antisemitic comments. He later apologized for these comments and went to rehab. He returned to the industry as creative director of Maison Margiela, a role he held from 2014 to 2024.

The Galliano show is poised to be the Costume Institute’s big May show for next year. But according to the Times, some have warned that mounting the show in that slot may not be a good decision.

As Times reporters Vanessa Friedman and Jacob Bernstein point out, the Met Gala, a highly publicized annual event associated with the Costume Institute’s spring show, is known for taking place on the first Monday in May. Next year, that Monday happens to be Yom HaShoah, otherwise known as Holocaust Remembrance day.

The Times reported that multiple donors have threatened to rescind or withhold gifts since the announcement of the Galliano show in July. Among those donors, it seems, is Glimcher, who reportedly emailed David Breslin, the Met curator in charge of the modern and contemporary art department, to describe his dissatisfaction.

“I don’t think you have considered the cost of this action and its reverberations to come,” Glimcher wrote in the email, according to the Times. He went on to write that he and his wife Milly were “seriously reconsidering other works that have been earmarked from our collection to the Met in our wills,” though it was not clear which works those were and whether or not Glimcher had formalized any promised gifts to the museum.

ARTnews has reached out to Pace Gallery for comment.

Glimcher has previously donated to the Met, gifting it works by Agnes Martin, Lucas Samara, Robert Mangold, and Mark Rothko over the years. With his son, Marc, and former daughter-in-law, Fairfax Dorn, they donated a 1981 Julian Schnabel painting on the ocassion of the Met’s 150th anniversary. All these artists have long been represented by Pace.

The Times article also quoted Elisha Wiesel, the daughter of the writer Elie Wiesel, who described the Galliano show as a “pretty bad idea.” The article also mentioned Julie Menin, the speaker of New York’s City Council, who reportedly wrote that the exhibition was “a serious mistake” in a letter addressed to Met director Max Hollein, Costume Institute head Andrew Bolton, and Vogue editorial director Anna Wintour, who has helped shape the Costume Institute into what it is today and is a co-chair of the Met Gala.

These criticisms have reportedly moved Met board members to discuss the show further. Andrew Solomon, one such board member, told the Times that “confronting cancel culture is a healthier way to go forward than bowing to it.”

Previously, the Times reported that the Met had conferred with representatives of Jewish groups on the exhibition.

In a statement to the Times this week, Hollein said, “The Met has no tolerance for antisemitism, racism or prejudice of any kind. We are in close consultation with Jewish leaders and other stakeholders, and we take the concerns we’ve heard very seriously.”

A Met spokesperson did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for comment.

item.title: The Photographers’ Gallery Examines Our Bond with Trees - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
There are more than 3 trillion trees on Earth, meaning there are 422 times as many trees as people. But that number is half the amount as existed at the beginning of human civilisation, with many cleared for agriculture and urban development. This destruction has accelerated since the Industrial Revolution, and in 2017, one football pitch worth of forest was cut down every second. Yet, they are amongst the most important things on our planet, bringing down temperatures in town and cities by up to 5 degrees; absorbing carbon dioxide; improving physical and mental health; and providing habitats for countless plants, animals and insects. They are, put simply, integral to sustaining life on earth. 

The Photographers’ Gallery presents Roots, a group exhibition that brings together eight internationally acclaimed artists whose work explores trees as the source of origin, memory and belonging. Through photography and mixed media, the show considers how trees are powerful symbols of the places, cultures and histories that shape who we are. Across different global landscapes, the plants symbolise cultural heritage, home and collective memory, and act as witness to the passage of time and the lives lived among them. Artists including Chrystel Lebas, Gohar Dashti, Julie Cockburn, Ingrid Weyland, Michael Kenna, Miho Kajioka and Paul Cupido presents works that reveal the relationships between people and place. 

Julie Cockburn is best-known for embellishing and altering found photographs, immaculately adding hand-embroidered shapes to vintage portraits and landscapes. It’s a craft she’s been honing since childhood, producing works that employ cubist marks, gradient outlines and geometric stamps. In this show, Cockburn adorns blossoms trees, making each individual flower stand out from the page, bringing the vibrancy of a spring day to life. In another image, colourful circles dangle from branches, almost like party decorations. There is a joyfulness to her works, simply reminding viewers that nature, and particular the fleeting moments that only appear seasonally, are something to be celebrated.  

Ingrid Weyland uses her platform to highlight the destruction of our natural landscape. Topographies of Fragility sees the artist manipulate, alter and enact “violent gestures,” contorting images until the landscape becomes something different altogether. Her images are made by crumpling photographs of natural scenery, taken by the artist across the world, before photographing the destroyed image again. The artist explains: “I suddenly realised that the act of crumpling my works on paper had taken on the role of symbolising our human manipulation of nature. My images are possible as they exist on the pulp of paper that was once a tree…the creased paper represents our destructive marks on the landscape.” 

In this show, the cypress tree is taken as a symbol of resilience and cultural identity. The Japanese Sakura cherry blossom signifies the fleeting beauty of life and the hope of renewal. Trees from childhood are revisited and forests reveal hidden histories. Trees become a way to remember and reflect on the fragile relationship between us and the natural world. The artists featured are disparate in their styles and creative methods, but together, they reveal how trees continue to shape our history, memory and culture. 

Roots is at The Photographers’ Gallery, London from 18 September – 15 November: thephotographersgallery.org.uk

Words: Emma Jacob

2. Michael Kenna, Heidodan Sakura Tree.
3. Julie Cockburn, Pink Tree.
4. Michael Kenna, Spring Poplar Trees.
5. Julie Cockburn, Crop.

item.title: Maybe This Fall Will Be Kind - Hyperallergic
item.description:
From a high platform in the Broadway Junction station, I see a forlorn cloud hovering over the rooftops of East Brooklyn. The sky around it is perfectly clear. The next morning, I find it still standing in the same spot, but it’s faded, famished. That’s how bad things have gotten: The loneliness epidemic has now reached the clouds. 

Espresso in Williamsburg, watermelon juice in Ditmas Park, writing session in Ridgewood, soccer camp in Bed-Stuy. At a street corner, a mural by @blkopslife shows a hand holding a famous 1964 photo of Malcom X leaning on the shoulder of his tuxedoed friend, Muhammad Ali. It’s in a Black neighborhood that’s been almost completely gentrified.

Dolly Parton suddenly dies at 80. She touched the hearts of millions working nine to five. Sliman Mansour dies at 79. He carried the weight of Palestinian pain on his back. I hope he catches a break in the afterlife. And then Yayoi Kusama follows, passing at 97. She’ll live on for eternity thanks to her Infinity Mirrored Rooms. At lunch, the guy from the falafel place tells me that all humans were created from a single soul. I say that sounds good, but no lettuce for me, please. I fear it more than death these days.    

I watch clips of China’s humanoid robot olympics and don’t know whether to be amused or frightened. One robot boxer keeps jumping and kicking long after its head is ripped off. At a cafe, I overhear a businessman on a Zoom call announcing, “We’re going to make a big AI push towards the end of the year.” On the other end of the call I see the workers who will probably be replaced by that AI.

I laugh at first when I hear that Vancouver police raided an art gallery because someone mistook a sculpture for a man in need of medical assistance. But then it turns out that passed out men are a common sight in the streets of the opioid crisis-stricken city.  

The moon is about to turn full, and a lot of aggression starts to make sense. A place called Insomnia Cookies is ironically most empty at night. Summer is on its hind legs, still acting out. Thousands flee for their lives from a huge wave in Nepal. But fall is pushing in, and I do believe it will be kind. 

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Yayoi Kusama, Artist of Infinities, Dies at 97

Artist Yayoi Kusama, who channeled psychological phenomena into impossibly kaleidoscopic artworks that enamored millions around the world, died in a hospital in Tokyo on August 14 at the age of 97. The news of her death was announced by her studio and David Zwirner Gallery today, August 26.

The labor-intensive quality of her works, combined with a Borgesian fascination with mirrors and the infinite, an openness about mental health struggles, and her ever-present red bob, rendered her an icon closer to a rock star or a spiritual leader than a contemporary artist. | Valentina Di Liscia

item.title: The After Nature Prize RevealsUntold Stories in the Landscape - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
This autumn, exhibition space C/O Berlin brings together works by Stelios Kallinikou and Susanne Kriemann, recipients of the After Nature Ulrike Crespo Photography Prize 2026. Every year, the award recognises two environmentally conscious lens-based artists, each taking away a €40,000 cash prize alongside an exhibition and accompanying publication. Established in 2024, the initiative reflects the growing urgency of artistic responses to the climate crisis. Its previous winners include image-makers from around the world, including Lisa Barnard, Isadora Romero, Laura Huertas Millán and Sarker Protick.

This year, the Prize presents Kallinikou’s (b. 1985) Cliffs Among Dreams, a collection of photographs, films and sculptural assemblages which explore the Akrotiri peninsula in southern Cyprus. This is a place where ecological diversity and military infrastructure are intertwined. Akrotiri is a Sovereign Base Area, which has remained under British sovereignty since Cyprus gained independence in 1960. It is home to both a Royal Air Force base and the island’s largest natural inland body of water. The Akrotiri Salt Lake is a major wetland and stopover for migratory birds. As such, Kallinikou’s compositions are full of contradictions: flamingos rest whilst antennas and radar systems soar into the air. Elsewhere, other wildlife, insects and rock formations intersect with military infrastructure, fences and air traffic. Kallinikou also turns his attention to the cliffs of Aetokremnos, one of Cyprus’s most important archaeological sites. The show raises geopolitical questions whilst touching on themes of migration, belonging and extinction, all set against the backdrop of an island which has been divided since Turkey invaded the north in 1974.

Kriemann (b. 1972), meanwhile, showcases Im Fieber der Sonne flattern Schmetterlinge im Bauch (In the Sun’s Fever Flutter Butterflies in the Stomach), which examines remnants of the industrial era and atomic age. The German artist’s long-standing engagement with radioactivity was initially motivated by the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, which has remained a recurring motif in her research. Now, her focus is on former uranium extraction sites in Saxony, Thuringia and the Limousin region in France – locations where radiation is present in architecture, flora and the soil. C/O Berlin presents Kriemann’s body of work Pechblende (Pitchblende), which employs a cameraless image-making process known as autoradiography, where radioactive substances directly expose photographic film to create an image. It also foregrounds her latest series, Pechblende (Fever), which incorporates samples of uranium-bearing ore and dried plant specimens, collected from former mining sites that have since been environmentally remediated. Other pieces on display were made by burying unexposed sheet film in a reclaimed mine waste heap near Dresden. Throughout, Kriemann’s experimental methodology brings traces to light that would otherwise go unseen.

Both Kallinikou and Kriemann take us to places where human activity has had a profound impact on ecosystems. They transport audiences to regions under military control, through contaminated landscapes and even deep into the soil itself. These are artists who make the invisible visible: demonstrating the enduring power of the photographic image to reveal truths that cannot always be seen with the naked eye.

After Nature Prize 26 is at C/O Berlin from 12 September – 20 January 2027.

co-berlin.org

Words: Eleanor Sutherland

item.title: Robert Indiana’s Maine Home Is for Sale, Despite Late Artist’s Intentions to Make It an Art Space - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The foundation established by Robert Indiana to preserve his legacy is selling the artist’s longtime home on the Maine island of Vinalhaven, despite instructions in his will that the property be transformed into an art space open to the public.

The Star of Hope Foundation, as the foundation is called, listed this week Indiana’s former home, a rambling 19th-century Odd Fellows lodge known as the Star of Hope, for $1.4 million, according to the New York Times. A second building Indiana owned, a few doors away, is being offered for $210,000. 

Indiana, best known for his “LOVE” series, with its iconic tilted O, moved to Vinalhaven in 1978 and spent the next 40 years living in the Star of Hope, a local landmark overlooking the island’s harbor. He died in 2018 at age 89. 

Indiana had specific plans for the building after his death. His will directed that the Star of Hope be restored “to museum quality” and used as an art environment open to the public for visits, classes and lectures and for the preservation and exhibition of his collection, according to the Times. The artist had established the Star of Hope Foundation to preserve his legacy, and the organization inherited his estate after his death. 

The foundation initially began working toward that goal, stabilizing and partly renovating the aging building. Now, however, it says its mission would be better served by getting out of the property-management business and putting its resources directly toward artists and arts organizations in Maine.

“These properties are not our purpose — supporting artists is,” Carole Martin, the foundation’s managing director, told the Times. “Selling these properties allows us to convert those assets into philanthropic capital and put resources directly into Maine’s arts community.”

The decision has drawn criticism from people who say selling Indiana’s home runs counter to the artist’s wishes. Kevin Lipson, a partner at Venable, the law firm that represented Indiana’s estate in litigation, called the decision “a remarkable repudiation of Robert Indiana’s testamentary intent” in an interview with the Times, adding that Indiana “wanted and expected a museum of some sort on Vinalhaven and that apparently is not in the cards.”

Marjorie Stratton, Vinalhaven’s town manager, who knew Indiana, also questioned the decision. Speaking in a personal capacity, she told the Times that Indiana had discussed using the building for art, education, and research and providing space where young people could work and learn about art.

“It just makes me sad that this foundation doesn’t seem to be following through with what he told me he wanted that to be,” Stratton said.

The Star of Hope was in rough shape by the time Indiana died. Its paint was peeling, clapboards were rotting, and a tarp covered a leaking roof, according to the Times. The foundation subsequently addressed some of these concerns, repairing its Mansard roof and restoring its windows and doors. But photographs accompanying the current listing show an interior still in various states of disrepair, including peeling paint, exposed framing and lath. 

The foundation said the building continues to present structural and regulatory problems and described selling it as a practical way to redirect its resources.

“We are one of many organizations trying to solve a hard problem — how to bring new life to a building that has sat empty for years,” Martin told the Times, adding that selling the property while investing directly in local artists and organizations was “the most honest path forward.”

Not everyone on Vinalhaven opposes the move. Elaine Crossman, who also knew Indiana and owns a motel and art gallery on the town’s Main Street, told the Times that the renovation appeared to have become an expensive quagmire. She hopes a new owner might return the building to active use, including reopening its first-floor storefronts.

“I’m optimistic that this is actually a really positive move,” Crossman said. “My hope would be that this is a big step in the right direction for that group to be able to do some positive work in the community.”

item.title: Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation Denied Use of Roy Cohn Portrait for New Biography Over Political Concerns - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation denied the use of a 1981 portrait by the artist of notorious New York lawyer Roy M. Cohn for the cover of a forthcoming biography, titled American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump, because of its negative affiliation with the sitting US president, according to the New York Times.

The portrait in question, simply titled Roy Cohn, captures the lawyer’s striking outward stare and scar-split nose head on, surrounded by a black backdrop, a signature of Mapplethorpe’s images during the final decade of his life.

At the time it was made, Cohn was the subject of an interview for an issue of Andy Warhol’s Interview magazine. Writer and book editor Steven M.L. Aronson, who authored the piece, convinced Cohn to pose for Mapplethorpe, who was at the peak of his fame at the time. By then, Cohn was a major New York figure who, by day, represented mobsters, moguls, and media barons, including then real estate developer and protégé Donald Trump; by night, he partied at Studio.

The subject was unusual, yet notable for Mapplethorpe, who during the 1970s turned his lens on New York’s S&M scene, most notably in his “X Portfolio” (1978); in the early ’80s, he was just beginning to start photographing high-profile celebrities, collectors, and artists. Despite being publicly anti-gay, however, Cohn himself was secretly closeted. Before the end of the ’80s, both Cohn and Mapplethorpe died from AIDS-related complications.

A print of the photograph was acquired by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the J. Paul Getty Trust, via a gift from the Mapplethorpe foundation in 2011.

The Mapplethorpe Foundation, which oversees the artist’s estate and collection, reportedly decided against licensing the image’s use for American Scoundrel, co-authored by Kai Bird and Susan Goldmark, because of President Trump’s negative characterization in the book. As a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit, the foundation is prohibited from engaging in certain political activities and was reportedly concerned that the image’s use on the book cover would be considered a political act. The artist started his eponymous foundation shortly before his death “to protect his work, to advance his creative vision and to promote the causes he cared about,” according to its website.

According to the Times, “the foundation’s board feared that Mr. Trump could retaliate, perhaps by threatening its nonprofit tax status,” if he took offense to his characterization in the book. For his part, Trump has been heavily involved in taking aim at cultural institutions during his second administration, including forcing changes at the Smithsonian Institution and taking control of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Bird told the Times he “thunderstruck” and “outraged” at the foundation’s decision, adding “It’s astonishing that these people are being so cowed, so easily.” The Mapplethorpe declined to comment to the Times about Bird’s comments. (A request for further comment from ARTnews was also not returned.)

Part of Mapplethorpe’s legacy is a controversy surrounding the censorship of his work. In 1989, months after his death, the now-defunct Corcoran Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., canceled its presentation of a traveling retrospective because of the inclusion of the “X Portfolio.” The institution had received a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts to realize the exhibition, which conservative politicians took issue with, catapulting Mapplethorpe’s to the center of the era’s culture wars.

“The idea that a photograph of a dead mobster lawyer could somehow qualify as political activity, even under the Trump administration, is hard to fathom,” Suzanne Nossel, a former chief executive of the free expression group PEN America, told the Times of the foundation’s decision. “And yet, we’re in an environment where no one feels they can rule anything out.”

item.title: Thieves Snatch $4.6M Diamond Necklace From Viennese Museum - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Two visitors smashed a display case and made off with a platinum and diamond necklace at the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna yesterday afternoon, August 27.

Per the Viennese daily newspaper Der Standard, the Van Cleef & Arpels necklace was last appraised at $4.6 million by Sotheby's. It was displayed as part of Glanzstücke, an ongoing exhibition featuring over 500 works gathered from the museum's design collection and the French luxury jewelry house.

The 200-karat, 673-white diamond necklace was designed in 1939 for Egyptian Queen Nazli on the occasion of her daughter Princess Fawzia's marriage to Iranian Prince Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, who later became Iran's last shah.

A press statement from the museum confirmed the theft, but officials declined to comment further due to the ongoing investigation.

Austrian media outlets reported that the two men paid for their ticketed entry into the museum before approaching the display case containing the necklace, a set of earrings, and a double-clip brooch from the same collection, along with two decorative wares.

item.title: The Belgian Exhibition That Strives to "Decenter" the West - Hyperallergic
item.description:
BRUGES, Belgium — With its cobblestone streets, glossy green canals, and stepped gable townhouses, Bruges has the self-contained and unchanging quality of a scene in a snow globe. Bigger Picture: Connected worlds of Bruges 900-1550 seeks to bust this myth, demonstrating the extent of the city’s historical connection with the rest of the world. The inaugural exhibition of BRUSK — “BRU” for Bruges and “SK” for schone kunsten (“fine art”) — a large new gallery attached to the Groeningemuseum, the show is guest curated by Peter Frankopan, an Oxford medievalist and author of a popular history of the Silk Road. In addition to demonstrating Bruges’s global connections, the exhibition also invokes the notion of decentering the “West” from its self-appointed position as the hub of civilization, via a video presentation, starring Frankopan, that plays at its entry. 

With these two somewhat contradictory briefs — to both decenter Europe and show Bruges’s centrality in international networks — the exhibition is off to a bumpy start. A further complication is the vast number and type of objects on display: There are over 250 items, ranging from a surprisingly covetable chain mail jacket and underwhelming shreds of ancient silk to significant paintings by Titian, Jan van Eyck, and Hans Memling, as well as religious relics, manuscripts of North African and European origin, Turkish carpets, Viking artifacts, coins, religious garb, and more.

To manage this vast range of materials, the exhibition is divided into four “worlds,” each defined by its own intricately designed enclosure delimited by hanging cloth. The “North Sea World,” for instance, is made up of triangular panels that recall sails, while the “Mediterranean World” is under a pavilion-style tent. Each world also has a distinct soundscape — the Mediterranean is evoked by a twitter of birds and the sound of creaking wagon wheels. “The World of Christianity” has bells and more birds. The “World of the Court” is accompanied, like a medieval feast, by gentle plucking on string instruments. In the darkened gallery, the worlds form dramatically lit islands, linked by white lines painted on the floor. Aided by the inventive but not illuminating animations playing in each world, the whole installation is reminiscent of the opening credits for Game of Thrones.

item.title: Demolition of Georgian Architectural Landmark Sparks Outcry - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Demolitions are underway on the Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall in Tbilisi, Georgia, prompting outcry from local community members and the architects who designed the two-structure complex. 

Set against the historic 19th-century buildings that define the capital city's dominant style, the landmark is known as the “Rike Tubes” for its futuristic appearance, a reminder of the country’s modernist push from the 2000s to the early 2010s.

The Tbilisi City Hall’s Architectural Service issued the demolition permit in June to the owner, Rike Dom, with the dismantling process commencing last month and due to wrap up by December. In interviews with Reuters and local outlets, many expressed concerns with the decision, describing the tourist hotspot as a defining feature of the capital city skyline.

Italian architects Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas, of Fuksas Studio, were asked to design the complex for musical performance and contemporary art exhibitions in 2010, under then-Prime Minister Nika Gilauri and United National Movement (UNM) President Mikheil Saakashvili (who has been in prison for nearly five years for abuse of power charges). Construction began on the glass-and-steel tubes in 2011. When the conservative Georgian Dream party came into power in 2012, officials froze construction, leaving the project unfinished.

item.title: China Pulls Artists from Gwangju Biennale as ‘Taiwan Pavilion’ Moves Forward - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Chinese ambassador to South Korea has ordered China’s artists to withdraw from the 16th Gwangju Biennale, which opens September 5, in protest of the Gwangju Biennial Foundation allowing Taiwanese exhibitors to participate under the name “Taiwan,” South Korean media reported today. 

In a meeting with Gwangju Mayor Min Hyung-bae at Gwangju City Hall yesterday, Ambassador Dai Bing expressed his “regret and concern” over the decision to restore the name “Taiwan Pavilion” at the request of Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture, the Munhwa Broadcasting Corporation (MBC) reported. 

Speaking on behalf of the Chinese Embassy, Dai then demanded Chinese curators and  installation staff to halt their preparations and withdraw from the Hajeongung Art Museum in Gwangju, which was set to host their special exhibition.

MBC reports that Min told Dai during their meeting that “political considerations should not affect the field of art.”

The Gwangju Biennale Foundation has been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute with Taiwan for more than year over the renaming of a satellite exhibition from the “Taiwan Pavilion” to the “NTMoFA Pavilion,” referencing its commissioning institution, the National Taiwan Museum of Fine Arts. The two parties disagreed over the circumstances surrounding the name change, with Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture ultimately accusing the GBF of “political censorship” in an August 15 statement.

GBF denied allegations that it had acted without Taiwan’s consent in an effort to appease Beijing, which does not recognize the sovereignty of the self-governed island. But the dispute quickly escalated into a reputational crisis for the biennale, with artists from Taiwan and China condemning the name change as a betrayal of its founding ideals.

The biennale was established in 1994 to commemorate the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, a deadly chapter in South Korea’s struggle against military rule, during which upwards of 2,300 South Korean civilians were estimated to have been killed.

On Tuesday, the GBF announced that Taiwan’s exhibition at its September edition can open as the “Taiwan Pavilion,” and be advertised as such in its promotional materials. 

In a statement to the South Korean press, the Gwangju Biennale said, “There is not much time left until the opening on September 5, and we are closely monitoring the situation, hoping the exhibition will proceed smoothly.”

item.title: Rotterdam’s Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen Embroiled in Alleged Bribery Scandal - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Two municipal employees in the Dutch city of Rotterdam have been dismissed following an investigation into alleged corruption involving construction contracts. They include work connected to asbestos removal at Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen, one of the country’s most important museums.

The employees were among three officials investigated after concerns emerged that municipal contracts had been approved at inflated prices. One of the three has since retired, while the other two were suspended and have now been fired.

Rotterdam mayor Carola Schouten said an internal investigation found that the two employees had violated the city’s code of conduct by accepting gifts from companies doing business with the municipality in return for possible preferential treatment. They are also suspected of forgery and passive bribery.

The allegations first came to wider attention in 2023, when Dutch newspaper NRC Handelsblad reported concerns about possible corruption surrounding construction projects at Rotterdam cultural institutions, including the asbestos treatment at Boijmans Van Beuningen. The city subsequently asked police to investigate, and a criminal inquiry by the public prosecutor remains underway.

The city’s executive board said information received from prosecutors in July indicated that the two employees’ conduct was “substantially worse” than had emerged during the initial internal investigation.
Diederik van Dommelen, Rotterdam’s head of financial affairs, told the Art Newspaper the ongoing criminal investigation limits what the city can disclose. The dismissed employees can challenge their termination through an employment tribunal.

Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen has declined to comment, saying responsibility for its buildings and their renovation rests with the municipality.

The museum closed in 2019 for a major redevelopment. Its collection has remained partly accessible through Depot Boijmans Van Beuningen, which opened in 2021 and houses around 154,000 works. The museum is currently slated to reopen in 2029 following the renovation, which includes making the building asbestos free.

item.title: What I Got Wrong About Krasner and Pollock - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Earlier this year, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced its forthcoming exhibition Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous on Instagram, alongside a photograph of the artists by Hans Namuth. Seething, I looked to the comments for affirmation. I didn't have to scroll for long. "Give her a solo show!"

Months earlier, I had visited the Pollock-Krasner House in Springs, East Hampton, knowing far more about Jackson Pollock than I did Lee Krasner. I am a painter myself, and I had come to Springs in the wreck of yet another failed relationship … with a painter. I thought I already knew Krasner's story. I thought her story was partly my own.

The first stop on the tour was Krasner's studio: a small second-floor bedroom overlooking Accabonac Creek. The guide told us Pollock would displace Krasner when it was too cold to paint in the barn, and how she would then work by the warmth of the kitchen stove: a woman in the kitchen in the 1950s, working around her husband's tempestuousness. In the living room, we learned how Krasner navigated gender bias, poverty, and Pollock's alcoholism while using her own credibility in the art world to promote his paintings, the sales of which supported their frugal life. I mourned all the paintings that could have been had she not been saddled with such a mess.

Then we crossed the lawn to the barn and its famous floor, where Pollock developed his drip technique. But I stared instead at the bare rectangles on the walls, fringed with splattered paint, the spaces where Krasner's canvases had hung. After Pollock's death, it took her a year to claim the studio. When she finally did, she painted at a sweeping scale and filled the barn with her own explosive work. As the guide described Krasner's grief-induced insomnia, I couldn't reconcile it: Why, when she finally had the studio her spirit and ambition deserved, when she was rid of the weight of that difficult man, was she so bereft?

The tour ended, and I grumbled my way into the gift shop. Still looking for an injustice to protest, I struck up a conversation with an employee about women painters. He placed a large yellow book in my hands, saying, "This is a wonderful introduction, not just to Lee, but to the other women of Abstract Expressionism." Only then did he introduce himself: Matthew Ward, director of the Pollock-Krasner House. I bought Mary Gabriel's Ninth Street Women (2018), and we said goodbye.

In the following months, I made a series of drawings from my photographs of the house and finished Gabriel's book. I sent Matt a short video of the work, and he suggested we discuss it over a call. About a week before we spoke, The Met announced the show. I assumed Matt would commiserate with me over the decision to exhibit Krasner alongside Pollock, but he was excited.

"A lot of people don't know this, but for two of the most avant-garde artists of their time, they led surprisingly domestic lives,” he told me. “They slept in separate beds, and they made appointments to visit each other's studios. The romance was in the passion for their art, in what the other was doing on canvas."

Throughout our conversation, I was struck by how often Matt said "they" and "them." He rarely referred to one artist apart from the other. Every time I tried to steer him toward Krasner's sacrifices, he returned to their partnership. "He was the face of their business, but she managed everything. I'm not sure Jackson would have kept painting if it weren't for Lee."

Then he offered a thought that astonished me. He described Krasner's habit of destroying and reassembling older paintings that no longer felt true to the artist she had become, and wondered whether she had done something similar with her memories of Pollock. She outlived him by almost three decades. Perhaps she had revised the relationship to align with the Lee Krasner she became.

Still, I couldn't imagine anyone who knew Krasner's life intimately thinking The Met's decision was right. When I googled "contact Mary Gabriel," the most promising result was an author page on her publisher's website. I sent my note into the void and began working on a backup plan. Four days later, the author agreed to a Zoom call from her home in Ireland.

item.title: UK Government Puts Temporary Export Ban on $97.2 M. Rembrandt Painting - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The United Kingdom’s government announced this week that it has put a temporary export ban on a Rembrandt painting valued at £71.7 million ($97.2 million).

The painting in question is Rembrandt van Rijn’s Portrait of Catrina Hooghsaet (1657), which has been on view in the UK since the mid-18th century, according to a release. It was most recently on view at the National Museum of Cardiff from 2016 to 2019.

Rembrandt’s portrait depicts Catrina Hooghsaet, a wealthy member of Amsterdam’s 17th-century Mennonite community who lived separately from her husband. Measuring around 49 inches by 37 inches, the dramatically lit painting shows Hooghsaet, wearing traditional clothing, seated as she stares off into the distance. She holds a white lace in one hand, and behind her is a intricate oriental rug used as tablecloth, as was the style during the period.

“Painted in the final phase of his career, Rembrandt’s portrait of Catrina Hooghsaet ranks amongst his finest achievements. It belongs to a rare group of large-scale three-quarter-length portraits and stands out for its delicacy, refinement, and exceptional finish,” Andrew Hochhauser, who chaired the committee that recommended the export band, said in a statement. “Rembrandt transforms her relatively ordinary features into a striking image of beauty through his sensitivity, honesty and profound psychological insight.”

The goal of the export ban is to prevent the work from “being taken out of the country permanently” and that a UK museum or institution have “the opportunity to save this masterpiece for the nation,” according to a press release. The hefty price tag is “the most expensive object ever to be given national treasure status,” per the release.

“The Portrait of Catrina Hooghsaet has been part of the UK’s cultural life for centuries,” recently appointed arts minister Ruth Mackenzie said in statement. “The scale, beauty and history of this masterpiece make it a priority for cultural partners, funders, philanthropists, and lovers of Rembrandt to help this masterpiece keep its historical place in the UK.”

The export ban, which will last until December 26 (inclusive), was recommended by the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest, which advises Secretary of State for Culture, Media, and Sport. After that period, the current owners will have 15 business days to accept any offers “at the recommended price of £71,696,324.90 (plus VAT of £754,698.15),” per the release. A second deferral period, lasting nine months, could also be triggered after the parties sign an option agreement.

The committee found that Portrait of Catrina Hooghsaet met the three criteria needed for an export ban, according to the release: “In this case, the painting was recognised for its strong connection with our history and national life, its exceptional aesthetic quality, and its importance to the study of Rembrandt and his work.”

“This is a painting of outstanding aesthetic importance, of outstanding significance to our cultural history,” Hochhauser, the committee chair, added in his statement. “It is also of outstanding significance to the study of the history of portraiture, the oeuvre of Rembrandt and the history of collecting his work in Britain. This enormously important painting should be saved for the nation and kept on public display in this country.”

According to the provenance provided by the UK culture ministry, the painting was first owned by its sitter, who died in 1685; it then passed to her third husband Jan Schildt, who died in 1686. Its fate for the next six decades is unclear until it entered the UK by 1752, when it was likely acquired by John Fane, Lord Le Despencer, 7th Earl of Westmorland, for his Mereworth House in Kent. It passed through the family until an 1831 sale and later sold at Christie’s twice more, in 1846 and 1860.

After that sale, the portrait eventually came into the possession of Colonel the Hon. Edward Douglas-Pennant, 1st Baron Penrhyn of Llandegai and seems to have remained in his family until a 2015 private sale by Sotheby’s. The most recent 2025 sale, which sparked the export ban, was privately brokered by Christie’s.

Artnet News reported market speculation that the painting’s seller is possibly Rosaline Wong, a Hong Kong–based art adviser who has been linked with some of China’s most important collectors, including Joseph Lau and Henry Cheng Kar-shun, the father of Adrian Cheng. In 2023, Wong was reportedly involved in the sale of two paintings by Gustav Klimt. (Christie’s declined to comment on the identities of its buyers or sellers.)

The outlet also reported that Old Master dealer Otto Naumann estimated that the painting could actually be worth about $150 million, or more than twice the value given by the UK government.

The UK government regularly issues temporary export bans on major artworks. The most high-profile of these recently is Joshua Reynold’s Portrait of Omai (Mai), ca. 1776, which received an export ban in 2022; the following year, the National Gallery in London jointly acquired the work for £50 million ($61.9 million) with the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, where it will go on view next month.

item.title: Chief Executive of Sydney’s Forthcoming $915 M. Cultural Institution Steps Down Amid Ongoing Investigations, 10 Weeks Ahead of Its Opening - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Just 10 weeks prior to the opening of Sydney’s latest cultural institution, Powerhouse Parramatta, its chief executive Lisa Havilah has stepped down amid ongoing “investigations into governance and procurement,” according to a statement released on Thursday from the office of Australia’s Minister for Arts John Graham.

Since her 2018 appointment, Havilah has been overseeing the $915 million build of Powerhouse Parramatta—the city’s most significant cultural infrastructure project since the Sydney Opera House, which opened in 1973 for an estimated cost of AU$102 million.

Havilah previously served as the director of Carriageworks in Redfern, a suburb of Sydney, for more than seven years. She joined Powerhouse, which is also known as the Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences (MAAS), as its CEO in 2019.

In Havilah’s absence, an interim team will oversee the organization in the months ahead of its inauguration, with Abbie Galvin, the government architect for New South Wales, stepping in as CEO and former Sydney Opera House CEO Louise Herron named strategic adviser; both are expected to start on September 1. The opening date of Powerhouse Parramatta, set for November 7, is not expected to be impacted.

“I think obviously, it’s challenging … these things are always somewhat surprising,” Powerhouse Trust president David Borger told radio station 702 ABC Sydney of Havilah’s departure. “Obviously it’s not an ideal situation this close to the opening.”

Earlier this year, Australian politician Chris Rath raised budget concerns that Havilah vehemently denied; however, it is unclear if this issue is directly connected to the current investigation.

A spokesperson for the Department of Creative Industries characterized the situation as “complex and involv[ing] multiple lines of inquiry” to Australian broadcaster ABC News, but offered no further details.

“The Department has a responsibility to address these matters with due diligence and procedural fairness,” the spokesperson added. “As the investigation is continuing and no formal findings or conclusions have been made, it would not be appropriate to provide further comment at this stage.”

Powerhouse Parramatta did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for further comment.

item.title: Kennedy Center Board Says It Will Delay Adding Trump’s Name to the Center by One Month - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Kennedy Center board told a federal judge on Thursday that it will halt efforts to add President Trump’s name to the building until at least October 8, delaying its plans by a month.

The announcement followed an emergency court hearing prompted by a Justice Department filing this week warning that the Kennedy Center could be demolished and potentially replaced with an outdoor amphitheater if the board is not allowed to close the building for two years for repairs. At the same time, the board is pushing to inscribe President Trump’s name on the front of the building, with the line “Restored and renovated by President Donald J. Trump” beneath John F. Kennedy’s name. 

President Trump’s name was added to the front of the building in December 2025, but U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ordered it removed in May 2026, ruling that only Congress has the authority to change the center’s name. The name was ultimately removed in June, but the board defied Cooper’s ruling and announced it would rename the building. A tarp has blocked the façade since.

During Thursday’s two-hour hearing, CNN reports, Cooper repeatedly pressed Justice Department lawyers to explain why Trump’s name needed to be added as soon as September 8. Cooper, an appointee of former President Barack Obama, called the date arbitrary and said he was prepared to issue a temporary order barring any renaming of the building while the legal battle continues. 

The Justice Department is arguing that Trump’s name should be added to the building to acknowledge his “ongoing” contributions to its upkeep. In a Monday court filing, the DOJ said Trump secured $258 million in congressional funding for capital restoration in 2025 and recruited donors to finance an endowment. His lawyers argued that his “efforts and prestige” provide the “sole hope for the Center’s financial survival and structural renewal,” and that without his involvement, the Kennedy Center will “continue to be in a financial and structural death spiral.”

The latest legal challenge was brought by Democratic Representative Joyce Beatty, an ex officio member of the center’s board who has led the months-long legal challenge against the DOJ. It argued that even if the court accepted Trump’s argument, renaming the Kennedy Center would violate congressional authority and Cooper’s prior order. 

DOJ lawyer Brantley Mayers reportedly framed the government’s main argument around the need to add Trump’s name to the center to ensure continued private donations, prompting a swift rebuttal from Cooper: “What does that have to do with what Congress intended in the statutes?” 

Cooper ruled earlier this year that the board violated federal law by renaming the venue “The Donald J. Trump and The John F. Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts,” which Congress designated as a living memorial to Kennedy.

The center has also proposed naming its plaza after Trump and adding another reference to him if its endowment reaches $100 million. The administration argues that naming the plaza for Trump would not violate the laws designating the center as a memorial to Kennedy. 

Cooper reportedly pushed back on the argument on Thursday, noting that the DOJ’s reasoning could allow the board to name the parking garage after former President Barack Obama or the campus after former President George W. Bush, effectively giving it broad authority to rename any part of the property.

“The whole thing would be for sale, basically — and that would be consistent with Congress’ overall scheme?” Cooper asked.

The DOJ offered no rebuttal.

item.title: PhotoDalkeith RSA200: Two Centuries of Seeing Scotland - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Photography does more than preserve history; it constructs it. At Dalkeith Palace, PhotoDalkeith RSA200 brings two centuries of Scottish image-making into dialogue, from the pioneering calotypes of David Octavius Hill and Robert Adamson to contemporary practices that question how place, identity and memory are represented. The exhibition forms part of the Royal Scottish Academy’s bicentenary programme, drawing on the institution’s collection while introducing new commissions and recent work. Rather than presenting photography as a straightforward chronology, its ambition is to reveal the changing ways in which Scotland has looked at itself, and how those images have, in turn, shaped cultural memory.

David Octavius Hill provides an important point of departure because his photographic experiments belong to a moment when the medium was still negotiating its relationship with art, evidence and observation. His collaboration with Robert Adamson produced some of the defining images of early Scottish photography, while the RSA’s own collection preserves a wider record of nineteenth-century practice. An album of early Scottish photographs held by the Academy, for instance, includes work by Hill, Dr Thomas Keith, James Good Tunny and Dr William Walker, documenting Edinburgh and other locations while recording buildings threatened with demolition. Photography therefore entered Scottish cultural history as a technology capable of preserving a world already undergoing change.

That relationship between image and disappearance remains relevant to the exhibition’s contemporary material. Landscape is never entirely innocent: it carries histories of ownership, labour, migration, tourism and belonging, even when a photograph appears to offer nothing more than an expansive view. Walter Dalkeith’s contribution, for example, places photography within the longer visual history of the Buccleuch estate, while the exhibition’s setting at Dalkeith Palace introduces another layer of historical consciousness. His earlier PhotoDalkeith project brought historic photographs from the Buccleuch family albums into conversation with new images of the same landscape, demonstrating how the archive can become a starting point for contemporary interpretation rather than a fixed record of the past.

Landscape consequently becomes a question of framing as much as geography. Thomas Joshua Cooper RSA, Wendy McMurdo RSA, Graham Fagen RSA and Calum Colvin RSA are among the contemporary artists whose work is brought into proximity with the historical material, creating a different understanding of what photographic representation can be. Cooper’s sustained attention to remote environments, for instance, positions landscape as an encounter rather than a backdrop, while other practices in the exhibition move towards constructed, mediated or technologically altered forms of image-making. Such contrasts prevent the history of Scottish photography from becoming a nostalgic sequence of views. Instead, they reveal a medium negotiating the distance between what is seen and imagined.

Curatorial decisions are therefore central to the exhibition’s argument. Calum Colvin RSA is amongst the curators, with the presentation combining works from the RSA collection with pieces from artists’ studios and new commissions created for the project by Colvin, Caroline Douglas, and Irvine & Spence. That arrangement makes chronology only one possible way of reading the exhibition; correspondence, interruption and reinterpretation become equally important. Historical photographs acquire different meanings when placed beside contemporary practices, while new work is inevitably affected by the visual histories surrounding it. The result is a conversation between generations of image-makers.

Caroline Douglas occupies an especially interesting position within that conversation. Her involvement in the new work for PhotoDalkeith RSA200, alongside the dedicated Hill & Adamson event later in the exhibition programme, brings contemporary practice directly into contact with the history of Scottish photography. The event, featuring Douglas alongside publisher Alexander Hamilton and historian Sara Stevenson, considers the continuing legacy of Hill and Adamson before a tour led by Colvin, Julie Lawson and Sandy Wood. This emphasis on return and reinterpretation reflects a broader shift within contemporary museum culture, where archives are increasingly treated not as sealed repositories but as active sites for questioning how histories are assembled.

Such questions become particularly charged when photography is considered as a record of identity. Portraiture has always carried an implicit claim to knowledge: to photograph someone is to propose that an image can communicate something about who they are. Contemporary artists complicate that assumption by foregrounding staging, mediation and the politics of looking. Within the wider selection, artists including Sekai Machache, Rachel MacLean RSA (Elect), Wendy McMurdo RSA and Leena Nammari RSA represent different approaches to a medium increasingly conscious of its own constructedness. Their presence alongside historical photography makes visible a profound change from the early belief in the camera’s evidential authority towards an understanding of the image as something culturally contingent.

The archive itself reinforces that tension. Nineteenth-century photographs can appear authoritative precisely because of their distance from the present, yet their survival is never accidental; institutions, collectors and families determine which images are preserved, catalogued and displayed. The RSA’s relationship with photography has developed through precisely these structures of selection, from its historic collection to awards, Academicians and contemporary commissions. Its bicentenary therefore offers an opportunity to examine the mechanisms through which continuity is produced. What survives becomes part of the story, while what remains outside the frame can be equally revealing.

Public space extends that argument beyond the walls of the Palace. Large-scale photographic installations and interactive frames across Dalkeith Country Park invite visitors to encounter the exhibition within the landscape itself, shifting photography from an object to be contemplated towards an activity that can be shared and reproduced. The gesture is apt in an era when image-making is no longer confined to artists, photographers or institutions. Smartphones, social platforms and digital archives have transformed virtually everyone into a producer of photographs, yet the sheer volume of images has not diminished their power. If anything, it has made questions of selection, attention and memory more urgent.

Photography’s contemporary condition also explains why an exhibition of historical material can feel unexpectedly current. The camera now operates across documentary journalism, personal archives, surveillance, advertising and algorithmic systems, making the boundaries between public and private images increasingly unstable. Against this accelerated visual culture, the act of looking at a nineteenth-century photograph can seem almost radical in its slowness. The historical image asks us to consider not only what happened, but what someone once decided was worth recording. PhotoDalkeith RSA200 uses that pause to connect the medium’s origins with the conditions of looking today.

The wider programme deliberately expands the conversation beyond photography itself. A performance and film event devoted to Ian Hamilton Finlay, a dramatic recreation of John Ruskin’s 1853 Edinburgh lecture, and Orkney Sequence, bringing Victoria Crowe’s paintings into dialogue with music by Gemma McGregor, place photography within a larger network of visual, literary and musical culture. That breadth matters because Scotland’s visual identity has never been produced by one medium alone. Landscape painting, architecture, poetry, music and photography have repeatedly borrowed from and challenged one another, shaping ideas of nation and place in the process. The exhibition’s events programme makes those connections explicit rather than treating photography as an isolated specialist history.

Scotland consequently emerges not as a single photographic subject but as a collection of competing viewpoints. Hill and Adamson’s 19th century Newhaven sits alongside contemporary explorations of landscape, identity and technology; archival photographs meet staged images; institutional histories encounter artists whose practices question established ways of seeing. That multiplicity is important in an era when cultural identity is often reduced to familiar visual shorthand – mountains, coastlines, historic buildings and romanticised rurality. PhotoDalkeith RSA200 suggests that Scottish photography becomes most revealing when those assumptions are made visible and then unsettled.

The exhibition’s significance lies in this movement between preservation and disruption. Its bicentenary context could have encouraged a conventional celebration of institutional achievement, but the combination of archival works, contemporary practices and new commissions creates a more complicated account of photographic history. The Royal Scottish Academy’s long relationship with the medium becomes a framework for considering how images are collected, interpreted and reimagined across generations. Dalkeith Palace adds another register, placing photographic histories within an architectural environment already dense with questions of ownership, heritage and memory. Two hundred years of photography therefore become less a story of progress than an ongoing negotiation over who gets to frame Scotland, and what those frames allow us to see.

What emerges, ultimately, is a more unsettled account of how histories are made visible. Hill and Adamson’s early experiments, the institutional archive and the speculative possibilities of contemporary practice belong to different moments, however, each is shaped by decisions about where to look and what to preserve. Photography has changed radically since the 19th century, but its relationship with memory remains unresolved. Perhaps that is precisely where its significance lies – not in its ability to give us an objective record of the past, but in its capacity to reveal how each generation chooses to see it.

PhotoDalkeith RSA200 is at Dalkeith Palace until 27 September: dalkeithcountrypark.co.uk

Words: Simon Cartwright

Image Credits:

1. Image courtesy of Philip Braham.
2. Thomas Joshua Cooper, Late Afternoon, Mouth Of The River Forth, (1991-2014).
3. Image courtesy of Dalziel + Scullion.
4. Alex Boyd, The Storr Impression From The East, 2013.
5. Julie Brook, Winter Wall, Setting Light, Aird Mhòr, Hebrides.
