item.title: Why Surrealists Turned to Animals to Plumb the Human Psyche - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Starfish, scorpions, swallows, and sheep—once you look, animals are everywhere in Surrealist paintings. These and many other creatures are the focus of Desmond Morris’sThe Surrealist Menagerie: Strange Beasts & Fantastic Visions, a new book that combines Morris’s longtime study of zoology (he had a doctorate from Oxford) with his own participation in the Surrealist movement. Morris died this April at the age of 98, and his work leaves us with a lingering question: Why did the Surrealists, in their efforts to plumb the depths of the human psyche, continue to turn to animals?

Morris’s book focuses only on the representation of real animals; cataloguing mythic and hybrid creatures would take another volume entirely. He identifies over 750 instances of animals featured in Surrealist artworks, 168 of which are pictured in The Surrealist Menagerie. The book is organized into sections ranging from broad categories (“The Invertebrates”) to the surprisingly specific (“The Elephants”).

Morris’s career was dedicated to demonstrating that humans have more in common with the rest of the animal kingdom than we tend to admit. In 1967, he made claims to humans’ apelike nature in his bestselling work of popular science, The Naked Ape. That book and subsequent publications stirred controversy as he doubled down on our essential animality as a species (and on some decidedly human, decidedly dated sexual politics).

With his final book, however, Morris refuses to draw conclusions, letting the ambiguity of Surrealists’ meanings stand. He wrote elsewhere that “Surrealists dislike having their work analysed.” In place of analysis, The Surrealist Menagerie provides a panoply of alternately delightful and disturbing creatures, generating unexpected pairings through its focus on the animal. An owl crouching at the base of Max Ernst’sMarlene (Woman and Child), 1941, finds a fellow in Morris Grave’sLittle-Known Bird of the Inner Eye (1941), works made in the same year but that may not otherwise have been considered together. Both artists, Morris points out, were working in the context of World War II, and the owl’s ability to both burrow and take flight may have appealed to feelings of entrapment and a desire to escape. Salvador Dali dominates the volume, as he often does in discussions of Surrealism, with 33 featured works, but there are a number of lesser-known and women artists included, especially the work of Leonora Carrington.

Art historians have been less reticent to assign meaning to the zoological Surreal. Kirsten Strom suggests that all the animal references point to the latent influence of Darwin, whose work dissolved perceived boundaries between the human and the animal and would prompt Freud to develop his own theory of psychic evolution. Animals could offer liberatory models to throw off bourgeois conventions, returning Surrealists to primal ways of being. Ernst, who once declared himself born from an egg his mother had laid in an eagle’s nest, used birds as totemic animals, appearing as an avian avatar in works like Loplop Introduces Loplop (1930). Other Surrealists, meanwhile, seemed to take from animals a license to exploit other (generally female) bodies, as in Clovis Trouille’sJustine(1937), in which both a naked female figure and a lion are bound and captive. The Surrealists were not a univocal movement, and it is striking the degree to which female artists were more likely to represent hybrid identification with their animal selves: Frida Kahlo appears intertwined with monkeys or as a wounded deer, Leonor Fini painted women cozied up with cats, and Carrington’s scenes imagine convenings with ferrets and foxes.

Carrington in particular models what some have termed an ecofeminist approach, one that does not appropriate animals for the artist’s own self-revelation but instead develops kinship across species. Carrington’s association with a hyena in Self-Portrait (Inn of the Dawn Horse) (ca. 1937–38) and her personal relationship to horses are well documented but, through her writing, Carrington makes clear that her aspirations go beyond the autobiographical. In her 1974 novel The Hearing Trumpet, a nonagenarian vegetarian heroine named Marian rebels against patriarchal institutions. Navigating a changing climate, Marian develops interspecies alliances on a quest for the holy grail. Ultimately, she envisions a planet populated with cats, werewolves, bees, and goats, hoping for “an improvement on humanity.” In the work of the female Surrealist, it is women’s solidarity with animals that creates the possibility for a more humane world.

item.title: Collector and Patron Hasnaine Yavarhoussen Is Determined to Bring Madagascar’s Art Scene to the Rest of the World - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In 2019, just four nations mounted their debut pavilions at the Venice Biennale. Madagascar was one of them, and Hasnaine Yavarhoussen’s sponsorship was largely what made it possible.

The year before, the Malagasy art collector and entrepreneur met with artist Joël Andrianomearisoa to discuss the country’s participation and his support. At the time of their meeting, Yavarhoussen had limited knowledge about Malagasy artists; his almost decade-old collection didn’t even include any artworks by them. But the chat with Andrianomearisoa, who splits his time between Paris and Antananarivo, Madagascar’s capital, was so convincing that it led Yavarhoussen to help fund the inaugural Malagasy Pavilion. It also inspired Yavarhoussen to collect work by Malagasy artists and to make plans to provide long-term support for other artists from Madagascar.

“I was thinking: Okay, what would be the impact on Madagascar?” Yavarhoussen recalled in an interview about that pivotal meeting.

A member of Tate’s Africa Acquisitions Committee, Yavarhoussen went on to found Fonds Yavarhoussen in 2019 with the goal of supporting and promoting Malagasy art and culture, both locally and globally; sponsoring the Malagasy Pavilion became its first initiative.

Following Madagascar’s showing at Venice Biennale, Yavarhoussen and Andrianomearisoa cofounded Hakanto Contemporary in February 2020, with the artist serving as artistic director. Hakanto Contemporary, which began as a modestly sized multipurpose art space and now occupies a nearly 2,000-square-foot renovated warehouse in Antananarivo, has helped make Yavarhoussen one of Madagascar’s most important art patrons. Its exhibitions, residencies, educational initiatives, and workshops have helped create an emerging local art scene and placed Madagascar on the global art scene’s map.  

Among Hakanto Contemporary’s most recent efforts is a 400-work survey of Pierrot Men, whom Yavarhoussen called “the most known Malagasy photographer today.” The collector, who owns photographs dating back to 1860, said the pioneering Malagasy photographer’s retrospective curated by Andrianomearisoa and Rina Ralay Ranaivo is a “very important step” in Hakanto Contemporary’s programming.

Yavarhoussen is the chief executive officer of Groupe Filatex, a Malagasy company with holdings in the real estate, hospitality, healthcare, and sustainable energy sectors. The company is said to provide about a third of Madagascar’s power needs; Yavarhoussen joined the family-owned company in 2011, having previously studied economics and management in France and Spain.

During the late 2000s, a visit to a friend’s Paris-based contemporary art gallery inadvertently kicked off Yavarhoussen’s art collecting journey. With the encouragement of his father, he later bought a work he liked by American artist David Ratcliff.

“There are two main themes in my collection,” he explained. “The first speaks to my sensibility and my taste: I buy what I like and what I want to live with and be surrounded by every day. The second is Madagascar. We buy modern Madagascar art, often works that left the country at the time of Independence [in 1960]. We acquire them and bring them back to the country. I sometimes refer to this as a ‘relocalization’ mission.”

His over 500-work collection now largely includes work by artists from Madagascar and across Africa, including Andrianomearisoa, Malala Andrialavidrazana, Christian Sanna, Ramily (Emile Rakotondrazaka), and Esther Mahlangu.

In addition to funding Hakanto Contemporary, Fonds Yavarhoussen sponsors projects by Malagasy artists and creatives outside the country. These include supporting Andrialavidrazana’s exhibition at Palais de Tokyo in Paris and Andrianomearisoa’s commission at Zeitz MOCAA in Cape Town, South Africa; partnering with the LAM Museum in Lille, France, on a Jessy Razafimandimby solo; and coproducing a recent project by dancer and choreographer Soa Ratsifandrihana that appeared this summer at the Venice Dance Biennale. The fund also powers the Yavarhoussen Scholarship, which collaborates with the Institut National d’Histoire de l’Art in Paris to research and publish books on Malagasy art history.

There are already signs that Yavarhoussen’s collecting and patronage has had an impact beyond Madagascar. Andrianomearisoa joined the roster of Almine Rech gallery in 2023 and is a nominee for the 2026 Prix Marcel Duchamp, France’s top art award. In 2024, Yavarhoussen donated Andrianomearisoa’s Les Herbes Folles du Vieux Logis (2022) to New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. The next year, the work went on view in the museum’s revamped Michael C. Rockefeller Wing for work from Africa, Oceania, and the Americas. Yavarhoussen also regularly loans work from his collection to international art spaces, the Ludwig Museum in Germany, Wiels in Belgium, and La Filature in France. 

Formerly a Zeitz MOCAA trustee, Yavarhoussen said he doesn’t want to keep the artworks he owns solely in storage, at home, or his corporate offices. Instead, he wants “these pieces to be shared and seen.” The donations and loans, he said, “are primarily intended to ensure greater visibility [for] Malagasy art” and also “breathe new life into the collection.” Thinking about what he’s accomplished since 2019 for Malagasy art, Yavarhoussen said, “I think we’ve fulfilled our mission.”

item.title: Pattern and Bold, Saturated Color Commingle in Ben Sledsens’ Rhythmic Paintings - Colossal
item.description:
In Ben Sledsens’ new body of work, An Apple for the Road, saturated fields of color meet methodical patterns constructed from grasses, leaves, brick, and more. The Antwerp-born artist conceives of vibrant, atmospheric paintings in which life pauses for a moment: there’s a swan hovering over its tinted reflection, a woman just stepping out her front door, and vivid still lifes in which clouds and soft breezes rustle through the windows.

Often beginning with drawings on paper before translating the most salient details to the canvas, Sledsens is interested in repetition and the visual power of pattern, which he layers to form dense thickets of willow trees or the tiles lining a boating dock. These motifs set the scene, in which the ordinary appears in a new, slightly skewed perspective.

While bold in color, the oil-and-acrylic paintings are quiet and intimate. Sledsens beckons the viewer into domestic spaces and serene pockets of landscape, while opting for soft light and the haze of dusk. By pairing recognizable imagery with a sense that we’re witnessing a fleeting moment, the artist invites questions about what sustains our attentions and what details we may never fully grasp.

An Apple for the Road is on view from September 3 to October 10 at Tim Van Laere Galler in Antwerp. Dive into the artist’s archive on Instagram.

item.title: For 20 Years, Turkish Media Star Vuslat Made Art in Secret. Now She’s on the Biennial Circuit - ARTnews.com
item.description:
For nearly two decades, Vuslat Doğan Sabancı lived two lives.

By day, she was one of the most powerful figures in Turkish media, serving as chief executive of Hürriyet, the country’s largest newspaper. At night—after work, dinner, and putting her children to bed—she went to her studio and made art. “Sometimes I would work until six in the morning,” Vuslat told ARTnews on a Zoom call from Istanbul.

The strange thing was that almost nobody saw what she made.

Vuslat, who goes solely by her first name professionally, drew, sculpted, worked in clay, and experimented with materials for nearly twenty years without exhibiting any of it. There was no gallery waiting for the work and, for much of that time, apparently no particular ambition on her part to pursue representation. Her first exhibition opened in 2022. Four years later, her art calendar is remarkably busier.

This summer alone, her work has appeared in New York, where she exhibited a room-sized installation, House of Silence, at the Conductor art fair; and in Rhodes, where dozens of her clay sculptures have been installed in a medieval former Greek Orthodox church. May We Meet in the Silence of Our Souls, her first monograph, was published by DISTANZ and the University of Chicago Press. It’s a startlingly fast career ascent for an artist who spent most of her life avoiding one.

The tension between public and private runs through much of Vuslat’s work. So does silence. When we spoke with her, she returned repeatedly to the idea of listening: to other people, to materials, to herself. These are not exactly fashionable occupations in contemporary media or contemporary life.

Vuslat knows something about the former. Before leaving the business, she spent years at Hürriyet, where her public life included advocating for freedom of expression, gender equality, and human rights. “I worked in media to create space for different voices,” she said.

But over time, she told me, something changed. Politics became more polarized. Media became increasingly driven by metrics. Everyone seemed to be talking, and fewer people seemed particularly interested in listening. Art offered another possibility.

Vuslat eventually gave the idea a name: emanet, a Turkish word without a neat English equivalent. Vuslat describes it as something entrusted to your care but not really owned. It can be an object, a memory, a story. Children can be an emanet. Nature, too. The responsibility is not merely to preserve what has been entrusted to you, but to care for it before passing it along.

The effect was simple: you shut up and sat in silence.

But silence, as she describes it, isn’t necessarily peaceful. Quite the opposite. Sit quietly long enough, and the first things that arrive can be judgment, guilt, and criticism. The trick is staying there. “If I stay patient,” she said, “clarity emerges — like clear water.”

Her materials tend to behave similarly. Vuslat works in marble, bronze, clay, felt, and even plants electroplated in silver. She has made monumental drawings using pigments gathered from the earth beneath the places where they are exhibited. For Tower of Babel (2025), she incorporated trees burned in the Los Angeles wildfires.

In Rhodes, where Vuslat is participating in the second Biennale of Contemporary Keramics, the material is simpler still: earth, water, and air. Her installation, May We Meet in the Silence of Our Souls, begins at the threshold of Our Lady of the Castle, a former Greek Orthodox church that later served as an Ottoman mosque. Small organic clay forms lead visitors from the entrance into the building. Vuslat describes them as resembling “the formless shape of breath.”

Another question hangs over Vuslat’s sudden arrival in the art world. She didn’t arrive as an unknown. As Vuslat Doğan Sabancı, she belonged to one of Turkey’s most prominent families and had already enjoyed a formidable career in business and philanthropy. Artists spend decades trying to get curators’ and institutions’ attention. Vuslat began showing her work in 2022 and, within a few years, had exhibitions at the Baksı Museum, Istanbul’s Tophane-i Amire, and the Museum of Troy. She knows hers is not the conventional route.

But the chronology complicates the obvious interpretation. Vuslat didn’t leave media, discover art, and rapidly reinvent herself as an artist. The studio came first. For years, it existed alongside her public career, unseen. By the time she finally exhibited at Pi Artworks in London in 2022, she had already spent nearly twenty years figuring out what she wanted the work to do. The critic Andrew Graham-Dixon captured the oddity when he wrote about Vuslat’s debut in her monograph. Vuslat, he wrote, seemed like “a novice and an old hand rolled into one.”

item.title: As New York Prices Artists Out, New Haven Is Drawing Them In - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Chiffon Thomas discovered pretty quickly that New York wasn’t going to work. An artist and sculptor who moved to the city after three years in Los Angeles, Thomas needed a studio with room to weld metal and a parking spot for his van. New York real estate was prohibitively expensive and he went in search of another solution. Detroit and Philadelphia have recently become outposts for artists as New York becomes ever more expensive. The move Thomas eventually made signals that there is another locale joining the mix: New Haven.

Thomas bounced between Bushwick and the Bronx. In Bushwick, the industrial spaces outside Manhattan that once attracted artists are now increasingly rented for all-night raves, co-working spaces, or even converted into a members’ only club. On some nights, Thomas said, events in the building made it difficult to get into the studio at all. The rent was around $4,000 a month. The Bronx was somewhat easier to work in, but it wasn’t much cheaper.

“I was like, this number is just way out of my bracket,” Thomas recalled. Eventually, he was paying around $4,000 for roughly 800 square feet of studio space—just enough to provide ventilation for his welding fumes, and to maneuver long pieces of metal. That came on top of the cost of an apartment in Brooklyn. So in January, Thomas began splitting time between New York and New Haven, where he had attended the Yale School of Art. The cost-of-living difference is almost comic. An 800-square-foot studio in New Haven costs $550 a month. An apartment runs another $1,400 or so.

All in, Thomas said, living and working costs less than $2,000 a month.

“I’ve been able to retain a lot of my income, so I can actually put it back into my studio practice, which is the point,” Thomas said. “You’re really just trying to maintain your small business.” Leaving New York part time, Thomas added, was simply “a business decision.”

There has been a lot of hand-wringing lately about whether artists can still afford to live in New York. Late last year, the artist Josh Kline gave this problem a name in a much-talked-about essay titled “New York Real Estate and the Ruin of American Art.” Kline argued that the city’s housing and studio costs weren’t simply driving artists out of New York, but changing the art that could be made there, pressuring artists into making easily marketable work so that they could sell enough to afford small studios. Experimentation and large-scale production, in Kline’s estimation, have disappeared in response. The essay kicked off a frothy argument in the art world, but the diagnosis was hard to ignore. A more interesting question may be what comes next. If artists can no longer afford New York, do they actually need to live there?.

Thomas is one of a growing group of artists in Connecticut, and especially New Haven, who believe they’ve found the remedy for a metastasized New York real estate market.

Some arrived for Yale and never left. Others came for residencies and decided to stick around. A few, like Thomas, trod the well-worth art world path that passes through New York and Los Angeles, before deciding to move back. New York is still a short train ride away, after all.

The New Haven experiment isn’t new. Dominic Chambers, an artist represented by Lehmann Maupin with works in multiple museums including the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden, the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, moved there in 2017 for Yale’s MFA program. Like plenty of young artists, he assumed New York would come next. 

“Every artist that goes to grad school, we all have dreams of going to New York,” Chambers said. “New York’s a fucking dynamic city. There are so many reasons to be there.”

But he’d also heard the horror stories: artists losing studios, rents jumping, people spending huge portions of their income simply holding onto enough room to work. New Haven offered a less glamorous proposition. It was practical.

Chambers’s first studio in New Haven was 1,200 square feet and cost $1,000 a month. His current studio is 1,700 square feet and runs between $1,500 and $1,800, depending on utilities. He lives about 20 minutes away in Meriden, where he owns a house. At first, staying was mostly about money. That isn’t really true anymore. 

“A lot of artists have really moved here,” Chambers said. “I haven’t seen a lot of these kinds of people leave.” Connecticut, he said, feels “less isolating” than it did when he arrived.

There are obvious tradeoffs. A curator in Manhattan cannot decide at three in the afternoon to swing by the studio on the way home. Chambers is aware of that. His answer is to make the trip worth taking: “We hope that people take a train ride up to visit us,” he said. “But really we let our work do the talking.”

There is also something to be said for not having the art world outside your front door.

Chambers thinks he might have been more distracted, or simply more anxious, had he moved to Brooklyn after grad school. New York offers extraordinary access to exhibitions and people, but access comes with its own pressure: openings to attend, dinners to go to, people to meet, a studio that must always be ready for someone to drop by.

“You go to New York, you invest so many years and so much capital into that city,” Chambers said. “You just feel like your dreams have not manifested materially yet, despite everything you poured into it.” Failure, or even just the normal slow development of a career, feels different when the rent is $1,000 than when it is $4,500.

And New Haven has affected the work itself. Chambers wanted a yard. He wanted dogs. He hikes. The woods and landscapes around him have gradually found their way into his paintings. New Haven, Chambers said, has given him “time to catch up with yourself in a way that New York doesn’t.”

Of course, it is difficult to talk about artists in New Haven without eventually arriving at Yale. For decades, Yale has brought a steady supply of ambitious young artists into a city of roughly 140,000 people. The traditional assumption was that many of them would leave after graduation, often for New York. What seems to have changed is the number who don’t.

Amy Smith-Stewart, chief curator at the Aldrich Contemporary Art Museum in Ridgefield, noticed that shift while organizing the museum’s inaugural decennial survey of artists living and working in Connecticut. 

The show, “I Am What Is Around Me,” takes its title from a line by Connecticut poet Wallace Stevens and is meant to be the first in a series the Aldrich will repeat every 10 years. Smith-Stewart organized it with curator Caitlin Monachino after more than 100 studio visits across Connecticut, eventually choosing 40 artists ranging in age from their thirties to their eighties. Geographic breadth was a focus. So was avoiding the easy version of a Connecticut show, one dominated by recent Yale MFAs or famous artists with country houses up north in the bucolic Litchfield hills. Artists who had already had solo museum shows in the state were nixed, as were people whose connection to Connecticut amounted to spending a few weekends there each year.

The idea is partly to correct for Connecticut’s strange place in the cultural imagination. Maine has artists. The East End has artists. Connecticut has hedge funds and nice schools, or so the stereotype goes. In reality, the state has a long artistic history and an unusually dense institutional one, from the Wadsworth Atheneum and the New Britain Museum of American Art to Yale and, more recently, NXTHVN (pronounced Next-Haven). New Haven itself is one of the most racially and ethnically diverse cities in the state, with Latinos, Blacks, and whites each making up about 30% of the population, accoding to 2020 U.S. Census data. Smith-Stewart said the influx has become especially noticeable since the pandemic.

Then there is Erector Square, an old toy factory in New Haven’s Fair Haven neighborhood where A.C. Gilbert once manufactured Erector Sets and American Flyer trains. After the factory closed in 1967, its new owners began carving the sprawling industrial complex into artist studios. Today, eight of its 11 buildings contain more than 175 studios, over 150 of them occupied. It is the sort of slightly battered former industrial space that artists once found all over New York, and that has become increasingly difficult to afford there.

Chambers described a burgeoning community in non-Yale New Haven: Artists stay, meet other artists, invite people into town, and give the next person one more reason not to leave.

“New Haven is a thinking person’s community,” Chambers said. “If people are interested in engaging and participating with ideas in a smaller community at a smaller scale than somewhere like New York, New Haven is a good place to start.”

NXTHVN has helped widen that circle.

Founded in 2018 by artist Titus Kaphar and investor Jason Price, the nonprofit runs a ten-month fellowship that brings artists and curators from around the world to New Haven. Fellows receive studio space, housing, and a stipend, along with mentorship and professional development. The latter was important to Kaphar, who wanted to provide the sort of practical education about sustaining a career that art schools often neglect. In other words, how to be an artist once school is over.

“There is a different type of community out here,” said Marissa Del Toro, NXTHVN’s director of programs and exhibitions (and a former curatorial fellow there). “Obviously a slower speed, but it’s still moving.” She said that around 15 alumni of the program, some of whom come in from overseas, now live in New Haven. 

Kristy Hughes is one of them. Unlike many of the artists who have settled in New Haven, she has no Yale connection. Hughes, who grew up in Texas and had most recently been teaching at the University of Vermont, came to the city through an NXTHVN fellowship. She had been deliberately applying to long-term residencies that could provide the community and access to a larger art world she wanted without requiring her to live in New York. “I can’t afford to move to New York City,” she said. It was a particularly bad fit for an artist making large sculptures.

Two years later, Hughes has stayed in New Haven. She now has two studios there, one for fabrication and another for painting, and says some warehouse space can still be found for around a dollar per square foot. More importantly, the space has allowed her work to grow. After visiting Hughes’s studio, Smith-Stewart asked her to make an outdoor sculpture for the Aldrich show. Hughes had wanted to work at that scale for years; suddenly she had a studio with 16-foot ceilings and enough room to actually do it. Another outdoor commission followed, and she has another coming up. “If I didn’t stay in New Haven, that wouldn’t have been possible,” Hughes said.


Hughes still goes into New York and has friends there, but the old choice between access to the art world and enough space to make her work no longer seems quite so stark. She has artists nearby for studio visits, fabricators who can help build the work and New York a train ride away. “I think I should just stay, you know, instead of keep chasing this thing,” Hughes recalled realizing. “Oh, I think we found it.”

The result is not exactly Brooklyn-on-the-Sound, nor does anyone seem particularly interested in making it that. Smith-Stewart sees New Haven as distinct from some of the other Connecticut communities that have attracted artists. Someone moving to Litchfield County may want acreage, solitude, or a barn that can be turned into a studio. New Haven still feels like a city. 

It also has Metro-North. The city works as an alternative to New York partly because it doesn’t require artists to abandon New York. “If people are willing to come to my studio and I don’t have to be in New York City and people will still come, then what am I doing?” Smith-Stewart said, describing the calculus she’s heard from artists. Outside the city, she added, they can put more money into materials and make work that would be harder to afford in New York.

SECTION BREAK

There are signs that the art world itself has not entirely adjusted to this new geography.

Thomas still maintains a room in Brooklyn and travels between New York and Connecticut. Part of the reason is practical. Some grants and residencies require artists to be New York residents, creating a paradox in which artists priced out of the city can also find themselves cut off from opportunities designed to support artists. 

“These are people who formerly resided there and now no longer can,” Thomas said. “Why are these opportunities snatched away from them?”

Thomas also admitted that returning to New Haven did not initially feel like some triumphant discovery of a better way to live. Quite the opposite. “I was incredibly resentful moving back here,” Thomas said. “I felt like I failed at something.” For generations of ambitious artists, New York was not merely a place to live. Getting there was part of the career itself. Leaving could look and feel like retreat.

Thomas is only now beginning to shake that feeling. Familiarity helped. So did returning to a studio building from the Yale years and finding a broader community nearby that were barely visible from the Yale orbit: working-class neighborhoods, Latino communities, taco trucks, people whose daily lives have very little to do with the university. “There’s a real culture here,” Thomas said.

item.title: Police Break Into Vancouver Gallery After Confusing Sculpture for Person - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Emergency personnel forced entry into Access Gallery in Vancouver on the night of August 14, after a 911 caller mistook a sculpture of an art preparator as a person in need of medical attention, as first reported by the local media outlet CityNews. 

Officers were dispatched to the downtown address after a witness reported "a person's feet protruding from behind a counter ... and believed medical assistance was required," a spokesperson for the Vancouver Police Department (VPD) told Hyperallergic. Emergency responders broke the gallery lock, breached the front door, and subsequently realized it was a false alarm.

As the gallery faces a 1,000 CAD (~$722) repair bill, the incident has sparked online speculation that the witness could have thought artist Allysa Pierre's “Untitled (the preparator)” (2024) was a person experiencing an overdose‚ a fairly common sight amid Vancouver's ongoing opioid crisis.

item.title: Demolition of Tbilisi Arts Complex Sparks Protests - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An arts complex in Tbilisi, Georgia, is being razed despite protests from its architects and some members of the local community. Following approval by Tbilisi’s city government in June, demolition work on the Rike Park Music Theatre and Exhibition Hall—colloquially known as Rike Tubes—began at the end of July and is scheduled to be completed by December.

The news was reported by Reuters following a photo-essay documenting the destruction of the complex and that of a second landmark, a Brutalist former flour mill known as Silo, published in Civil Georgia.

The Rike Tubes are a connected pair of glass-and-steel structures designed by Fuksas Studio, an Italian architectural firm led by husband-and-wife architects Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas. Built in the final years of United National Movement (UNM) rule (2004–2012), their ultracontemporary design symbolized the pro-Western approach of the UNM’s leader, Mikhail Saakashvili.

The current governing party came to power in 2012, and the complex, reported to have cost about 75 million lari ($29 million US) of public money, never opened. The 108,000-square-foot site was privatized, and the current owner—a subsidiary of Maqro Property called Rike Dom—is planning to build a hotel on it, though details have not been released.

While members of the public and the architectural community have criticized the Rike Tubes for altering the character of Tbilisi’s historic old town, some favored relocating them to a more suitable setting rather than demolishing them. But protests—including appeals from the architects, who offered to help authorities repurpose the complex—have failed to halt their destruction. The worry now is what may take their place.

item.title: Neolithic Figure Astride a Leopard Unearthed in Turkey: ‘Unlike Anything Seen Before’ - ARTnews.com
item.description:
An 11,000-year-old statue depicting a person on the back of a leopard was unearthed by archaeologists at a Stone Age site in southern Turkey, the country’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism announced in a statement on August 25.

The find from the Neolithic site Karahan Tepe measures about 28 inches tall and would have sat on a platform along the wall of a larger round building roughly 10 feet in diameter. Notably, the style of the composite statue is “unlike anything seen before,” Turkey’s Minister of Culture and Tourism, Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, said.

Experts believe the statue may have symbolized masculinity, virility, strength, and courage. “Leopards were common feline predators in the region,” Jens Notroff, a Neolithic archaeologist at the German Archaeological Institute, told Live Science. “They are vigorous, dangerous animals, so probably challenging game for skilled hunters. That might have added to their symbolic meaning.”

He added, “An individual fearlessly shown among these animals […] or even apparently mastering one, as in this new sculpture from Karahan Tepe, could be read as maybe a symbol of power, of control over this vigor and danger.”

A similar statue was found at the same site years before entering the Şanlıurfa Museum’s collection. Still, this latest discovery raises questions and offers new information about the region’s earliest human settlements.

Constructed around 9750 BCE in the Urfa (or Şanlıurfa) province, Karahan Tepe is one of the oldest known villages in the world, alongside others like Göbekli Tepe.

item.title: At Peter Marino’s Foundation, Centuries of Art History Devilishly Collapse into Each Other - ARTnews.com
item.description:
The Peter Marino Art Foundation occupies the former Rogers Memorial Library, a charming historic building in Southampton, New York, that its namesake has transformed into something much stranger inside. 

This summer, the iconoclastic architect and collector has placed portraits by Robert Nava alongside those by Y.Z. Kami; abstractions by Betty Parsons and Carla Accardi share a wall. Nearby is a magnificent room filled with Tiffany silver, while a luscious, red-painted space is filled with Viennese paintings and objets d’art from the 1900s. Elsewhere are bits and pieces from Marino’s collection: a Rashid Johnson here, a Sanford Biggers there, a slew of Eugène Atget prints over yonder. There are more than 500 works at the foundation, and that’s just a fraction of what Marino has acquired over the years.

Part of the joy of walking through Peter Marino’s private museum is that there is quite literally stuff everywhere. Marino doesn’t treat the building as a series of hermetically sealed exhibitions, instead art from one century flows into work from several centuries later.  Ferdinando Tacca’s 17th-century bronze, Hercules Capturing the Cerynitian Stag, for example, is flanked by photographs and prints by Andy Warhol. Peppering the room are carved wooden reliquaries from Central Africa, 19th-century ceramics by Théodore Deck, and Les Lalanne’s designs. The hang is constantly in flux; if Marino thinks an object belongs in another room because it will look better there, he simply moves it. 

During my visit, the Velvet Underground’s first record played softly through the speakers, and I got the sense that I was strolling through Marino’s mind. “It’s kind of a little bit of an amalgamation of all the things that he loves,” Curtis Clarizio, Marino’s chief of staff, told me as we walked through the foundation on a recent rainy morning. 
 
Now 77, Marino has been collecting since he was 22, and his tastes have always extended well beyond the art of the moment. “Art history is about 5,000 years and some people today are only interested in work made in the last three years,” Marino told me later in the day at his palatial Southampton home. “That’s not really collecting for me.” 
 
A collection, he explained, should equally include contemporary art, bronzes, antiquities, rare books, ceramics, arms and armor and design. A point of inspiration are European collections accumulated over generations, where hundreds of years of art coexist because they simply kept growing. On the foundation’s second floor, for example, the room devoted to Viennese objets d’art is next to one devote to all things Tiffany: silver, flatware, tea sets, hammered pitchers, vases, tankards, candlesticks— installed at different heights on mirrored or highly polished metal plinths.
 

Marino also has a penchant for seeing affinities in the work of two artists who paths likely never crossed, as is the case with his two-person exhibition of Parsons and Accardi. In the foundation’s Cathedral Gallery, he has installed the two artist’s paintings in a dense, salon-style hang, where large abstractions sit beside more modestly scaled ones. The juxtaposition of the gallery’s double-height, vaulted timber ceiling with its warm parquet floor adds to this play in scale, giving this chapel-like space an intimate, domestic feeling.

Walk through another door and the mood changes again. A wood-panel floor and black wall is the setting for a sparsely hung display dedicated to Kami’s quiet, meditative dome paintings that mimic the ceilings of Byzantine churches and mosques.

While Marino has worked with some of the world’s top collectors, from Bernard Arnault to David Martinez, his taste is one that doesn’t hew at all to market trends. Marino pays attention to prices, certainly, but has little interest in being told what he ought to want. “I don’t really care what other people think,” he said. When dealers tell him an artist is “really hot,” he dismisses it as sales talk. “They should be selling shoes.” 

That comment made me think back to a room at the foundation devoted to Robert Nava, a market darling who had a show at Pace Gallery in New York that didn’t strike a chord with me. At Marino’s, I found myself surrounded by a funny menagerie of animals and mythical creatures: a lion here, a dragon there, a castle further along. The installation has the feeling of creatures moving around the room, as if in a carousel. These pictures don’t take themselves too seriously, and neither does anything at the foundation.

How Marino approaches a new acquisition might have something to do with. His own test to decide on whether to purchase an expensive artwork is simple: He gives himself a week. If it keeps crossing his mind “every morning, noon and night,” that’s an indication he should buy it. “I like to take my time.”

item.title: Virginia and Leonard Woolf's Hogarth Press Gets an Exhibition of Its Own - Hyperallergic
item.description:
SUSSEX, England — Ouch!

Yes, there’s often a bit of a sting in Virginia Woolf’s comments, even about people of whom she is fond. “I’ve got a confession to make,” she once wrote. “I’m going to marry Leonard Wolf [correct spelling: Woolf]. He’s a penniless Jew. I’m more happy than anyone ever said was possible.” Is that spoken from a great height or not? After all, she was the daughter of the esteemed author Sir Leslie Stephen, hem hem.

“Wolf” and she married. They were both writers. And amongst the remarkable fruits of their union was a decision to open a small press, which in time grew into something far from small.

It was called the Hogarth Press, and an exhibition tells its story in a farmhouse set very much within Woolf country, by which I mean the Firle Estate in Sussex. In 1916 Virginia was out walking on the Downs, a ridge of hills smooth as the nap of a snooker table when seen from below, that runs along that part of the coast of England. She could see it from above: a house that became known as “Charleston.” 

It was a former farmhouse with a sheep barn and threshing barn in close attendance. Virginia recommended it to her sister, painter Vanessa Bell, who was looking for somewhere to live. Vanessa was a conscientious objector who had left London to find manual work on a farm — penance for her disobedience to a country at war. She and Duncan Grant bought the place which became their on-and-off home for more than half a century. In time they filled it with many interesting people, artists and writers for the most part, some of whom lived there for a while. They became known as the Bloomsbury Group.

Now, in a building that almost nudges at Charleston’s door, the exhibition puts on display about 200 books, all published by the Hogarth Press, telling the story of the press from its first beginnings in 1917.

It began with the purchase of a hand press by Leonard and Virginia, which was set up in the basement of Hogarth House, their home in London. The books were all handmade, which made for a lot of inky fingers. Each letter of each book had to be plucked out and locked into place. Virginia loved it. It gave her the freedom to do what she wanted with her own words. She had grown sick of the slowness and the tyrannizing of male editors. The press published her own novels, from Jacob’s Room (1922) and on. You can see them all in a single bookcase, Virginia’s books, with their wayward covers designed and realized by her sister Vanessa — the two sisters were true collaborators in the venture. 

The press even proved to be a commercial success. It published established writers such as E. M. Forster, and others — and especially women — who were daring to experiment. It published the very first complete UK edition of T.S. Eliot’s The Waste Land in 1922. Tom Eliot was a frequent visitor to the house. Virginia liked him, in her ouch, waspish way. 

“Yes I like talking to Tom,” she once wrote. “A glorified boy scout, he is tight & shiny as a wood louse. But there is well water in him, cold & pure.”

Virginia Woolf and the Hogarth Press continues at Charleston in Firle (East Sussex, BN8 6LL, England) through September 6. The show was organized by Ben Majchrowicz and Stephen Barkway.

item.title: ‘Handmade Utopia’ Relishes the Architecture of California’s Back-to-the-Land Movement - Colossal
item.description:
When I was about 10 years old, my parents organized a vacation to a tiny enclave called Orr Hot Springs just outside of Ukiah, California. Nestled in the mountains with a history dating to 1858 as a stagecoach stop with redwoods shading the trails, the property has a uniquely layered architectural history. We stayed in what my dad called “Art’s cabin,” which turned out to have really been built by a guy named Art in the mid-1970s. A giant tree intersected the middle of the structure.

Art’s cabin is one of few remaining buildings from the property’s back-to-the-land era, before it became today’s modern yet earthy resort. In 1974, my dad and a group of friends from Berkeley teamed up to buy the hot springs. Over time, a small community developed as people purchased “shares” in the property. Attracted by the cooperative nature of the place and the opportunity to escape the city, people came and went, sometimes staying for a couple of weeks and sometimes for a couple of years. To make income, my dad recalls leading week-long carpentry courses, during which visitors and community members alike constructed what he describes as tiny, “very not-code” cabins, some of which were finished and actually lived in for a time. There was a buzz around building.

As my dad and I both paged through my hot-off-the-press copy of Handmade Utopia: Back-to-the-Land Architecture in Northern California, published by DAP/Edition Patrick Frey, I could tell that a lot jogged his memory. I grew up hearing stories about the ups and downs of running an intentional community in the hills during the 1970s, and his experience is but one among many thousands. Having also lived in Humboldt County for a time myself, I enjoy the striking sense of continuity throughout the past five decades that author David Jacob Kramer and photographer Michael Schmelling capture in this hefty tome. The work represents a counterculture that, though changed, is still alive and well.

The vernacular of Northern California architecture in the late 1960s and 1970s is a result of resourcefulness, timeliness, and a staunch desire to do things one’s own way. Scrounged from discarded redwood left over by the region’s logging industry and salvaged architectural details and appliances from historical homes, the houses cover a broad range of styles. Think triangular windows, diagonal paneling, cylindrical or octagonal footprints, and ad hoc additions.

Often, builders had no plan, constructing their dwellings to whatever standard they were able. They used plastic to cover windows and sometimes innovated with compositing toilet solutions or solar. The buildings were hardly ever up to code, and many lived with the constant anxiety that their homes could be condemned and they’d be evicted by local authorities. But the risk outweighed a mainstream alternative that felt too limiting or oppressive. “In pursuit of something better, back-to-the-landers radically reappraised what a home could and should be—and how it might inform the lives of its inhabitants,” Kramer says in the introductory essay.

Some homes of the era draw their inspiration from Buckminster Fuller’s geodesic dome design, while others take cues from neolithic forms or Indigenous structures around the world. Many examples of these were published contemporaneously in popular books like Lloyd Kahn’s Shelter, which itself was a spinoff of his editorial contributions to Stewart Brand’s counterculture magazine, Whole Earth Catalog. The legendary publication described itself as an “access device” that served as a kind of ultimate peer-to-peer DIY guide for living and building.

My first impression of Handmade Utopia was that it felt like a kind of reverent extension of Barry Shapiro and Art Boericke’s seminal 1973 photo book Handmade Houses: A Guide to the Woodbutcher’s Art. By comparison, this fresh look at the stylistic movement is a more personal expression of wonder and fondness for not only a particular style of architecture but the societal complexities that spawned it.

Kramer and Schmelling adventured through the NorCal countryside over the course of four years to touch base with people who still make their homes in the woods. Even those who no longer live in their decades-old dwellings can retrace their steps to see what remains. And the foundation of every one is composed of ingenuity and independent spirit. In addition to thoughtful introductory texts, the bulk of the book is chock full of photographs, archival material, and anecdotes by the folks whose structures the authors visit.

Rather than a comprehensive study of hand-built Northern California architecture, Handmade Utopia reads more like an homage to what Kramer calls the “audacious hope” of the back-to-the-land movement. And this hope isn’t relegated to its historical roots, as young people today are confronted by the prohibitive cost of both homes and land. “Schmelling and I felt an urgency in capturing these homes before they literally went back-to-the-land, disappearing along with the generation who built them,” Kramer says.

Handmade Utopia is officially slated for release on September 1. Find your copy in the Colossal Shop. You might also enjoy a tour of Ricky Boscarino’s whimiscal hand-built home in New Jersey or Matt Bua’s “repurposed city” in Upstate New York.

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article ‘Handmade Utopia’ Relishes the Architecture of California’s Back-to-the-Land Movement appeared first on Colossal.

item.title: Thieves Steal One of Europe’s Most Significant Bronze Age Gold Collections, Frieze Abu Dhabi Announces Exhibitors, Growing Pains in Britain’s Expanding Cultural Scene, and More: Morning Links for August 27, 2026 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • Thieves have stolen most of Spain’s Treasure of Villena, one of Europe’s most significant Bronze Age gold collections, in just four minutes.  
  • Frieze is heading to Abu Dhabi for the first time this November, unveiling a line-up of 84 galleries for its inaugural edition.
  • Britain’s cultural scene is showing signs of a new “cool Britannia,” but does the country risk squandering its creative advantage without a stronger culture of private patronage?

The Headlines 

SMASH-AND-GRAB. Thieves have stolen most of Spain’s Treasure of Villena, one of Europe’s most significant Bronze Age gold collections, in a raid lasting just four minutes, the Guardian reported. The gang broke into the Villena Museum in Alicante province early Thursday, escaping between 5.20 a.m. and 5.24 a.m. The haul includes gold bracelets, bowls, bottles, and other objects dating to around 1000 BCE. The collection, discovered in 1963, has an estimated gold value of €1.7 million ($1.98 million), though its historical worth is considered incalculable. Police are investigating whether a separate alarm at a nearby sports center was used as a diversion. The theft follows several major European museum raids. 

BIG FRIEZE IN THE DESERT. Frieze unveiled a line-up of 84 galleries for its inaugural edition in Abu Dhabi this fall, ARTnews reported. More than 40 percent of exhibitors are from the SWANA region, reflecting the fair’s focus on building a stronger platform for galleries from the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia. The international roster includes major names alongside younger and regionally focused galleries, with the fair taking place from November 19–22. The fair’s presence in the region marks another significant step in Abu Dhabi’s push to establish itself as a major global art-market hub, as competition between Gulf cultural capitals continues to intensify.

The Digest

Long-running efforts to revive Glasgow’s People’s Palace have received a fresh funding boost, with the city submitting a new National Lottery Heritage Fund bid for the £36 million ($48.9 million) restoration. [BBC]

For the first time, 26 Islamic masterpieces from the Louvre are heading to the US, with the treasures going on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art this September. [Smithsonian Magazine]

The UK government has been urged to strengthen protections for exceptional natural history specimens, ensuring British museums have the opportunity to acquire them before they are sold overseas. [Museums Association]

A monumental Isamu Noguchi sculpture titled Mississippi Fountain (1961–62) is heading to the New Orleans Museum of Art, where it will be installed at the museum’s Beaux-Arts entrance this fall. [The Art Newspaper]

The Kicker

COOL BRITANNIA. Britain’s cultural scene is showing signs of a new “cool Britannia,” but the country risks squandering its creative advantage without a stronger culture of private patronage, Yana Peel, president of arts, culture, and heritage at Chanel, argued in the Financial Times. She highlighted the growing importance of wealthy individuals and businesses in supporting museums, artists, and cultural institutions as public funding remains under pressure. Britain still has major advantages, from world-class museums and galleries to a thriving creative economy, but competing internationally will require more ambitious philanthropy. The argument is ultimately that cultural investment should be seen not simply as charity, but as a strategic investment in Britain’s global influence and economic future.

item.title: Brussels Is Building an Art Scene Without a Centre - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Brussels’ artistic identity lies in its overlaps: between galleries and artist-run spaces, established institutions and experimental initiatives, the commercial and the independent. This September, RendezVous – Brussels Art Week brings more than 80 participants across the capital, but its significance lies less in the scale of the programme than in the network it makes visible. Moving through Molenbeek, Anderlecht, Forest, the Sablon, Ixelles, Saint-Gilles, Uccle and the city centre, the second edition resists the logic of a single art-world destination. Instead, it asks audiences to encounter Brussels through the relationships between its different cultural communities. The result is an art week that is as interested in the conditions surrounding artistic production as in the exhibitions themselves.

The city has developed a cultural landscape in which different models of practice exist unusually close together. International galleries including Mendes Wood DM, Nosbaum Reding, Bernier/Eliades, Nino Mier, Almine Rech and Martins&Montero operate alongside established local spaces such as Xavier Hufkens, Maruani Mercier, Spazio Nobile, rodolphe janssen, Sorry We’re Closed and STEMS. Younger and more experimental spaces, including Damien & The Love Guru, KIN, IN-GATE and the nomadic initiative SYBIL, occupy another position, while newer arrivals continue to shift the city’s gallery geography. What emerges is not a neat hierarchy but a series of overlapping communities. Their proximity creates the possibility of exchange without erasing the differences between them.

That diversity becomes particularly visible when attention moves beyond galleries. RendezVous includes institutions, private foundations, artist-run initiatives and temporary projects, while its Open Studios programme gives audiences access to selected residencies and collective artist studios. The distinction matters because an art scene is sustained by far more than its public exhibitions. Studios, informal networks and independent spaces provide the conditions in which practices can develop before they enter more established circuits of visibility. By bringing these structures into the same framework, RendezVous makes a case for looking at the infrastructure around art as closely as the art itself.

Curatorial strategy is therefore central to the project. Rather than asking audiences to remain within a single district, the focus days trace different parts of Brussels, moving from Molenbeek, Anderlecht and Forest to the Sablon and city centre, before reaching Ixelles, Saint-Gilles and Uccle. Geography becomes a form of interpretation: the route between venues is part of the experience, placing exhibitions within the social and architectural conditions of the neighbourhoods where they take place. This approach also resists the compression of an art week into a sequence of openings and appointments. Brussels remains visible as a city rather than disappearing behind the event that temporarily brings its cultural activity into focus.

Forest offers a particularly useful case study. Situated close to WIELS, the Salon de RendezVous will be designed by Espace Aygo as an immersive environment containing a bar, pop-up bookshop, intimate cinema and stage for talks and performances. Known for its emphasis on recycling and circular design, the collective is creating a large-scale, site-specific installation that will also mark the end of its four-year presence in Brussels before travelling to Jester in Genk. Its temporary status is important. Rather than functioning as another permanent cultural monument, the Salon is conceived as a setting for activity – a structure whose purpose is to bring different practices and audiences into contact.

Performance unsettles that architecture further. Stina Fors, Teo Ala-Ruona and Ivan Cheng will engage with Espace Aygo’s installation through interventions inspired by cabaret, introducing live action, sound and duration into an environment already shaped by design. The choice of cabaret is particularly apt for a project concerned with encounter: historically, such spaces have blurred the boundary between performance and social life, spectacle and participation. Here, the audience is not simply positioned in front of a work but within a setting activated by different forms of practice. Talks and artist conversations developed with NW, WIELS, Bozar, Belgian Art Prize and La Loge extend the Salon’s emphasis on exchange.

Moving-image adds another dimension to this porous structure. A newly introduced cinema will host The Artist Moving Image programme, curated with Argos Centre for Audiovisual Arts, participating galleries and film curator Max Ferguson, alongside selected graduation projects. Film occupies a particularly fluid position within contemporary art, moving between the gallery, cinema and performance space without belonging entirely to any one of them. Its inclusion therefore reinforces a wider curatorial argument: that contemporary practice increasingly happens across disciplines rather than inside fixed categories. The Salon becomes a place where these different forms of attention can coexist. A visitor might encounter a film, then a performance, then a conversation, with each experience altering the context of the next.

Artist-run spaces provide another perspective on how cultural scenes are sustained. RendezVous includes CCINQ, Celador, Gilbard, Hectolitre, Komplot, Level Five, MINERVE, SB34, SPASSS, Superdeals, The Green Corridor, The Smoking Room – Chez Michel and URBAN SOCIETIES, among others. These initiatives operate differently from major galleries and museums, often creating room for collective practices, experimentation and emerging forms of discourse. Their inclusion is significant because it prevents Brussels’ cultural identity from being defined solely through its most visible institutions. A more complex picture emerges when commercial, institutional and artist-led structures are understood as different parts of the same ecology. Each contributes to the conditions in which the wider scene can function.

Visibility, however, brings its own complications. Any attempt to present a local art scene to an international audience risks turning complexity into branding, particularly when a city is reduced to a sequence of fashionable neighbourhoods, galleries and names. RendezVous was founded in 2024 by Laure Decock and Evelyn Simons with the aim of creating a shared framework for Brussels’ diverse cultural community, fostering connections while increasing international visibility. The more interesting question is whether visibility can be expanded without flattening the structures that make the scene distinctive. RendezVous’ dispersed format offers one possible answer: rather than creating an image of Brussels from above, it allows audiences to move through the places where its artistic relationships already exist.

Decock and Simons bring complementary experience to that task. Decock has worked with galleries including Almine Rech, Albert Baronian and Axel Vervoordt, alongside fundraising and institutional roles with WIELS, La Loge and Netwerk Aalst. Simons has worked independently as a curator for Fondazione Prada, Casino Luxembourg, KANAL and FOMU, as well as in artistic-direction roles at Horst Arts & Music and Fondation CAB; she is also co-artistic director of the Busan Biennale 2026. Their backgrounds span commercial galleries, foundations, public institutions, curating, strategy and partnerships. That mixture is reflected in RendezVous itself, which does not treat these sectors as separate worlds. Its structure instead acknowledges that contemporary art depends upon the movement of people, ideas and resources.

Public space completes the picture. Park Poétik will activate the neighbourhood surrounding the Salon through projects and events, while the Brussels City Guide for Art Lovers, produced by MER. Books / Borgerhoff & Lamberigts in collaboration with Glean, offers walking and cycling routes through selected cultural destinations and independent initiatives. These elements transform movement through Brussels from a practical necessity into part of the cultural experience. They also place the programme within a wider understanding of how art can operate in cities – through streets, temporary spaces, conversations and encounters as much as through formal exhibition venues. The city becomes both context and material.

RendezVous is compelling because it avoids presenting Brussels as a finished cultural proposition. Its programme reveals a city whose artistic life depends upon movement between commercial and independent spaces, institutions and collectives, exhibition and performance, established practices and emerging ones. The Salon provides a physical meeting point, but the more significant structure extends beyond it, through the relationships connecting the programme’s many parts. Brussels Art Week consequently becomes less a survey of what the city has to offer than an opportunity to examine how an art scene is made and maintained. Its real subject is the space between the venues – the exchange, friction and collaboration that allow a city’s artistic culture to remain in motion.

Brussels Art Week runs from 10 – 13 September: brussels.be

Words: Shirley Stevenson

item.title: Yayoi Kusama Dies at 97 - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Yayoi Kusama, one of the world's most popular artists, died at a Tokyo hospital on August 14 at the age of 97. Her studio shared the news last night. Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia remembers the idiosyncratic Japanese artist, who reached legend status during her lifetime.

If your art history leans Western, you likely know them as Indian “miniature paintings” — but let’s put a stop to that. A recent book on art from the Pahari region reviewed by Nageen Shaikh argues that the term is, well, minimizing. Besides, the name actually derives from the use of the red “minium” pigment, so, bit of a misnomer anyway — and as we know from running an art publication, words matter. 

History will come to life — and to Dallas — in the form of an exhibition of more than 160 treasures from Pompeii, drawn from the National Archaeological Museum of Naples. But important things are happening in this millennium, too: A former member of the feminist protest and performance art group Pussy Riot claims that she was recruited by Russia to spy on other artists, and painter and printmaker Elizabeth Peyton is being sued for copyright infringement. 

Plus, an artist introduces a device that slows a bike’s brakes in less-affordable neighborhoods, turning wealth inequality into physical sensation. That’s what art can do: Make ideas visceral.

—Lisa Yin Zhang, associate editor

Artist’s Device Slows Down Citi Bikes in Less Affordable Neighborhoods

While biking the perimeter of Prospect Park in Brooklyn, New York, on a sunny August afternoon, the pedal strokes are smooth. On the Citi Bike, I ease through all of Park Slope and most of Windsor Terrace, but as I bike through Prospect Lefferts Gardens, also known as Flatbush, tension builds. When I enter the park at Lincoln Avenue, where Flatbush begins, there is a massive shift in my ability to move. It is jarring, and I’m forced to dismount.

I’m riding around with a device attached to the e-bike that manipulates the brakes depending on the levels of rent affordability in the neighborhood you’re biking through. The device is an artwork called “Ground Truth,” Justin Blinder’s latest creation and part of an exhibition with the same name. | Eliana Perozo

item.title: A Major Display of Lee Miller’s Photography - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Lee Miller is a singular figure in 20th century art. Her work defies categorisation, and throughout her life she moved between muse and artist, model and innovator, effortlessly turning her hand to portraiture, avant-garde Surrealism and war reportage. Miller went where the action was, diving into the heart of the 20th century, from the horrors of WWII to the dynamic, thriving art scenes of New York and Paris. The result is a life entirely dedicated to creativity, in almost every form imaginable. Now, the Art Institute of Chicago presents Lee Miller: Fearless, gathering 150 works from across the major episodes of her career. Matthew Witkovsky, Curator at the Art Institute of Chicago, says: “Lee Miller was a complex figure, at once complex and conflicted, plainspoken in her words yet with a flair for mystery in her art. She excelled at collaboration but also forged paths entirely on her own. Her breakthroughs in fashion and Surrealism from around 1930; her frank, disturbing images from the camps at Buchenwald and Dachau in 1945; and her sensitive portraits of fellow artists throughout her multifaceted career, are all highlights of this exhibition.” 

Born in New York in 1907, Miller moved to Paris at 20 years old, simultaneously seeking work in front and behind the camera. It was here that she met Man Ray, a leading figure in Surrealism, quickly becoming his partner both in art and life. Their collaboration produced some of the era’s most innovative photographic experiments, notably the solarisation technique, which created striking halo-like reversals of light and dark. Miller herself pioneered Surrealist techniques and took on daring subjects with a readiness that inspired experimental artists and fashion editors alike. She excelled at portraiture and pictured a range of cultural figures in the 1930s – from Charlie Chaplin to Pablo Picasso – most of them personal friends. By the time she turned 30, Miller had run commercial studios on both sides of the Atlantic, becoming a haute couture icon and cult cinema idol, establishing herself as a major force in contemporary art. 

In 1939, WWII broke out, and Miller’s work took a radical departure from the avant-garde worlds in which she had previously operated. In London, she became a leading photographer for British Vogue, but her images of Blitz-torn London – works like David E. Scherman Dressed for War (1942) featured in Art Institute of Chicago’s exhibition – transcended fashion reportage. Her work contrasts the turmoil of the war with the indomitable human spirit that often shines through in times of struggle. Later, she travelled from France to Romania, spending a momentous two months in Germany just as the concentration camps were being liberated. Her photographs are some of the first of the atrocities, documenting the realities for millions just as the world began to realise the extent of the inhumanities. Two rooms of the show are given over to this chapter of Miller’s life, when she became one of the most important voices in wartime news.

Her time spent in Germany also expanded to the political realm. Away from the front, and her role as one of the only female reporters allowed to travel with Allied troops, she spent time in Hitler’s private apartments in Munich. In one infamous shot, taken by David E. Scherman, Miller washes in Hitler’s bathtub, taken coincidentally on the same day that the dictator died. The photographer also captured others in the field, turning the lens on her peers and fellow photojournalists. Lee Miller: Fearless includes a shot of Margaret Bourke-White, the first American female reporter to travel with the United States Army Air Force. In Miller’s image, Bourke-White is crouched underneath an aircraft, clutching her camera. It’s a shot that really captures the passion felt by the few women allowed access to such a male-dominated world, providing a vital lens on one of the defining moments of the entire century. 

To try and encompass the almost countless facets of Lee Miller both as a person and as a practitioner is no easy feat. With this new show, Art Institute of Chicago goes some way to proving it is possible. In 150 photographs, great swathes of Miller’s person – and our shared cultural – history are put on display. Audiences walk through a life dedicated to exploration, adventure and, crucially, a refusal to shy away from where our attention is most needed. In fashion, Surrealist photography and, most powerfully, the atrocities of WWII, the artist created an oeuvre that continues to resonate with global audiences today.

Lee Miller: Fearless is at Art Institute of Chicago from 29 August – 7 December: artic.edu

Words: Emma Jacob

item.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi Lines Up 84 Galleries for Inaugural Edition in November - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Frieze Abu Dhabi announced today the 84 exhibitors who will participate in its inaugural edition, scheduled to run November 19–22 at Manarat Al Saadiyat, in the city’s Saadiyat Cultural District.

The fair will bring together galleries from 63 cities in 36 countries, including 36 galleries (around 43 percent) with locations in the SWANA region. They include Carbon 12 (of Dubai), The Third Line (Dubai), Dastan (Tehran and Toronto), Gypsum (Cairo), Loft Art Gallery (Casablanca and Marrakech), and Sfeir-Semler Gallery (Beirut and Hamburg).

They will show alongside international blue-chip enterprises such as Gagosian, Pace Gallery, Thaddeaus Ropac, Victoria Miro, Galleria Continua, and Perrotin, which opened a space in Dubai in 2022.

In addition to the main Galleries section, Frieze Abu Dhabi will also include a Focus section for solo or dual presentations of emerging artists with experimental practices. The six galleries in this section will also receive bursaries to offset costs with participating in the fair, according to a release. The include Dala Nasser at Commonwealth and Council, Tahir Karmali at Management, and Jawad Al Malhi at Iyad Qanazea Gallery.

A new section for the fair, Global Futures, will be curated by independent curator and writer Tarini Malik and feature the work of artists “whose practices engage with histories and

ideas that resonate across the UAE and the wider region,” per a release. Among the highlighted artists are Abdullah Al Saadi (at Aisha Alabbar Gallery), Ala Younis (Taymour Grahne Projects), and Seta Manoukian (at Marfa’).

The Frieze Masters section in Abu Dhabi will organized by independent curator Marika Sardar and feature art and objects from antiquity to the 20th century, with a focus on the Indian Ocean as a theme, “encompassing the historic movement of objects, people and ideas through trade, collecting and cultural exchange,” per a release.

“Across the main section and Focus, galleries will present ambitious, thoughtfully considered booths, while the curated sections – Global Futures and Frieze Masters

Abu Dhabi – will introduce fresh perspectives and avenues for critical inquiry,” Frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh said in a statement. “Frieze Abu Dhabi will be a catalyst for knowledge production, art market integration and meaningful participation in global discourse for the whole region.”

Frieze Abu Dhabi, established with the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi, takes over from the Abu Dhabi Art fair, which operated in the city for 17 years. It is also the second fair this year to launch in the region, after Art Basel Qatar debuted this past February.

“The inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi begins with the depth and ambition of the UAE and wider WANASA art scene and reaffirms our commitment to fostering meaningful dialogues on the global art stage,” Kristell Chadé, executive director of fairs for Frieze, said in a statement. “Complementing Frieze’s expansive reach, the fair amplifies voices from the region in an international context, establishing a key moment of convening and exchange for galleries, artists, institutions and collectors from across the world.”
