item.title: Yayoi Kusama, Avant-Garde Artist Who Pursued Infinity, Has Died at 97 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Yayoi Kusama, whose obsessive repetitions of dots and nets became a means of expressing infinity, leaving an indelible mark on contemporary art worldwide, died on August 14 of multiple organ failure at a hospital in Tokyo. She was 97. Her death was reported on Thursday by Kyodo News and later confirmed by her David Zwirner Gallery, her longtime representation.

“It’s been one of the great privileges of my professional life to have been able to represent Yayoi Kusama’s extraordinary art for the last fifteen years,” wrote David Zwirner in a statement. He continued, “The last time Kusama visited New York, a city where she lived for many years, was in 2013. During that visit, she opened the first of many exhibitions in our galleries that had an hour-long lines for the chance to experience her work… At the time of her passing, Kusama was, without a doubt, the most famous living artist in the world. I will miss her terribly.”

Kusama developed a singular visual language that drew on the hallucinations she had experienced since childhood. She emerged as a significant figure in New York’s avant-garde scene in the late 1950s and continued working for more than seven decades, moving freely among painting, sculpture, installation, performance, literature, and fashion. Major surveys of her work have been staged at museums around the world, while her striking likeness eventually transcended into a global brand onto itself, making her the most instantly recognizable artist to emerge from postwar Japan.

From Hallucinations to Art: Matsumoto to America

Born in Matsumoto, Nagano Prefecture, Kusama was the youngest daughter of a family that ran a seed nursery. As a child, she routinely ventured into the fields of violets and other flowers around her home to sketch them. From an early age, she experienced visual hallucinations, which she once described as “flashes of light, auras, or dense fields of dots.” Animals, too, appeared to speak to her, she said. To cope with the intensity of these experiences, Kusama turned to drawing, a practice that would become the foundation of her artistic life. A portrait of her mother, made when Kusama was around 10 years old, for example, is set against a sea of dots. The motif would grow alongside both her compositions and her legend, first engulfing frames, then rooms, and finally entire galleries.

In 1948, at age 19, Kusama enrolled at the Kyoto Municipal School of Arts and Crafts, where she studied nihonga, or traditional Japanese-style painting. She held her first solo exhibition in Matsumoto in 1952 and continued to exhibit in Japan. But she increasingly chafed against what she saw as the constraints of postwar Japanese society, coming to believe that her art required a freer, more expansive environment.

One figure who encouraged her ambitions was Georgia O’Keeffe. Kusama tracked down the American artist’s address and sent her a letter, along with several of her watercolors, asking for advice. O’Keeffe replied. In 1957, at age 28, Kusama left Japan for the United States.

The Birth of the “Infinity Nets” in New York

After spending time in Seattle, Kusama moved to New York and began working in Manhattan. Money was scarce, but her output was prodigious.

It was during these years that she created the “Infinity Nets,” the first major series of her career. The paintings—vast canvases covered edge to edge with minute, repeated loops of paint—drew attention when they were shown at New York’s Brata Gallery in 1959. The exhibition was reviewed by publications including the New York Times and ARTnews.

The obsessive repetition of these marks would become closely associated with Kusama’s concept of “self-obliteration”—the dissolution of the boundaries between the self and the surrounding world, as she described it.

Writing in ARTnews, Donald Judd, then an emerging artist and critic, praised Kusama’s work and purchased one of her paintings. Other artists, including Frank Stella, also took notice. Working as a Japanese woman within the largely white, male New York avant-garde, Kusama gradually established herself as a distinctive presence in the city’s rapidly changing art scene.

Happenings, Narcissus Garden, and the Avant-Garde

In 1965, Kusama debuted Infinity Mirror Room—Phalli’s Field, a mirrored environment filled with soft, phallic forms covered in red polka dots. The mirrors multiplied the objects—and the viewer—seemingly without end. The Infinity Mirror Rooms would ultimately become among the most celebrated works of her career.

Against the backdrop of the antiwar movement and the counterculture of 1960s America, Kusama also staged a series of performances, or “happenings,” often involving nude participants whose bodies she covered in polka dots.

In 1966, during the 33rd Venice Biennale, Kusama staged Narcissus Garden without an official invitation, installing 1,500 reflective silver spheres on a lawn outside the exhibition grounds. Beneath a sign reading “YOUR NARCISSISM FOR SALE,” she attempted to sell the spheres for $2 apiece until Biennale officials intervened.

The gesture provocatively blurred the distinction between artwork and commodity while taking aim at the institutional and commercial structures of the art world. Kusama later reflected on her conception of the avant-garde in her 2013 memoir, Polka Dot Autobiography: “To look back at one’s place in society and create a new history—that, I believe, is what it means to be avant-garde.”

Her guerrilla-style interventions expanded to include nude demonstrations, “Love Happenings,” and polka-dot body painting. Against the backdrop of the Vietnam War and the broader counterculture, her work became increasingly intertwined with political and social concerns.

Kusama also ventured into musicals, filmmaking, and fashion, continually expanding the boundaries of her practice and establishing herself as one of the era’s most singular avant-garde figures.

Return to Japan and International Rediscovery

In 1973, after roughly 16 years in the United States, Kusama returned to Japan. There, however, the sensational aspects of her New York activities initially drew more attention than their art-historical significance, and the critical standing she enjoys today was far from immediate.

During this period, Kusama increasingly turned to writing in Japanese. Fiction and poetry offered another means of exploring the self, distinct from her visual practice. Beginning with her debut novel, Manhattan Suicide Addict, she went on to publish novels, short-story collections, and poetry while continuing to make art.

During the 1980s, Kusama exhibited regularly at venues including Fuji Television Gallery. The pumpkin, perhaps the most recognizable motifs in her oeuvre today, became increasingly prominent in her work during this period. A major catalyst for Kusama’s international reassessment came in 1989, when the Center for International Contemporary Arts in New York organized a retrospective of her work. The exhibition renewed attention to her New York years and the pioneering role she had played in postwar art.

Then, in 1993, came a decisive turning point. Kusama was selected to represent Japan at the 45th Venice Biennale, with art critic Akira Tatehata serving as commissioner of the Japanese Pavilion. Twenty-seven years after her unauthorized presentation of Narcissus Garden in Venice, she returned as Japan’s official representative.

Tatehata’s presentation foregrounded Kusama’s pioneering position in a New York art world transitioning from Abstract Expressionism to Minimalism and Pop, while also introducing her more recent work. The Japanese Pavilion became a crucial moment in cementing her reputation, both in Japan and internationally.

In 1998, “Love Forever: Yayoi Kusama, 1958–1968” opened at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art before traveling to the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis, and the Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo. The exhibition prompted a major reassessment of the radical work Kusama had produced during her New York years.

At 70, Kusama’s Career Takes Off Again

Rather than slowing down as she entered her 70s, Kusama continued to expand her practice throughout the 2000s.

Beginning in 2004, she produced the monochrome drawing series “Love Forever.” In 2009, she embarked on “My Eternal Soul,” an expansive series of large-scale acrylic paintings filled with blazing color and motifs resembling faces, eyes, and organic forms. By the time the series concluded in 2021, Kusama had produced roughly 900 works over 12 years.

Her output continued unabated. In 2021, she began a new painting series, “Every Day I Pray for Love,” returning to themes that had occupied her throughout her life: infinity, love, life, and death.

By then, Kusama was an undisputed market force. In a landmark feat for a woman artist, she became the top-selling contemporary artist of 2023, generating $80.9 million at auction and surpassing the previous year’s record-holder, David Hockney, by more than $30 million. Her highest-selling work that year was the 2014 painting A Flower, which sold at Christie’s Hong Kong for nearly $10 million. The year marked the peak of a career-best run for Kusama’s market. Her auction sales had surged nearly 160 percent in 2021, climbing to $183.5 million.

A Kusama blockbuster was a guaranteed draw at museums worldwide. Tate Modern in London mounted a major retrospective in 2012. In 2017, “Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors” opened at the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C., before traveling across North America. Her “Infinity Mirror Rooms,” which placed visitors inside Kusama’s endlessly reflected environments, generated extraordinary demand, with lines stretching around the block.

In 2022, M+ in Hong Kong staged “Yayoi Kusama: 1945 to Now,” a sweeping retrospective featuring roughly 200 works spanning nearly eight decades. Even into her 90s, Kusama remained the subject of major exhibitions around the world.

Her imagery also proliferated far beyond museum walls. In 2012, Kusama embarked on her first major collaboration with Louis Vuitton. The partnership was revived on an even larger scale in 2023, when monumental polka dots and animatronic figures modeled after Kusama transformed the fashion house’s stores in New York, Paris, Tokyo, and other cities, becoming a global social-media phenomenon.

In Japan, her yellow Pumpkin on the island of Naoshima became one of the country’s most recognizable works of public art. Large-scale works by Kusama are permanently installed at institutions and sites across the country, including the Matsumoto City Museum of Art in her hometown. In 2017, the Yayoi Kusama Museum opened in Tokyo’s Shinjuku district, establishing a permanent institution dedicated to preserving and presenting her work.

Kusama received the Praemium Imperiale in 2006, was named a Person of Cultural Merit by the Japanese government in 2009, and received the Order of Culture—one of Japan’s highest honors—in 2016.

“Even After My Death”

Kusama continued working into the final years of her life, driven by an unwavering determination to leave her mark on art history.

In Polka Dot Autobiography, Kusama wrote of what she hoped would happen to her art after she was gone: “I hope that the polka dots will continue to proliferate and carry my message to people everywhere. And even after my death, I would be happier than anything if the traces I have left could extend far and deep, continuing without end to reach generations to come. From today to tomorrow, and from tomorrow to the day after, I want to keep working, step by step, to move people through my art.”

item.title: LACMA Hit With Class Action Lawsuit Over Data Breach of Employee, Visitor Information - ARTnews.com
item.description:
A former employee of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art has filed a class action complaint against the institution over a 2025 data breach that he claims has compromised sensitive visitor and employee information, including Social Security numbers.

The complaint accuses LACMA of acting negligently by waiting nearly a year to inform its staff of the breach and seeks unspecified damages, as well as a court-ordered assurance of stronger security measures. 

The lawsuit, reviewed by ARTnews, was filed Tuesday in the Superior Court of the State of California by Adam Piron on behalf of “all persons” whose information was compromised by, what the complaint describes as, LACMA’s failure to protect the personal data with which it had been entrusted. It also asks that LACMA be compelled to maintain adequate security practices and act with swift transparency after any future data breach.

“By obtaining, collecting, using and deriving a benefit from the plaintiff’s and class members’ [personal information], LACMA assumed legal and equitable duties to those individuals to protect and safeguard that information from unauthorized access and intrusion,” the complaint reads.

LACMA is the largest art museum in the Western US, with a collection of some 155,000 objects, spanning six millennia of history, according to its website. Earlier this year, it opened its long-awaited David Geffen Galleries to showcase the permanent collection, which ARTnews described as having the “potential to rewrite art history.” It attracts over 1 million visitors annually, per the suit.

According to the complaint, LACMA experienced a data breach on or around July 11, 2025, during which cybercriminals accessed “personally identifiable information,” including addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license information, health insurance details, and financial account numbers.

LACMA publicized the data breach this past Monday in a statement posted to its website, which confirmed that suspicious activity was detected on their computer systems last July. “We immediately began working with third-party cybersecurity experts to investigate and remediate that activity,” the statement reads. “In August 2025, the investigation found that an unauthorized third party gained access to a portion of our computer network from July 7 to 11, 2025.” 

LACMA did not immediately reply to ARTnews’s request for further comment.

The museum’s statement lists the same personal information identified in the complaint as having been compromised, and added that categories of data varied across individuals. “We also notified law enforcement. We are providing notification to affected individuals under applicable law and posting notice to our website,” the statement adds.

Piron, 40, of San Bernardino County, worked as an assistant film curator at the museum from 2018 to 2020, according to his LinkedIn. He said he learned of the data breach prior to Monday’s statement, in June 2026. Still, nearly a year after the incident, he and others affected were left “unable to take the necessary precautions to prevent future fraud and mitigate damages,” the complaint states.

It adds that the plaintiff and museum goers “now face years of constant surveillance of their financial and personal records, monitoring, and loss of their rights.”

item.title: Lush Foliage Permeates Xanthe Burdett’s Delicate Portraiture - Colossal
item.description:
For Xanthe Burdett, the boundary between humans and nature is thin, malleable, and always in flux. The Devon-born, London-based artist works largely in a palette of greens, layering leaves and vines atop faint figurative silhouettes. Invoking mythology and ancient cosmologies, her paintings suggest that people and plants are not only interconnected but also intrinsically one.

Beginning with a sketch, Burdett employs the Renaissance-era cartoon method of transferring her drawings to canvas, which involves layering a substance like charcoal between the preparatory composition and the substrate and tracing the initial linework. After, the artist adds various greenery until she’s reached a lush density.

Burdett considers superimposition to be a way of “reimagining the body as a site of ecological and mythic transformation,” she says. “In an age defined by environmental catastrophe—wildfires, biodiversity loss, and climate anxiety—the work functions both as a refuge and as a space for imagining alternative ways of being with the more-than-human world.”

Presented as “host and terrain,” Burdett’s figures encompass a sense of growth and regeneration as “flesh gives way to nettles, brambles, and tender green shoots,” she adds. Many also invoke mythic deities, including Venus, the Roman god of beauty and fertility, and Janus, the god of transitions and beginnings.

This fall, the artist will be in residence at Soho Revue working on a collection exploring the Greek tale of Daphne, who morphed into a laurel tree, as a way to conceptualize transformation amid climate catastrophe.. Keep up with that new series on Instagram.

item.title: Artist Elizabeth Peyton Sued Over Painting of Oasis Brothers - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Welsh music photographer Justin Thomas is accusing painter Elizabeth Peyton, David Zwirner Gallery, and Sotheby's of copyright infringement on his 1995 photograph of British pop star brothers, Liam and Noel Gallagher of the British rock band Oasis.

In an August 20 lawsuit filed in the Southern District of New York, Thomas's attorney, Terry Parker, calls Peyton's painting, "Earl's Court (Liam + Noel)" (1996) a "slavish copy" of the 1995 photograph, according to court documents first covered by the legal blog Copyright Lately and reviewed by Hyperallergic.

Peyton's painting resembles a zoomed-in portion of Thomas's photograph, which captures the notoriously feuding siblings and Oasis musicians, in a rare moment of embrace. The iconic image bolted to fame during the British pop music wave throughout the United Kingdom, and a black-and-white print embellishes the cover of Thomas's 2024 photography book, How Does It Feel? - Oasis 1995/2002.

Under copyright law, a person accused of infringement must have significantly adapted the appearance of the copyrighted original to a "transformative" degree. The filing alleges that the similarities are far too many: "The only transformation is the medium itself, and Peyton’s slight cropping of the Copyrighted Work and adding different coloring and brush work." In her painting, Peyton adds details such as a blue flower-patterned sleeve.

item.title: Ex-Pussy Riot Member Says She Was Recruited by Russia to Spy on Artists - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Margarita Konovalova, who went by the alias Rita Flores as a member of the Russian punk feminist band and anti-Putin artist collective Pussy Riot, recently claimed that she was coerced into spying on other dissident artists for the last three years by the Russian national security service (FSB) after they threatened her and her family's lives.

Having fled Russia with the help of her lawyer earlier this month, Konovalova spoke freely about her experience for the first time in an exclusive interview with an independent news outlet for dissident Russian journalists called Port Media. She explained that after an FSB officer raided her apartment in February 2023, she was detained and threatened into cooperating.

“It was just like in a movie: they sat me down at the table, I couldn't move, I couldn't look away,” Konovalova recounted in her interview. “They started recruiting me: they threatened me in every way, mocked me, said unpleasant things, threatened to kill my family, and said I'd never be able to prove who killed my mother.”

The artist and activist said she was also threatened with criminal prosecution over social media posts criticizing the fatalities during the Battle of Bucha — part of the Russian offensive in Kyiv in 2022. She recounted signing a non-disclosure agreement and additional paperwork outlining her cooperation with the FSB, after which she was reportedly assigned to research and write profiles on contemporary artists for the security service. She also claimed that the FSB seized all of her documents, except her Russian internal passport.

item.title: Historic Sulfur Emissions Likely Damaged Murujuga Rock Art, New Study Finds - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Ancient rock art at Murujuga, or the Burrup Peninsula, in Western Australia, has seen much larger damaged than previously anticipated due to industrial pollutants found in air emissions.

About 932 miles north of Perth, Murujuga contains one of the world’s most significant and dense collections of ancient petroglyphs, dating back about 50,000 years. These tens of thousands of petroglyphs depict animals, spiritual figures, and sacred stories.

Since the 1950s, however, Murujuga has also become one of Western Australia’s largest industrial areas, home to a major fertilizer plant and gas facilities, with the world’s largest urea plant expected to begin operations next year.

The Rock Art Monitoring Report, compiled over the last three years by members of the peninsula’s five Aboriginal language groups and a team of more than 50 Curtin University scientists, found that carvings closest to industrial projects degraded faster than normal, and current activity is not thought to be accelerating this deterioration.

The damage includes changes in the rocks’ porosity, or tiny hole structures on their surfaces, believed to result from historical emission levels. According to the report, sulfur dioxide emissions from burning fuel had the greatest effect on the petroglyphs.

“Transport fuels, shipping fuels industry all have some level of sulfur in their fuel,” lead scientist Ben Mullins told ABC News. “There’s a lot of evidence that that was a lot higher in the 70s and 80s, and even since 2010, shipping fuels have massively reduced sulfur levels and sulfur dioxide emissions.”

The report’s release coincides with a recent decision by federal Environment Minister Murray Watt to extend the North West Shelf gas project through 2070, and with Murujuga’s inclusion on UNESCO’s World Heritage List.

“This latest report provides further confidence that the monitoring program is building the evidence needed to support the long-term protection of our rock art and cultural landscape,” Murujuga Aboriginal Corporation (MAC) director and cultural adviser Belinda Churnside told National Indigenous Times. “World Heritage recognition brings new responsibilities for all of us. MAC will continue working with government, industry, scientists, and our Elders to ensure Murujuga’s outstanding cultural values are protected and cared for long into the future.”

A memorandum of understanding currently exists between the MAC and the state government to fund long-term monitoring of the area beyond 2026, but negotiations have not yet been finalized.

“As Traditional Owners and Custodians, we know that protecting Murujuga requires both cultural knowledge and robust science. These findings are an important step forward in helping us better understand the landscape and ensure it is protected for future generations,” Churnside added.

item.title: Can We Stop Calling South Asian Painting "Miniature"? - Hyperallergic
item.description:
In the vibrant 1760 painting “Taking of the toll (Dana-Lila),” Radha, the Hindu goddess of devotion, arrests a rattled Krishna for stealing toll money from his maiden companions, the gopis. Scholars believe that the work is similar to two other paintings based on a drawing model from a workshop, but they are uncertain about the place of origin. Formal analysis reveals that “Dana-Lila” most likely came from the 18th-century kingdom of Chamba, which then was home to at least 16 established artist families. Chamba, along with Kangra, Nurpur, and others in India, is located where the Himalayas meet the plains of Punjab in the state now known as Himachal Pradesh, together comprising the Pahari region.

The substantial new catalog Pahari Paintings: Art and Stories (2026) is based on now-dispersed works amassed by scholar Catherine Glynn Benkaim, whose collection has been acquired by the Cleveland Museum of Art, the Cincinnati Art Museum, and the National Museum of Asian Art. This full-blooded hardcover catalog includes knockout reproductions, a crisp opening essay by curator Sonya Rhie Mace and art historian Sarang Sharma, and comprehensive analytical entries. Building on pioneering studies on Indian painting by B. N. Goswamy, the book zooms in on the prolific ancestral network of artists and workshop systems in the Pahari region.

Unlike the more widely recognized traditions of Rajput painting from the independent Hindu Rajasthani courts or Mughal (Indo-Persian) manuscript illumination, Pahari painting most often centralized the loving relationship between Radha and Krishna. Painters, such as court artist Sajnu, were highly mobile across the established kingdoms in the Western Himalayas. Art historian Debra Diamond writes that in the folio The goddess Sumukhi, from a Mahavidya (circa 1800), Sajnu and other workshop artists merged styles from Kangra and Mandi, resulting in gods with more pronounced features and jaunt expressions. In the rare cases when artists traveled out of state, we read about Purkhu, who left his family business in Kangra to work for Maharaja Ranjit Singh in present-day Lahore.

item.title: Wildlife Photographer of the Year Whittles More than 65,000 Entries to the Top 100 - Colossal
item.description:
More than 65,000 images by photographers in 121 countries presented a staggering challenge for the jurors of this year’s Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition. Of these entries, 100 were selected for the prestigious contest’s shortlist, showcasing the world’s diverse creatures and their habitats.

The top images also demonstrate an array of realities across a number of categories, from animal behavior to portraits to photojournalism. Viewers are treated to the beauty and tenderness of inter-species cooperation and also confronted with the poignancy of family and the sometimes troubling impacts of human intervention.

In Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen’s capture of orcas off the coast of Norway, we witness a grieving parent supporting the body of a calf as they swim. And Pietro Rojas’ documentation of a brown bear in a circus, muzzled and strapped to a bicycle cart for a performance, acknowledges the toll of human interference on wild animals. “Many countries have banned the use of wild animals in circuses,” says a statement. “Where brown bears are used, they often are trained to perform in unnatural postures like standing upright for long periods of time, contributing to health and behavioural problems.”

Most of the images snap animals in their native habitats, such as a polar bear peeking furtively through a hole in the ice, which Audun Rikardsen captures from a seal’s-eye view. Ernest Porter times an oxpecker’s beak-cleaning ritual on the snout of a rhinoceros so well that it lends an air of affection, as if the bird is giving the mammal a hug. And Jens Cullmann chronicles a humorously candid “fail” when an African bullfrog dramatically misses its meal.

Winners are slated to be announced on October 13. Explore hundreds of photos from past years in the online gallery, and visit this year’s exhibition, which runs from October 16 to July 11, 2027, at London’s Natural History Museum.

item.title: Artist's Device Slows Down Citi Bikes in Less Affordable Neighborhoods - Hyperallergic
item.description:
This story was copublished with Next City, a nonprofit news organization reporting on solutions for more sustainable, accessible, inclusive, and equitable cities.

While biking the perimeter of Prospect Park in Brooklyn, New York, on a sunny August afternoon, the pedal strokes are smooth. On the Citi Bike, I ease through all of Park Slope and most of Windsor Terrace, but as I bike through Prospect Lefferts Gardens, also known as Flatbush, tension builds. When I enter the park at Lincoln Avenue, where Flatbush begins, there is a massive shift in my ability to move. It is jarring, and I’m forced to dismount. 

I’m riding around with a device attached to the e-bike that manipulates the brakes depending on the levels of rent affordability in the neighborhood you’re biking through. The device is an artwork called “Ground Truth,” Justin Blinder’s latest creation and part of an exhibition with the same name.

Blinder is a researcher, biker, scientist, and, at his most vivid, an artist. The exhibition explores New York City’s affordability crisis and, through the device, makes the disparities felt on a physical level. While not publicly available, he created the device for both the Lyft manual and e-bikes and has biked over 35 miles across New York City himself with it installed. 

This work was made possible with money from Idle Hands, an art incubation program founded in 2025 by Linden Renz and Gabrielle Sirkin. Blinder was the Idle Hands Incubation award’s inaugural winner, cashing out $10,000 and loads of professional support to make Ground Truth a reality.

item.title: US State Department Takes Down “Woke” Kehinde Wiley Painting - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The Department of State removed Kehinde Wiley's 2015 commissioned painting from the United States embassy in the Dominican Republic this month, claiming that the artist's “violent and racist words and depictions” have no place in the foreign relations agency.

In a statement shared with Hyperallergic, a spokesperson said that the department has consulted legal representatives to “ascertain whether the art can be sold.”

Leah Campos, the Trump-appointed US Ambassador to the Dominican Republic as of 2025, posted a video of the painting's removal on Instagram on August 11. The post's caption read: “In the Trump Administration and under my leadership we are turning away from globalist and woke ideologies and instead embracing American patriotism and the beauty of our great country! 🇺🇸”

Wiley, known for painting Barack Obama's presidential portrait in 2018, was commissioned in 2013 by the State Department to create “Young Artists After Siamesas 1960” for its Santo Domingo embassy. The painting depicts four individuals — two standing together as if they're about to dance, and two seated on the floor at their feet — against a floral-patterned backdrop. Wiley studied the work of Dominican artists Celeste Woss y Gil and Gilberto Hernández Ortega in preparation for the work, which he completed with the help of local art students.

item.title: Chinese Artist Gao Zhen Gets 3-Year Prison Sentence for Mao Sculptures - Hyperallergic
item.description:
The 70-year-old Chinese dissident artist Gao Zhen has been sentenced to three years in prison for his sculptures of communist revolutionary and leader Mao Zedong. The verdict was issued in the Sanhe City People's Court in Hebei Province on Tuesday, August 25, as reported by the New York Times. 

The three-year sentence falls under an amendment passed by People’s Republic of China (PRC) leader Xi Jinping in 2021, which prohibits any perceived slander of China's deemed heroes and martyrs. Prosecutors pointed to sculptures created between 2005 and 2009, which include depictions of the communist leader repenting, or aiming fire at Jesus. Another is an enlarged bust of Mao with a cartoonish nose and enlarged breasts.

The New York-based artist works with his younger brother Gao Qiang under the moniker “Gao Brothers.” The two are known for producing satirical and critical sculptures of the PRC founder and former Chinese Communist Party Chairman, including in the Miss Mao series, which they made from 2006 to 2009. The duo was the subject of a major retrospective from 2010 to 2011 at the Kemper Museum of Art in Kansas City entitled Grandeur and Catharsis. 

Zhen was arrested during a family visit to Hubei province in August 2024, marking the beginning of a tedious legal ordeal that other Chinese artists, such as Ai Weiwei and Guo Gai, have faced in recent years. Chinese officials not only ignored international protests and artist petitions surrounding Zhen’s arrest, but have continued to block his wife and son from leaving the country.

item.title: Leslie Wayne’s ‘The Unintended Blues’ Contemplates Rising Seas and Vulnerable Shorelines - Colossal
item.description:
In Leslie Wayne’s exhibition The Unintended Blues, large-scale paintings may a first read as photographs. Melting icebergs in the Arctic Circle, the island of Manhattan, harbor construction projects, and coastlines around the U.S. that are vulnerable to rising sea levels take center stage. The closer one approaches, however, the more fluid the imagery becomes, as some shapes and shorelines appear nearly abstract.

These latest works follow Wayne’s series titled This Land Is Your Land, in which trompe-l’œil paintings of airplane windows depict aerial views of the American West based on photos the artist snapped while in flight. For The Unintended Blues, she expands this idea beyond the frame and turns her attention to watery landscapes around the world.

“Artists are in a unique position to bring awareness to issues of great urgency like this by reaching the hearts and minds of viewers, not just with information but with the poetic force of their creativity,” Wayne says in a statement. “For this exhibition, I hope to achieve that by transporting viewers with paintings that portray the splendor of what we stand to lose by our inaction.”

Displayed out in the open and supported by an armature of metal posts to present two canvases back-to-back, the paintings become not only sculptural but environmental. Viewers circumnavigate the works, traveling to different locations and climates while experiencing a kind of everywhere-all-at-onceness. We’re reminded how melting ice sheets and rising sea levels aren’t a localized phenomenon; it’s happening everywhere. The United Nations refers the planet’s rising waters as a global crisis for the billion people who rely on coastlines for their livelihood.

The Unintended Blues is presented as part of the Lower Manhattan Cultural Counsel’s 2026 River to River Festival and is on view through September 27 at the Arts Center at Governor’s Island. See more on Wayne’s Instagram.

item.title: Fabrizio Plessi, Pioneering Italian Video Artist and Experimenter, Dies at 86 - ARTnews.com
item.description:
Fabrizio Plessi, a pioneer of video art, died on August 23 in Venice at 86. His death was reported by La Repubblica.

Plessi was best known for engaging history and tradition with the digital, creating installations that took on an architecture of their own. A true experimenter, he also had a flair for eschewing one medium for another, moving between water, fire, stone, memory, and most recently glass.

As a teenager, Plessi moved to Venice, first to study at the city’s Art High School and then at its Academy of Fine Arts. He completed his degree in 1962 and was appointed professor in painting. During this period, in the early ’60s, he began to research water as a subject and conceptual medium spanning time, memory, and movement—a concept that would continue throughout his career.

In the ’70s, bodies of water would become central to his practice, featuring in performances, films, and videos. He created his first video works in 1973 as part of a collaboration with the Visual Activities Center at Palazzo dei Diamanti in Ferrara, Italy. In 1981, he presented Underwater at the Venice Film Festival; it subsequently showed at the Centre Pompidou in Paris. In the 1980s and ‘90s, he drew inspiration from light and stone after spending time in and continually returning to Mallorca, Spain.

Much like the transformative powers of water and light, Plessi also found the digital to be spiritual. “Everyone thinks of digital as connected to material technology, when it is the most immaterial element there is,” he once told Repubblica. “Painting and sculpture are material. LED lights, light, are immaterial. I draw continuously, every day for at least three hours. I draw light, I draw ideas and what we will then see thanks to the luminous pixels.”

He saw no difference between the stained glass windows in Gothic cathedrals (“nothing more than large pixels of light”) or televisions (whether “80-kilogram black-and-white boxes” from the earliest part of his career or the “elegant, minimalist forms” of today). “[N]othing has changed. Technology doesn’t exist. It only exists as we use it, as we humanize it,” he said. “In a video, we see something that has no substance and then evaporates. That’s why, for me, it’s the most spiritual thing there is.”

Born on April 3, 1940, in Reggio Emilia, Plessi had a long-standing relationship with the Venice Biennale, having both exhibited in the main exhibition and mounted presentations in multiple editions. At the 1986 Biennale, for example, he represented Italy, debuting his video installation Bronx (1986). Featuring 26 shovels placed in the center of 26 television monitors set inside a dark, narrow iron structure, that installation also included video footage of running water that reflected off the surfaces of the shovels, a metaphor for the changing industrial landscape of its namesake New York borough. The following year, he showed at Documenta 8 in Kassel, Germany, which led to further international acclaim.

“La Biennale di Venezia loses an artist who accompanied and, in many moments, anticipated the transformations of contemporary language,” the Venice Biennale said in a statement. “His work brought the ancestral force of the elements into dialogue with the immaterial dimension of technology, restoring to the electronic image a surprising physicality, and to matter a new possibility of movement, light and memory. Fabrizio Plessi’s long history with La Biennale di Venezia thus remains a significant part of the history of the institution and of artistic research: a history that spans more than fifty years without ever losing its visionary force.”

In 1999, Plessi was honored with two major international awards: the 13th Rome Quadriennale and the Kunstpreis der Nord/LB in Hanover, which named him Germany’s Artist of the Year. The following year, he once again represented Italy on the international stage, first at the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea and then at Expo 2000 in Hanover, Germany.

Additionally, Plessi’s works have been shown at major institutions such as the Centre Pompidou in Paris and the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, and in 2014, the Ludwig Múzeum in Budapest mounted a retrospective of his work, titled “Liquid Labyrinth.”

Even among the darkest times, Plessi never stopped creating. In 2020, at the height of the pandemic, for instance, the city of Venice honored his 80th birthday with a digital installation spelling out “Pax Tibi” (or “Peace be with you” in Latin) on the windows of the Correr Museum to which Plessi responded by creating a 32-foot-tall “Christmas tree” comprised of 80 LED monitors in the Piazza San Marco.

Most recently, Plessi took up a new medium: glass. Working alongside master glassblowers in nearby Murano, he created a series of objects that were exhibited last year, in the final show he realized during his lifetime, “Perdersi in un bicchier d’acqua” (Getting Lost in a Glass of Water) at Barovier&Toso Arte in Murano.

“His works always brought light: a physical light and, at the same time, an idea of energy, the future, and rebirth. Fabrizio knew how to look at Venice without nostalgia, creating a dialogue between its history and the contemporary, to the point of presenting our city as ‘the grammar of his artistic work,’” Venice Mayor Simone Venturini said in a statement. “We will work to ensure that his message continues to resonate in the works and initiatives of many other artists who will create art following his example.”

item.title: Barbara Hammer Through Her Own Lens - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Barbara Forever (2026) sets itself apart from most biographical documentaries early on by eliding the first three decades of its subject’s life. In voiceover, the late Barbara Hammer avers that her life did not truly begin until she started making films and came out as a lesbian in the early 1970s. Hungry to make up for lost time, she reinvented herself with admirable speed, separating from her husband, with whom she lived in the woods of Northern California, and integrating into Berkeley’s queer and experimental filmmaking scenes. 

The documentary proceeds through the groundbreaking feminist filmmaker’s life and work chronologically, studying how her artistic practice and political convictions evolved. Save for some new interviews with Hammer’s longtime partner, Florrie Burke, the film is constructed almost entirely from archival materials. Hammer was meticulous in her self-documentation, saving reams of personal photographs, notes, videos, and voice recordings. It is in this way that she narrates her own life, with help from director Brydie O’Connor’s editorial interventions.

Those interventions mean that while the film’s timeline is linear, Hammer’s thoughts are not. Many of her audio recordings were made in her final years as she endured endometrioid ovarian cancer and mortality spurred her to evaluate her life. It was also in this context that she created her performance piece The Art of Dying or (Palliative Art Making in the Age of Anxiety) in 2018, one year before her death.

item.title: Björn Persson’s New Book Highlights the World’s Incredible and Endangered Wildlife - Colossal
item.description:
From the Tanzanian grasslands around Mount Kilimanjaro to the ever-evolving icy realm of Antarctica and beyond, Swedish photographer Björn Persson captures the majesty of the natural world and its wild denizens. His bold, tonal style of portraiture taps into the drama of running giraffes and a stoic American bison in profile, but he also homes in on family-centric moments as a lioness plays with her cubs, for instance, or a coalition of cheetahs’ perch calmly atop a knoll.

Persson’s emotive photographs meander between intimate, tender vignettes to striking and powerful demonstrations of brute strength and presence. In many cases, the animals look directly at the viewer, as if we’re being stalked. Others look away, scanning the grasses for prey or for other members of their cohort.

Dozens of Persson’s photos fill the pages of The Earth We Share: Extraordinary Photography of Our Vanishing Species, forthcoming from Rizzoli. The volume also includes a preface by the late Dr. Jane Goodall, who completed the writing shortly before she died last year. Indeed, Persson’s goal is to encourage care, spurring conservation efforts and portraying wildlife through a lens of hope and possibility rather than discouragement.

With a reverent eye, Persson focuses specifically on endangered creatures, which face dwindling populations due to poaching, habitat loss, and the effects of the climate crisis. “He believes that by portraying animals as sentient beings, he can inspire people to acknowledge the intrinsic beauty and worth of these extraordinary creatures,” says a statement. The book is an extension of this vision, with the aim of inspiring not only awe but action.

The Earth We Share is slated for release on September 8. Pre-order your copy from Bookshop, and explore more on Persson’s Instagram.

item.title: Claudia Pagès Rabal Plays in the Ruins of Settler Colonial Time - ARTnews.com
item.description:
In Typo-Topo-Time Aljibe (2024), a video, shown on an undulating screen, follows Claudia Pagès Rabal as she descends into an 11th-century Moorish water cistern in Xàtiva, Spain—wetsuit on, 360-degree camera strapped to her body. She swims through murky water, plunging and surfacing as a techno score drops and swells with her. The walls around her are scribed with marks spanning centuries—penises, names, legal contracts—all cut into the same damp stone, none claiming priority over the others. This is what Pagès Rabal calls “settler time”: Markings and materials pile up as one civilization is superimposed onto the next.

The cistern sits on a site first built during the Roman Empire, then reconstructed under Islamic rule to supply water to a palace. That palace was later demolished to build a Christian convent before eventually getting absorbed into a boutique hotel. Each conversion tried to erase what came before, but instead created “a physical cartographic time in superposition,” as the artist put it when we spoke. The writings on the wall evince colonial histories settling like sediment.

Pagès Rabal doesn’t theorize settler time from a distance but wades into it. With her bodycam, the Barcelona-born artist circumnavigates the cistern. Her practice is rooted in performance, but, as she explains, “[I] started making videos because I wanted to choreograph not only bodies and language and music, but also cameras and points of view.” For instance, she shot the flooded chamber in a single continuous take. The camera scans the walls, evoking video-game navigation. In her solo show at SculptureCenter in New York in 2024, the video’s custom LED screen was shaped like a wave or an open book, its radiating light extending the feeling of immersion into the room itself.

In Aljubs i Grups (2024), first shown in Manifesta 15, five figures appear onscreen, navigating twin cisterns—one of them the same structure from Typo-Topo-Time Aljibe. Three dancers move through the spaces in what looks like a ritual, a trancelike dance. Pagès Rabal and another performer deliver a scripted dialogue she wrote as a rhythmic spoken-word exchange, set to music. The whole thing plays like a homemade music video: The group appears to be having fun as they dance and rap while exploring the chambers together.

Where work addressing colonial violence tends to lean grave, Pagès Rabal’s videos, as she puts it, look “very DIY and casual.” She explains that “even though the topics come from histories of violence, I try to think in ethics, not morality.” Where morality pronounces from above, ethics requires situating yourself inside the mess. So she straps her camera on and moves with the people beside her.

item.title: Remembering Sliman Mansour - Hyperallergic
item.description:
Sliman Mansour, a major figure in Palestinian art, died yesterday at age 79. Drawing from the bleeding wound of the Nakba and the fight for liberation, his work is a defiant response to those who wish Palestine was just a distant memory. Mansour painted the pride and dignity of his people. There is no anger in his canvases. No call for revenge. Just a people who deserve to live on their land. I know for a fact that he wished none of these paintings had to be made in the first place.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

How AIDS Activists Turned Graphic Design Into a Weapon

In the mid-1980s, as the AIDS crisis simmered hotter and hotter in the apartments and bathhouses of New York, a band of frightened, fed-up young men took to copy shops around town. They were watching friends, partners, and lovers waste away with a mysterious virus, blamefully dubbed the “Gay Plague” by some. These kids knew what they were doing when they took jobs at Kinko’s. Clandestinely running the printers after hours — a so-far-indifferent corporate America owed the public more than the cost of a couple print-outs, they reasoned — they produced graphically stark, zanily colored flyers, posters, and stickers. In other words, a PR toolkit. Then, they wheat-pasted New York with abandon, demanding action. | Amy Levine-Kennedy

item.title: Reimagining Environments for the Contemporary Moment - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
“I don’t think that architecture is only about shelter, is only about a very simple enclosure. It should be able to excite you, to calm you, to make you think.” These are the words of Zaha Hadid (1950-2016), one of the most influential architects of the 20th century. Her statement speaks to the ways that buildings can shape our experience, our day-to-day movements and, fundamentally, how we see the world. In fact, there’s neuroscience to back up this way of thinking, with the BBC reporting that “cities can affect our mood and well-being, and that specialised cells in the hippocampal region of our brains are attuned the geometry and arrangement of the spaces we inhabit.” Artist Yuange Sheng (b. 1999) follows this design philosophy, exploring the shifting relationship between structure, material and life. 

The artist begins with grids, modules and architectural fragments, transforming them through sculpture and image-making into unstable systems where structures collapse, deform and reorganise as ongoing processes of becoming. He draws on a combination of organic and artificial materials, with resulting pieces that echo the relationship between the natural world and human constructs. Works also engage with memory and accumulation, using fragmented materials to construct pieces that resemble fossils and remains, reminding audiences that the traces of what we build extend far beyond the current moment. 

Scaffolding is a sculptural work that reimagines the architectural unit as a fractured, body-like form, suspended between collapse and reconstruction. The piece is cast in both concrete and plaster, creating a delicate balance between the artificial and organic – an aesthetic that is characteristic of the designer. Sheng plays with the idea of a scaffold, taking it from a traditional support system to a “mechanism of intervention – piercing, binding and stitching the form together.” The mesh textile runs along the edge of a fissure, acting almost like broken skin or a medical gauze. It gives the impression that these architectural repairs are almost surgical, revealing the human hands that often shape seemingly natural environments. 

Meanwhile, Tetris Skyline reinterprets urban spaces by carving Tetris-like voids into building facades. The geometric openings reveal fragments of the sky – daylight, sunrise, nighttime – creating a contrast between dense structures and the expansive sky. The artist uses photography and digital compositing to suggest that “the sky we see is not entirely free, but shaped and defined by the built environment.” Residue Habitat continues to explore the urban environment, using lighting infrastructures to explore how organic life emerges within the remnants of existing systems. Here, lights nestle within nests of feathers, with a faint glow emerging from the narrow gaps. A particularly fun feature is his Stratified Tiramisu piece, which uses the layered dessert as a medium to translate personal memory into a form resembling geological stratification. Sheng explains: “as an edible object, the dessert can be cut, shared and consumed, transforming memory from something preserved into something gradually dissolved.” 

Sheng’s work is a refreshing perspective on architecture. The artist has a diverse portfolio – from feathers to tiramisu – but manages to maintain a singular vision, asking how the buildings we construct influence not only humanity, but the natural world around us too. More than this, the artist’s practice has a profound understanding of where buildings sit on both contemporary art and modern life, something that aligns him with the major names who came before. There’s a universality to his work, reminding us that what we make has effects that ripple out far beyond the obvious realms and into our everyday existence. 

Words: Emma Jacob

Image Credits:

All images courtesy of Yuange Shang.

item.title: In Conversation with Installation Artist Chiharu Shiota - Aesthetica Magazine
item.description:
Chiharu Shiota’s (b. 1972) work is some of the most recognisable in contemporary art. Red thread engulfs entire rooms, forming dense networks that obscure personal belongings, architectural structures and, at times, sleeping figures. The evocative installations, rendered primarily in red, black and white, are often rooted in the artist’s own personal experiences, including being diagnosed with cancer. This autumn, Shiota’s monumental works will occupy the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts in her largest solo exhibition to date. The show, titled The Soul Trembles, covers three decades of creative output, paying tribute to the artist’s poetic and sensitive practice. The exhibition includes celebrated works like Where Are We Going (2017/2026), an installation suspended from the ceiling, composed of boats that are filled with sheets of white thread, as well as In Silence (2002/2026), which sees a piano and chairs surrounded by a cloud of black yarn. We caught up with Shiota ahead of the show’s opening to discuss what it is like to look back at 30 years of artistic output and what continues to drive her creative practice. 

A: Could you take us right back to the start. When did you begin working as an artist? 

CS: I knew I wanted to be an artist when I was 12 years old. Even when I was younger, I already loved to draw and would do this much more than other children, and people would compliment my pictures. When I was drawing, I forgot time, and it felt like I could create my own personal world. I wanted to make paintings and I really dreamed of being an artist. I’ve never wanted to be anything else.

A: Why are you drawn to large-scale installation. What does it allow that other practices do not? 

CS: Even though I wanted to be painter, after the first year of art school, I had to stop painting. I could not find my identity in the medium. Everything I created looked like someone else’s work. It had no feeling to me. I searched for other materials and when I started working with thread, it felt like an extension of the line from the canvas into space. For me, it’s like a three-dimensional drawing. An installation can convey emotion immediately, and when the viewer enters the space they are immediately involved in the work. 

A: You often take something deeply personal – for example in Out of My Body, which was made in response to your second cancer diagnosis – and turn it into something universal. How do you determine which stories to share and which will strike a chord with audiences?

CS: My work always starts with a personal feeling and then extends into something universal. When I was creating art during my chemotherapy, it was about my own existence, but I believe people who have not encountered this can still relate to the feeling. The experience of illness or confronting death is not unique; anyone can go through it. Viewers have empathy and can imagine this feeling for themselves.

A: Tell us more about your use of thread. Where did this initial come from? 

CS: I started using thread when I was still in my studies and moving away from painting, making early works like Accumulation (1994) and for From DNA to DNA (1994). I was experimenting with different materials during that time but this specific way of creating a web began when I was living in Germany. I had moved nine times in three years at this point and I was sitting in my bed and began weaving around my body, creating my own space. In the beginning it was more like making a drawing, but later the focus of the webs has become connection. We are all linked by an invisible line and I want to make this visible. 

A: What is the act of constructing a piece like? Is it a meditative experience? 

CS: We have to construct the installation quite systematically, beginning by weaving from the ceiling and then wall, and then connecting both while working from top to bottom. Weaving the whole room is like meditation. I make the same movement over and over again and put all my feeling into it. 

A: After three decades of creating installations that are rebuilt and transformed from one place to another, what does permanence mean to you?

CS: For me, it’s all about memory. My installations simply can’t exist forever, the material is always going to be impermanent, but the visitor can keep their experience of the installation in their minds forever. Memory shapes our existence and without it I could not explain myself, or connect with audiences. 

A: This is the largest solo exhibition of your work to date and covers three decades of creative output. What is it like to have so much of your artistic life laid out in one exhibition? 

CS: When I walk through the show, I can see how my work presents turning points in my life. It is interesting to see how my practice has changed over the years, where I was emotionally in the beginning and where I am now. Alongside this solo exhibition, I have continued to create new work.

A: The exhibition moves from your early work through to more recent installations, creating a kind of journey through your artistic life. How did you decide on the sequence in The Soul Trembles?

CS: Mami Kataoka invited me to show a solo exhibition at the Mori Art Museum, and we went through all my work and as the curator, she decided what to display. She created this journey through my work itself. At the time I was also going through chemotherapy and was thinking a lot about death and what my daughter was thinking about the soul. This was inspiration for the title. 

A: Looking back, what has changed about your practice over the past three decades? Do you see moments of departure, or is there a sense of continuation? 

CS: I have had cancer twice, and you can see these experiences in my work. After my studies, I had stopped drawing and painting for 10 years, but when I got cancer the first time, I began drawing again. I understood that it’s not about technique but feeling and I was drawing every day like it was my journal. The second time I was diagnosed with cancer, I thought a lot about soul. And it was the first time I wanted to include my body again in my work, but this time mainly from other materials like bronze. A substance that would exist forever in comparison to my body. My work is always connected to my life. 

A: The pieces invite audiences to step inside and interact with the works. What do you hope they take away from that experience? 

CS: Every single person thinks differently, and there is no one true answer in contemporary art. I want the visitors to Montreal Museum of Fine Art to feel free to think or feel whatever they will. 

Chiharu Shiota: The Soul Trembles is at Montreal Museum of Fine Art from 26 September – 14 February: mbam.qc.ca

Words: Emma Jacob & Chiharu Shiota

item.title: At Joy Machine, Emmy Star Brown and Danym Kwon Revel in Memory and Childlike Wonder - Colossal
item.description:
Joy Machine is thrilled to present The Peace of Wild Things, a duo exhibition by Chicago-based American artist Emmy Star Brown and San Jose-based Korean artist Danym Kwon. This is Brown’s second exhibition at Joy Machine and Kwon’s third.

Drawing its title from Wendell Berry’s often-quoted poem, The Peace of Wild Things is a return to wonder through disparate yet complementary practices. For both Brown and Kwon, color and layering become a means of self-discovery and a way to tap into the emotions, dreams, and memories that might not surface otherwise. Their practices diverge in notable ways—Brown works abstractly, while Kwon turns to surreal representations of care and domestic life—but when presented together, they enter into a harmonic dialogue about the ways experiences linger long after a moment has passed.

Whether working on a monumental mural or intimate painting on canvas, Brown revels in riotous geometries of color. Amorphous forms and clean lines commingle in compositions that conjure the emotional power of magenta, peach, cobalt, or goldenrod. Describing her studio practice as the space in which her inner child emerges, the artist harnesses the playful energy we typically associate with adolescent imagination. In both her canvases and irregularly shaped found-cardboard pieces, each line resists being bound by the edge of the frame, instead appearing to continue onward on its own course.

Inversely, Kwon nests tiny scenes of family life into stacks of folded clothes and bulbous vessels evocative of Korean Moon Jars. Holding the mundane with affection, the artist preserves small acts of care by placing them securely inside these larger forms. Rendering elements at different scales echoes the ways experiences fade and reappear over time, while the soft, pastel color palettes suggest a tenderness toward quiet intimacies.

Kwon also draws on her Korean heritage and training in Asian painting traditions, the latter of which informs her understanding of negative space. In the diptych “What We Hold Dear,” she pairs a trio of vignettes depicting outdoor adventures with hands cradling the small findings from such endeavors. The pieces are presented in a folding frame with soft, rounded edges inspired by Korean design.

For both Brown and Kwon, painting offers the necessary space to process the past and imagine the future. Perhaps more importantly, though, the practice demands one’s presence and creates the conditions that spark wonder and joy.

The Peace of Wild Things is on view from August 28 to October 17, 2026. RSVP to the opening reception from 6 to 8 p.m. on August 28. Brown will be present.
